name: DHH
domain: software design and engineering opinions: simplicity, programmer happiness, conventions, the majestic monolith, testing and TDD, dynamic versus static typing, code review, cloud exit, small teams, and AI coding

sources.title: DHH on agentic engineering: Omarchy Quattro, 100% agent-written code, and why Linux wins
sources.originalTitle: DHH: Future of Programming, AI, Agentic Engineering, Vibe Coding & Linux | Lex Fridman Podcast #501
sources.summary: DHH explains his shift from hand-chiseled Ruby to running parallel agents, shipping Omarchy Quattro without hand-writing its code. He covers vague prompts over specs, the shrinking payoff of beautiful code, AI pull requests in open source, Linux as the agentic OS, and fast installs as pursuit of excellence.

principles.text: Agent-era work is bottlenecked on ideas, vision and taste, not implementation; human layers slow agents down.
principles.quote: Most organizations don't know what they want. They don't know how to make it better. They're not bottlenecked on implementation. They're bottlenecked on ideas. They're bottlenecked on vision. They're bottlenecked on taste.

principles.text: Don't over-specify to agents; be vague, then use the result to discover what you want (agile applied to agents).
principles.quote: The way you arrive at good software is you write a little bit of software and then you try to use it. It is in the process of using software that you discover what you really want.

principles.text: The economic payoff of sweating beautiful code is diminishing as agents do the modifying.
principles.quote: What I'm coming to realize is that the economic payoff of that sweat is diminishing rapidly.

principles.text: The programmer's remaining job is editor-like judgment: proportions, shape, and telling agents to make it simpler.
principles.quote: I can tell you when the shape isn't proportional to the problem or when it just feels like it's too complicated. And shockingly often, it just works.

principles.text: Agent-written pull requests are a gift to open source maintainers; declining them hurts no human's feelings.
principles.quote: I would rather get an agent written pull request to one of my projects than I'd get one written by a human.

principles.text: Have a differently sourced second model review the first one's work, just as you'd want a human peer review.
principles.quote: I would actually rather have two differently sourced sort of I mean they're not mid-tier, they're all frontier, but have let's say Opus 5 and Codeex and have one check the other's job.

sources.title: DHH on Lex Fridman: Ruby, Rails, small teams, dynamic typing, cloud exit and AI coding
sources.originalTitle: DHH: Future of Programming, AI, Ruby on Rails, Productivity & Parenting | Lex Fridman Podcast #474
sources.summary: A long conversation where DHH explains why Ruby's focus on programmer happiness shaped Rails, and why he defends dynamic typing, the majestic monolith and tiny teams without managers. He also covers leaving the cloud, writing code by hand versus vibe coding with AI, and open source as a gift exchange.

principles.text: Optimize for programmer happiness, even at some cost to performance or strictness.
principles.quote: his number one goal was programmer happiness. That his number one goal was the affordances that would allow programmers to articulate code in ways that not just execute it correctly, but were a joy to write and were a joy to read.

principles.text: Dynamic typing is the essence of Ruby; static typing adds repetition and ugliness he doesn't want.
principles.quote: I hate repetition. We've just talked about how much I love that Ruby boils all of these expressions down to its essence.

principles.text: Convention over configuration: pick sensible defaults so people focus on decisions that matter.
principles.quote: No one cares about whether it's post_id or post ID or PID.

principles.text: Prefer the integrated monolith; microservices are premature decomposition for small teams.
principles.quote: The first rule of distributed programming. Do not distribute your programming.

principles.text: Small teams beat large ones; default team of two, no managers, long uninterrupted focus.
principles.quote: our default team size is two. One programmer, one designer, one feature.

principles.text: Cloud is not cheaper or easier; owning hardware saved millions with no extra staff.
principles.quote: we're now saving literally millions of dollars, projected about 10 million over five years.

sources.title: Rails World 2026 Keynote: DHH on the end of handwritten code and the agent era
sources.originalTitle: Rails World 2026 Opening Keynote - DHH
sources.summary: DHH argues Opus 4.5 on Nov 24, 2025 was the Kodak Brownie moment for programming, and that 37signals has gone "pencils down" on handwritten code. He covers native apps with Rust backends driven by agents, rethinking abstractions, CLIs over embedded chatbots, and choosing optimism.

principles.text: Handwritten code is now the exception; treat it like a bug to fix in the factory.
principles.quote: Writing code by hand at 37 signals is now an exceptional state. It is like seeing a bug in sentry.

principles.text: Agents make small teams able to ship native apps, so web apps chosen for team size lose their reason to exist.
principles.quote: They're going to be native applications because the price of developing those things has gone to damn near zero.

principles.text: Let agents write verbose Rust you never read; judge it as a black box by outcomes.
principles.quote: Rust is amazing if you never ever ever have to look at it yourself.

principles.text: Rails conventions pay off in the agent age: token efficiency and one-developer frameworks.
principles.quote: Everything that we've worked on for the past 25 years, convention over configuration leads directly to things like token efficiency.

principles.text: Abstractions and DRY must be re-evaluated, since repetition is nearly free and many agents mutate code at once.
principles.quote: The reason we did abstractions was in part not to repeat ourselves. Well, now the price of repetition has gone to near zero.

principles.text: Skip embedded chatbots; expose a CLI so users bring their own agent.
principles.quote: Save your tokens, bro. Let me bring my own butler to the party. Let me interact with your applications through a CLI.

sources.title: Rails World 2025 keynote: DHH on simplicity, local-first dev and owning the stack
sources.originalTitle: Rails World 2025 Opening Keynote - David Heinemeier Hansson
sources.summary: DHH rants that web development has regressed (deploys slower than 1999 FTP, brittle stacks) because we embrace complexity instead of proudly being CRUD monkeys. He argues for maximalist, end-to-end frameworks, then shows what 37signals pruned (system tests, cloud CI, Puma-dev, Docker-for-everything) and demos Omarchy, local CI and cloud exit.

principles.text: Merchants of complexity only win because developers buy; embrace being a CRUD monkey and keep things simple.
principles.quote: The only reason they can sell that and grow so big is because you don't buy it. It takes someone to purchase from a merchant of complexity for the merchant of complexity to make any money at all.

principles.text: Solve the whole problem end to end with a maximalist framework, not tiny isolated slices.
principles.quote: This isn't about minimalism. In fact, in many ways, it's about maximalism. It's about solving all the little annoying problems that we all share when we're working making web applications.

principles.text: System tests are brittle, slow and not worth it; keep only a handful of smoke tests.
principles.quote: System tests in theory are wonderful. You get to test everything end to end and flow through the browser and you test your HTML and you test your back end and the [ __ ] doesn't work. It never worked.

principles.text: Run the test suite locally on fast modern hardware instead of paying for slow cloud runners; pin versions to avoid works-on-my-machine.
principles.quote: The vast majority of you should be able to replicate these numbers and run your entire test suite locally.

principles.text: Trust developers: a human sign-off that tests passed is an effective merge gate.
principles.quote: Trust works. In most organizations, your employees are not [ __ ] They're actually programmers who want to ship working software and they know that if they lie on the attestation here, they will get fired.

principles.text: Own and be free to change your whole stack; sharp tools, freedom and ownership over vendor dependence.
principles.quote: I pride the fact that we use sharp tools in the Rails community and we are not afraid of our citizens propriet. We have full ownership of what we work on.

sources.title: Rails World 2024 keynote: Rails 8, no build, and leaving the cloud
sources.originalTitle: Rails World 2024 Opening Keynote - David Heinemeier Hansson
sources.summary: DHH launches Rails 8 as the bridge from Hello World to IPO: no build, no PaaS, and a one-person framework. He argues for invalidating stale patterns, deploying your own servers on cheap hardware, and collapsing queues, cache and cable into one SQLite/database stack.

principles.text: Ship working software as the monument that ends the argument that your approach can't work.
principles.quote: the best way to refute that is not to get into an argument it is to ship working software and once you've shipped that working software you have a monument to the argument that is simply immovable

principles.text: Rails extracts proven solutions from real production apps rather than building speculative frameworks.
principles.quote: we are not in the business of making speculative Frameworks in the rails community we are in the business of taking solutions that we have proven to work in real applications with real customers under real production pressures

principles.text: Complexity is a necessary step toward progress, but you're only done once it's made simple.
principles.quote: we're not done by the time we've solved it we're done by the time we've made it simple

principles.text: Optimize for limited human brain capacity so one full-stack developer can hold the whole problem in their head.
principles.quote: the purpose is to optimize for our limited monkey brains they simply can't fit that much

principles.text: Optimize for getting to the billions, not for the hypothetical scaling pain after you have them.
principles.quote: the problem to optimize for is how do we get to the billions that's the path

principles.text: Rails should let you deploy to your own hardware without paying a PaaS; cloud fear is marketing-induced learned helplessness.
principles.quote: rails will be a framework not just now but going forward that does not require you to pay a commercial vendor to go to production in a way that feels reasonable and approachable

sources.title: Rails World 2023 keynote: DHH on no-build, Solid Cache/Queue, Kamal and the one-person framework
sources.originalTitle: Rails World 2023 Opening Keynote - David Heinemeier Hansson
sources.summary: DHH opens Rails World on the 20th anniversary, arguing the zero-interest era bred a productivity dark age of over-specialisation and complexity. He tours seven tools (Propshaft, Turbo 8, Strada, Solid Cache, Solid Queue, Mission Control, Kamal) that push toward simplicity and a one-person framework, with no-build JavaScript/CSS and cloud exit as through-lines.

principles.text: Progress need not mean complexity; complexity is a bridge you cross to reach simplicity.
principles.quote: progress is not synonymous with complexity complexity is a bridge we use to get to Simplicity

principles.text: Cheap money bred indifference to productivity and over-specialisation; pressure restores full-stack capability.
principles.quote: we should be working on designing and installing and maintaining and knowing how to do all of these things ourselves and being capable of doing all these things ourselves

principles.text: No build beats the fastest build: ship plain JavaScript via import maps and plain CSS straight to the browser.
principles.quote: no built is way better than fast built you can make the build as fast as possible but it's never going to be as fast as no build

principles.text: Choose progress over stability, replacing bloated legacy with a clean-sheet, far smaller implementation.
principles.quote: you have an order of magnitude less code to deal with you'll have an order of magnitude or maybe even two orders of magnitude less issues to content with

principles.text: Rails should stay free, open source and independent of commercial vendors end to end; vendors may add alternatives, never be required.
principles.quote: Ruby un rails from end to end should be free open- source software that is not owned by any commercial entity

principles.text: Rails should be a one-person framework, enabling Renaissance developers who handle design, implementation and deployment.
principles.quote: rail should be a oneperson framework that one individual should be able to make everything happen from start to end

sources.title: DHH on going agent-first: how 37signals and Omarchy build software with AI now
sources.originalTitle: DHH’s new way of writing code
sources.summary: DHH explains why his opinions on AI didn't change but the tools did: agent harnesses plus Opus 4.5 crossed his quality bar. He covers his tmux/Neovim agent workflow, senior-vs-junior leverage, small teams, designers as product people, beauty in code, and avoiding burnout.

principles.text: Beautiful code is likely correct; craft and aesthetics matter in the interior as much as the exterior.
principles.quote: I think aesthetics is truth. When something is beautiful, it's likely to be correct.

principles.text: Agent code must meet the same style bar as human code; he won't merge sloppy agent output.
principles.quote: when I'm using agents to work on Ruby code I want their code to look as good as mine I'm not going to merge their stuff if it's sloppy

principles.text: Autocomplete AI was annoying; agent harnesses with tools plus a strong model were the real unlock.
principles.quote: I thought the way of using the models with autocomplete versus agent harnesses was just dreadful, annoying.

principles.text: Running agents feels like a mech suit, not project management; it makes programming more enjoyable.
principles.quote: running a bunch of agents feels less like being a project manager for agents and more like stepping into this super mech suit

principles.text: Senior developers benefit most from agents because they can judge whether output is fit to ship.
principles.quote: the most successful and applicable agent acceleration that I've seen at 37 signal has been from the most senior people

principles.text: Start products with a tiny team until the shape is found; piling people onto uncertain direction slows you down.
principles.quote: I've found that you actually go slower if you pour a bunch of people into a direction that is uncertain.

sources.title: DHH on AI and coding: why he still hand-writes his Ruby (for now)
sources.originalTitle: DHH: Why AI Isn't Writing My Code (Yet)
sources.summary: DHH explains why AI isn't writing his code yet: he still cares about how code looks, uses AI mostly to learn faster, and sees no proof yet that AI lets companies cut half their programmers. He also covers cloud exit savings, small-team leverage, and open-sourcing Fizzy as marketing.

principles.text: Balance AI hype against reality: AI isn't writing his production code from scratch yet.
principles.quote: on my reality train, AI is not writing busy. is not writing anything from scratch.

principles.text: Use AI to learn faster and get smarter, not just to offload code writing.
principles.quote: It's not just about making the AI do things for me. It's about using the AI to make me smarter.

principles.text: Code craft still matters; hand-writing code stays competitive and enjoyable, like a saddle maker's work.
principles.quote: I still care about how code looks. I still care about the beauty of it. I care about finessing it.

principles.text: Outsourcing everything to AI erodes your competence; keep your skills trending up.
principles.quote: I can feel the competence dripping out of my fingers.

principles.text: Skeptical AI lets you fire half the programmers; he applied the same test to the cloud.
principles.quote: the fundamental test of can we do more with fewer people for less money never penned out

principles.text: Developer productivity and small teams were always the Rails premise; AI plus Rails is best.
principles.quote: The framework for the single developer was what Rails always tried to be

sources.title: DHH on Basecamp 5, agents, and Rails' stable foundation
sources.originalTitle: DHH: Basecamp 5, Vibe Coding, and the Future of Rails
sources.summary: DHH explains why Rails' stable back end let Basecamp 5 evolve on a 2013 chassis, and how AI agents change his workflow. Agents produce code fast but bolt on rather than refactor, so architecture, taste and human review still matter. He sees agents opening Rails to non-programmers.

principles.text: Rails' stable back end lets investment in its DSLs pay off for two decades.
principles.quote: Active record, that was an investment you could amortize over literally two decades.

principles.text: Brownfield and greenfield Rails apps look alike; only the front end dates an app.
principles.quote: I can open today models in the basecam codebase that would look absolutely right at home in Fizzy even though fizzy was just written five minutes ago.

principles.text: Don't bake fast-moving agent conventions into the framework yet; stale agent files can hurt.
principles.quote: any agents MD file that was written three model jumps ago is not only going to be outdated, but it's literally going to be harmful to your agent's ability to do work

principles.text: Agents bolt on code instead of reshaping architecture, so care for design must stay human.
principles.quote: agents can make very hard changes and it's perfectly happy writing 1,200 lines of code on something when a architectural twist could have reduced that to 20 lines of code.

principles.text: Cheap implementation lets you discard and compare many versions to find the shape you like.
principles.quote: I don't feel bad at all about flushing a thousand lines of code down the toilet because I know these agents will happily charge me for the tokens to build another implementation

principles.text: Learning AI tooling is a professional obligation, and Rails should welcome non-programmers building with agents.
principles.quote: I do actually think it is a professional obligation of every programmer to take this revolution seriously, to dedicate time to coming up to speed on it

sources.title: DHH with Matz and Jeremy Daer: Ruby, agents, and why programmers become software makers
sources.originalTitle: Ruby, Rails, and the future of programming - Matz, DHH & Jeremy Daer
sources.summary: A panel with Matz and DHH on how agents are changing programming. DHH argues acceptance comes first, that human value is taste and joy rather than hand-typing code, and that the "slop" critique is cope. He says to trust agents the way you'd trust a senior hire, and that agents will speak Ruby to you if you ask.

principles.text: Move through denial and bargaining to acceptance: agent-driven programming is coming for everyone and you can't opt out.
principles.quote: None of us has the power even if we wanted to.

principles.text: Human value in the agent era is taste, proportion and beauty; being a software maker is more satisfying than being a software writer.
principles.quote: What is the human value we add when we're working with agents? It is taste. It's a sense of proportion. It's a sense of beauty.

principles.text: Agents free us from ego about lines of code, so we attach only to better ideas.
principles.quote: you're not attached to the lines of code anymore. That's a blessing.

principles.text: The "slop" critique of agent code is cope; agent-written code is already high quality and improving fast.
principles.quote: The idea that agents cannot write original high quality code free of bugs is just at this point delusional.

principles.text: Trust agents like human hires: extend autonomy as competence is demonstrated, and accept that they, like us, will occasionally err.
principles.quote: And their competence is measured in your trust that the last pull request was handled correctly, just like you would any human.

principles.text: Agents are fluent in any language, so have them speak Ruby to you, the best language for humans to read.
principles.quote: If you want them to speak to you in Ruby, they will speak to you in Ruby.

sources.title: DHH on Ruby, programmer happiness, open source as gift exchange, and no-build
sources.originalTitle: DHH Is Right About Everything
sources.summary: DHH explains why Ruby's aesthetics and metaprogramming made programming itself the reward, why competence and understanding beat copy-paste or AI crutches, and why open source is a meritocratic gift exchange. He defends plurality of languages, refuses static typing in Ruby, and defends no-build JavaScript.

principles.text: Pick the language that makes you want to program; the act of programming should be its own reward.
principles.quote: ruby made me want to go out and do programming or go in and do programming as it is and I think that part of it was a huge push for my career

principles.text: Make the learning ramp soft at the start, but let it keep climbing toward real competence indefinitely.
principles.quote: the ramp needs to be soft but it needs to go to Infinity

principles.text: Open source is a meritocracy, not a democracy: those doing the work set the direction, and maintainers owe users nothing.
principles.quote: you want the most capable competent people who are doing the goddamn work to set set the direction

principles.text: Embrace a plurality of languages and frameworks; don't converge, and don't bolt static typing onto a dynamic language.
principles.quote: static typing is the one thing I will literally die on the hill for for Ruby we're not [ __ ] putting static typing into Ruby

principles.text: No-build JavaScript works in production, and many small cached files beat one bundle that churns on every change.
principles.quote: when you have one bundle the entire bundle turns over every single time you change a goddamn semicolon anywhere right that's not great for caching Dynamics

principles.text: Use AI as a better Google or pair programmer, but keep writing the code yourself; training wheels left on forever prevent real understanding.
principles.quote: the training wheels are great when you're first learning to balance but if you keep an on forever you're never gonna [ __ ] find balance

sources.title: Is TDD dead? DHH on mocks, test-induced damage and self-testing code
sources.originalTitle: Is TDD dead?
sources.summary: DHH, Kent Beck and Martin Fowler discuss TDD after DHH's RailsConf critique. DHH separates self-testing code from TDD, objects to mock-heavy isolation that distorts architecture, and says red-green-refactor is a personal preference, not a mandate.

principles.text: Unit tests forbidden from touching collaborators, DB or filesystem gave DHH nothing useful.
principles.quote: I wasn't getting anything useful out of unit tests that weren't talking to any collaborators

principles.text: Driving design through mocks and isolation causes test-induced damage to architecture.
principles.quote: this is test induced damage that the architect is actually suffering damage from this drive towards unit testing all the things

principles.text: Programmer happiness matters; red-green-refactor is a personal preference, not a mandate.
principles.quote: that whole feeling of feeling great about your development style feeling programmer happiness as as Matt would always put it um just wasn't I wasn't getting that from tdd

principles.text: Confidence comes from self-testing code; TDD is only one path to it, so don't conflate them.
principles.quote: tdd is One path of getting to that place I'm seeing though a lot of people are mistaking those two things

principles.text: A more unit-testable system is not automatically a better-designed system.
principles.quote: a easier to unit test system was a better design system and that's the main sort of the heart of the fallacy that I want to take a real big swing at

principles.text: Don't discard productive patterns like Active Record just to satisfy fast, isolated unit tests.
principles.quote: we were discarding all sorts of really useful techniques really useful patterns like active record because it didn't fit this notion of unit tests that had to run in 300 milliseconds

sources.title: Is TDD dead? Part II: DHH on test-induced design damage, mocking and indirection
sources.originalTitle: Is TDD dead? [Part II]
sources.summary: DHH debates Kent Beck and Martin Fowler over whether TDD pushes designs toward needless indirection. He argues that isolating every layer for fast unit tests (hexagonal, command and repository patterns) hurts clarity and cohesion, rejects internal mocking, and gives up on TDD as a universal path to good design.

principles.text: Don't mock your own collaborators; mock only true externals like payment gateways.
principles.quote: I don't want to do even one degree of mocking internally in my application I'm fine with mocking externals if you're talking to a payment Gateway of course that payment Gateway should be marked out

principles.text: Test-induced design damage is indirection and layers added only to make unit tests easier.
principles.quote: additional layers of complexity that we inject into the application for the purpose of testing it easier

principles.text: More code for the same outcome is bad unless it reflects real domain complexity; each layer costs understanding and change.
principles.quote: my position is that uh more code to do same things bad unless it's part of the sort of inherent complexity of the domain

principles.text: Trade high coupling for high cohesion: hardcode dependencies in controllers and accept they're hard to unit test in isolation.
principles.quote: I'm willing to suffer suffer High coupling because I also get high cohesion out of it

principles.text: Making code more testable doesn't always make it better; sometimes there is no win-win design.
principles.quote: I think sometimes the answer is there's not an answer you're not going to produce better code by making it more testable

principles.text: Believing TDD will eventually lead to the right design is faith-based; he abandoned it as a universal principle.
principles.quote: faith-based tdd this belief that tdd will eventually even though we cannot see it and we have no evidence for it today will leave you to the right design

sources.title: Is TDD dead? Part IV: DHH on over-testing, test-first dogma, and the hidden costs of TDD
sources.originalTitle: TW Hangouts   |   Is TDD dead? [Part IV]
sources.summary: In the fourth Is TDD dead? hangout, DHH argues that TDD nudges teams toward over-testing, high test-to-code ratios and worship of testing infrastructure. He wants testing treated as a tradeoff: calibrate coverage to how much the code matters, keep the code as the top authority, and rank design clarity above measurable test metrics.

principles.text: Large test-to-code ratios are a smell: tests are code too, and they make changing behavior expensive.
principles.quote: the whole notion of having multiples of test code to single lines of production codes to me is often not a good thing

principles.text: Most code changes alter behavior, not just structure, so behavior tests must change too. Heavy test code multiplies that cost.
principles.quote: far more of my code changes are actually driven by wanting to change the actual Behavior

principles.text: Don't test everything first. Declarative framework statements like validations aren't worth stacked unit, functional and system tests.
principles.quote: see people write maybe five line of testing code to test that one declarative statement

principles.text: Coverage should vary by how critical the code is; well below 100% is fine for code that rarely breaks.
principles.quote: quite comfortable with significantly less than 100%

principles.text: Tune testing to the team: a stable product team with low rotation can accept 60-80% coverage, unlike a consultancy handing code to strangers.
principles.quote: most of the time 60% coverage or 80% coverage buys me enough confidence in making changes and catching errors that that'll do

principles.text: Design clarity and user value outrank measurable test metrics; don't get lured into chasing speed, coverage and ratios.
principles.quote: test speed coverage and ratio are quite far down the list

sources.title: Is TDD dead? Part III: DHH on the costs of testing, QA, and overconfidence in green bars
sources.originalTitle: TW Hangouts   |   Is TDD dead? [Part III]
sources.summary: In the third Is TDD Dead hangout with Kent Beck and Martin Fowler, DHH argues that TDD's success bred overconfidence and led shops to drop QA. He says the costs of testing are rarely discussed, and that real-world feedback such as on-call and customer complaints catches what green tests miss.

principles.text: Programmer-written tests aren't enough; someone who isn't the author needs to test the software too.
principles.quote: I don't think you can work on anything of material quality and produce great software without having somebody who's not you test it

principles.text: TDD's success gave programmers overconfidence, so many shops cut QA and shipped lower-quality software.
principles.quote: it gave them overconfidence in the quality with which they can produce software through testing

principles.text: Testing has real costs. The conversation only chases more, faster, better tests and ignores what you give up.
principles.quote: when I say stuff like testing does damage I see this look in some programmer's eyes just going what the hell are you talking about

principles.text: Coverage has sharply diminishing returns, like uptime nines. Each extra nine costs exponentially more.
principles.quote: to get to say 99 59s of coverage it's going to be exponentially more expensive than to get to 99 and even getting to 99 is going to be so much more expensive than getting to 80

principles.text: How much testing is right depends on how critical the domain is. Dogmatic 100% coverage contradicts that trade-off.
principles.quote: you can't on the one hand claim well we need 100% coverage because that's our design methodology and then at the same time also feel like oh well we're doing a trade-off that depends on the criticality

principles.text: Real-world feedback from users, customer service, and on-call is a vital loop that green tests can't replace.
principles.quote: it's also the information feedback loop right it's the feedback loop that goes beyond just I wrote my own test I'm deciding my own feedback loop here's the actual real world flowing into that

sources.title: RailsConf 2014 keynote: Why test-first design hurts clarity and programmers should think like writers
sources.originalTitle: RailsConf 2014 - Keynote: Writing Software by David Heinemeier Hansson
sources.summary: DHH argues most information-system work is closer to writing than to hard science. He says TDD optimizes for ease of testing and metrics (coverage, ratio, speed) at the cost of architecture and comprehension. He favors coarser system-level tests and aiming for clarity by reading, writing and rewriting lots of code.

principles.text: Programming information systems is writing, not engineering; clarity should be the top goal.
principles.quote: Writing is a much more apt metaphor for what we do most of the time than engineering is. Writing is about clarity.

principles.text: Designing for testability does not make code simpler or clearer; ease of testing is a poor measure of quality.
principles.quote: Is it simpler? Is it clearer? No. It's easier to test. And that's the important point, right? That's the important point in all these debates.

principles.text: Test at coarser levels; splitting code up for unit tests destroys architecture and comprehension.
principles.quote: Splitting up functions to support the testing process destroys your system architecture and code comprehension along with it. Test at a coarser level of granularity.

principles.text: Coverage, test ratio and speed are easy to measure but are not what matters; whether the whole system works is.
principles.quote: Just because something is easy to measure doesn't mean it's important.

principles.text: Regression tests have real value; driving design test-first rarely does.
principles.quote: Testing absolutely has value. Regression testing absolutely has value. Driving your design through test first, in my mind, rarely has value.

principles.text: Become a good programmer by reading, writing and rewriting a lot of code; first drafts are never final.
principles.quote: The only way to become a good programmer, where by definition I define good programmer somebody who program, who writes software with clarity, is to read a lot of software, write a lot of software.

sources.title: Code comments are a smell: extracting a constant and a create_or_find_by pattern
sources.originalTitle: On Writing Software (well?) #1: Pilot Episode
sources.summary: DHH walks through a Basecamp 3 refactoring session, treating code comments as a smell and replacing them with clearer code (an extracted private constant). He also weighs conflicting aesthetic conventions and shows pushing a recurring pattern, create_or_find_by backed by a unique index, upstream into Rails.

principles.text: Code comments are usually a smell; make the code itself explain the intent.
principles.quote: more often than not I tend to look at code comments as a bit of a smell why are you explaining something that isn't apparent or clear from the code itself

principles.text: Replace magic numbers with a named constant, declared privately and placed next to where it's used.
principles.quote: how far away are they from their usage and is this a general constant that someone should consider as a Pollak public constant or is it more of a private thing

principles.text: When style conventions conflict, choose by what makes code easiest and most pleasant to read; automatic style checkers can't make that call.
principles.quote: these two considerations that are somewhat in conflict you have to choose which one is more important to you

principles.text: The goal of refactoring is code that is easier and more aesthetically pleasing for the programmer to read and come back to.
principles.quote: it's just make this easier for me to read more aesthetically pleasing for me to read easier to come back to

principles.text: Model domain concepts as first-class objects (an administratorship join model) rather than boolean flags.
principles.quote: I really like encapsulating these domain objects and being able to reason about them and giving them a place to live and giving them a whole concept rather than just giving them boolean

principles.text: Prefer one insert guarded by a database unique index over a racy find-then-create; extract the pattern as create_or_find_by.
principles.quote: we're basically just doing one insert and relying on the unique index in the database to throw an exception if this person already exists

sources.title: DHH on callbacks: tracing the Basecamp mentions feature to manage auxiliary complexity
sources.originalTitle: On Writing Software Well #2: Using callbacks to manage auxiliary complexity
sources.summary: DHH walks through the Basecamp 3 mentions feature, tracing it from controller through concern, callbacks, background job and eavesdropper class. He argues callbacks push auxiliary complexity off to the side so the main flow stays simple, and that opt-out via suppression is the key to using them safely.

principles.text: Callbacks move incidental complexity aside so most code can pretend to be on a simple default path.
principles.quote: I think callbacks allow you to take incidental complexity and considerations and move them sort of off to the side since that most of the code can just pretend to be in a simple default path

principles.text: Side effects are a feature, not a smell; use them to progressively enhance a main flow.
principles.quote: I think side-effects are wonderful for a whole host of uses and I love having side effects that as I said sort of go off and adorn or progressively enhance a main flow

principles.text: Callbacks need an opt-out; design a suppression mechanism for the non-default path.
principles.quote: the thing about callbacks is you want to use them on the default path you want it to happen most of the time but there are scenarios where you don't want them to happen

principles.text: Push non-essential work into background jobs so requests do less blocking work.
principles.quote: if we take some of that work that is not required to happen at the same time as the recording of the message and shove it up on basically a different queue and have it happen in a job then we're doing less work that's blocking

principles.text: Don't move auxiliary logic into a service object or transaction script; it doesn't get clearer, and it deserves to sit on the side.
principles.quote: I don't think any of these things get clearer if you do that the fact is mentions is an auxilary concern it's not the main purpose of what we're doing here

principles.text: Concerns let you treat an aspect as one cohesive unit without burdening the main class.
principles.quote: We don't have to burden the recording class itself with all this logic and all this setup to it we can treat this whole aspect as one cohesive unit

sources.title: Using globals when the price is right: Rails Current at Basecamp
sources.originalTitle: On Writing Software Well #3: Using globals when the price is right
sources.summary: DHH defends globals as a "sharp knife" for request-scoped context, showing how Basecamp's Current class (extracted into Rails 5.1) carries the current person, account and request details into event tracking without threading them through every call. He warns to keep Current small so it doesn't become a crutch.

principles.text: Globals aren't inherently harmful; they fit request-scoped context in web apps well.
principles.quote: I think Global's have a great place in all sorts of applications and especially web applications since a lot of these all of these operate within a request cycle

principles.text: Rails deliberately ships sharp knives; a framework shouldn't withhold precise tools just because they can be misused.
principles.quote: it's not a sin of a framework or language to provide you with really sharp niall knives that could cut your hand off if you use them wrong but they can also provide just the incision that you need

principles.text: Don't thread auxiliary context like request ID, user agent and IP through every layer; it adds hassle, not clarity.
principles.quote: imagine having to pass this amount of detail the request ID user agent an IP address all the way from the top of the chain all the way up from the controller action down through the creation of a recording down to through the creation of the event and so on it would just be a real hassle

principles.text: Pluck ambient context like the current person from globals so callbacks need no parameters.
principles.quote: after create is a callback that doesn't take any variables right like you don't have to pass anything into it to be able to to call this

principles.text: Keep auxiliary concerns off center stage so readers focus on the main behavior.
principles.quote: passing this stuff around all the time is actually not an advantage it doesn't make the code clearer it makes it more convoluted

principles.text: Use globals deliberately and with pride, but keep Current small; a long list is a smell that code needs refactoring.
principles.quote: if you end up with a current that has 10 15 20 different things yeah okay maybe you're off into the weeds somewhere and you should take a step back

sources.title: Testing without test damage: real models, real controllers, fixtures, no mock soup
sources.originalTitle: On Writing Software Well #5: Testing without test damage or excessive isolation.
sources.summary: DHH walks through how Basecamp tests a lockable Document feature. He defends tests that hit the real database and render real views over isolated unit tests with mocks, uses fixtures instead of factories, and keeps assertions minimal. Fast-enough tests that give confidence beat the fastest possible tests.

principles.text: The goal of tests is confidence that shipped features work, not fast tests.
principles.quote: the purpose of developing software is not to have fast tests the purpose of testing new software is to have high confidence that the features that you're shipping are of high quality

principles.text: Don't trade realism for speed by piling on mocks and stubs; test the real thing with the real database.
principles.quote: I think in the majority of cases you're better off testing the real things interfacing with the real database interfacing with the real generation of HTML and controller

principles.text: Stub as little as possible so tests stay close to the metal and readable, without needless setup complexity.
principles.quote: you're testing the real thing under you mocking and stopping as little as possible as you can get away with such that your tests remain as close to the metal as close to the to the real thing

principles.text: Use fixtures as a base world instead of per-test factories; only create new records for what's particular to the test.
principles.quote: fixtures is this a wonderful concept of where you basically configure a base set of characters in a world that you can pull upon whenever you want to play a certain part

principles.text: Controller tests should be integration-style, covering HTTP request through view rendering and the database, stopping short of a real browser unless JavaScript needs testing.
principles.quote: it's stopping just short of using the browser to drive the interaction because using the browser to track the interaction adds sort of an order of magnitude of delay to it

principles.text: Reject one-assertion-per-test; use as many assertions as needed to cover an aspect fully. Prefer plain assert and assert_equal.
principles.quote: I think you should have all the assertions that you need to feel comfortable about testing one aspect of what you're doing

sources.title: How Basecamp actually deletes data: the incineration pattern, 30-day grace, backups scrubbed
sources.originalTitle: On Writing Software Well #6: Actually deleting data, not just pretending to
sources.summary: DHH argues programmers owe users real deletion, not a hidden flag, and walks through Basecamp's "incineration" code. Command objects traverse the account, buckets and recordings tree, scheduled 30 days out, with a trash stage, a short grace period and backup wipes.

principles.text: Deleted data should truly disappear, not just be flagged inaccessible. Programmers have an obligation to do it.
principles.quote: if you delete your data it should be gone it shouldn't be accessible years later for employees to access to be subpoenaed by someone suing you or the government the data should be gone

principles.text: Real deletion is deliberate engineering work. It never happens automatically in a multi-tenant database.
principles.quote: this doesn't happen automatically this is something you actually have to program

principles.text: Reserve a precise domain word for a precise process instead of overloading generic terms like delete or destroy.
principles.quote: we've come up with this term this notion this word of incineration and we're reserving that term to mean this specific thing

principles.text: Extract lifecycle behavior into a concern on the root object so it can be treated and discussed separately.
principles.quote: it's an aspect of the account I separated out from the account object itself such that we can treat and talk about it in separation

principles.text: Reuse the same deletion machinery at every level of the data tree: deleting a project is a subset of deleting an account.
principles.quote: we lean on the fact that the leading part of the Tree of data is a subset of deleting the entire tree of data

principles.text: Stage deletion with grace periods to protect users, while still honoring the promise to delete for real.
principles.quote: we kind of try to give as many steps as is reasonable while still honoring the principle of deleting the when it actually needs to be gone

sources.title: Push specifics down: replacing type checks with polymorphism in a Basecamp pull request
sources.originalTitle: On Writing Software Well #7: Move the specifics down as far as it'll go when evolving your codebase
sources.summary: DHH walks through a real Basecamp pull request (skipping reminders for already-answered questions) to show how to evolve code without degrading it. Keep generic classes stable by pushing type-specific logic down to the concrete classes via message passing, and choose names from everyday domain vocabulary.

principles.text: Changing existing code well means making it a little better along the way, and at the very least not worse.
principles.quote: the mission that we have is as part of writing software well to make things a little better along the way and at the very least not make them worse

principles.text: Keep generic classes free of knowledge about specific types; push specifics as far down as they go.
principles.quote: trying to push down the behavior that is specific to specific classes as far down as we possibly can get it

principles.text: A type check inside generic code is a smell; replace it with message passing (polymorphism) and let the concrete class answer.
principles.quote: as soon as you see type checks it's a smell and innocent indication that you can replace that type check with message passing

principles.text: Separate change schedules: a generic class shouldn't change when a specific rule's strategy changes, even if the inlined version reads clearer.
principles.quote: the reminder delivery should be on its own change schedule it shouldn't be changing when we're changing the strategy for figuring out whether a question has been answered or not

principles.text: Name methods in casual domain vocabulary; 'needed' beats 'pertinent' because it's what you'd say in conversation.
principles.quote: something that's as close as possible to the domain vocabulary that you would use in common conversation about this

principles.text: Pushing logic down prevents mega classes bloated with type tags and per-object exceptions as the system ages.
principles.quote: we won't get these mega classes that aren't large because they do a lot of stuff but because they have a lot of type tags that sort of have exceptions for for different objects

sources.title: Why 37signals dropped TypeScript from Turbo 8 and what DHH thinks of the flame war
sources.originalTitle: TypeScript Drama and Open Source Opinions
sources.summary: DHH explains why the Turbo team removed TypeScript: the people building it weren't enjoying the work, so they pulled it out in about 40 minutes. He frames static versus dynamic typing as a tribal, identity-driven fight, defends open source as a gift made for himself, and explains why internet backlash doesn't faze him.

principles.text: If the team building a tool isn't enjoying how they write it, change the approach; enjoyment is a valid engineering criterion.
principles.quote: does anyone like this way of working anymore like any of the people who are at the company um are we enjoying ourselves writing this software in this way and we were all like well not me not me not me

principles.text: Prefer dynamically typed languages like Ruby and JavaScript for their loose, permissive, freedom-loving feel.
principles.quote: my preference is for dynamically typed languages like the Ruby language that we predominately use and been using for 20 years like JavaScript itself

principles.text: Static vs dynamic typing is a debate nobody wins by argument; opinions rarely change, so don't try to debate your way out of it.
principles.quote: this is one of those things we can't debate our way out of

principles.text: Appreciate other paradigms by visiting them, then return to what suits you; diversity of tools is healthy.
principles.quote: I can appreciate these other ideas I think it's fun to spin them around but this is what speaks to me

principles.text: Open source is a gift made primarily for yourself; maintainers owe no one refunds or the gift they wanted instead.
principles.quote: I'm predominantly doing open source for me I love sharing also but like I'm not just doing it for the sharing I'm like I'm not here showing up as a volunteer labor force for whatever gifts you would like to have

principles.text: Online outrage is loud but small; ignore it, and say out loud the contrarian things many people privately believe.
principles.quote: I like to be of service to say things out loud that other people are hesitant

sources.title: AI Revisited: why DHH flipped on AI coding once agents moved to the terminal
sources.originalTitle: AI Revisited – REWORK
sources.summary: DHH explains why AI finally clicked for him in late 2025: agent mode in the terminal, not autocomplete, produced work he kept about 80% of. He covers toil-reduction uses at 37signals, shipping AI features only when clearly useful, and staying optimistic without hype or doom.

principles.text: Autocomplete-style AI interrupted his thinking; terminal agents running on their own fit how he works.
principles.quote: I did not like this idea that I have a thought in my head coming out through my keys and then boom, the AI tries to did you think of this? Did you think of that?

principles.text: The real shift was agents producing work he keeps: roughly 80% right, with him finishing the last 20%.
principles.quote: I've been shocked how often it's like 80% there.

principles.text: Use AI on internal toil first: triaging noisy security reports, patient log reviews, and on-call investigations.
principles.quote: AI turns out to be really good at that, right? Like it's really good at filtering noise from signal.

principles.text: Don't ship AI features as stickers; wait until the product is uniformly better, even if that means arriving late.
principles.quote: it's about putting on a sticker of something where it's not uniformly better after we've introduced this. And that's not what we want to launch.

principles.text: Non-programmers get more magic from AI than experts, in the way Excel and FileMaker democratized building programs.
principles.quote: we're democratizing the access to creativity in a way that very few moments in history have done so broadly.

principles.text: Stay curious and optimistic about what AI can do now; nobody knows where it goes, so skip hyperbolic extrapolation.
principles.quote: nobody knows where this is going.

sources.title: Cloud exit: why 37signals left rented clouds for owned hardware
sources.originalTitle: Fintech Daydreaming S07E09 - Cloud Exit with David Heinemeier Hansson
sources.summary: DHH explains why 37signals is leaving AWS: the promises of smaller teams, lower cost and less complexity never materialized, and a $3.2M annual cloud bill could shrink dramatically on owned hardware. He argues for "sovereign clouds" in colocated data centers.

principles.text: The cloud's promises (smaller teams, lower cost, less complexity) did not materialize for a stable, profitable business.
principles.quote: the promises of cloud that you could do more with less less complexity less cost um faster execution um smaller teams all of these fundamental promises as to why we should pay a premium for renting computers in the cloud versus buying our own turned out not to be true

principles.text: Cloud's real edge is instant elasticity, which is not worth a big premium for steady, predictable workloads.
principles.quote: that advantage of being open to spin up 100 servers by the snap of your fingers was just not worth that much it was not worth the the premium

principles.text: Run the numbers: managed cloud services are the costliest, and owned hardware can cut that spend by roughly two thirds or more.
principles.quote: we could take that 2.4 million and cut it down to less than nine hundred thousand and that would include buying all the replacement gear amortizing that over five years

principles.text: Companies buying compute at scale are software companies, so running infrastructure is a core competency to keep in-house.
principles.quote: if you are spending uh hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars buying compute directly from rental clouds you are a software company and the sooner you realize that the better off you are

principles.text: Running your own hardware is not exotic or risky; the industry has developed amnesia about it.
principles.quote: there's this General Amnesia in the industry that um over the past year it seemed or past five years let's say five to seven years it seems like everyone has forgotten what it takes to operate and own your own hardware

principles.text: Cloud consolidation into three vendors undermines the decentralized design of the internet.
principles.quote: if we handle all over all our Computing just to three companies then we've really destroyed this wonder of the world

sources.title: The Rails Doctrine: DHH's nine pillars of Rails philosophy
sources.originalTitle: The Rails Doctrine
sources.summary: DHH's founding essay lays out nine pillars behind Rails: programmer happiness, convention over configuration, omakase, no single paradigm, beautiful code, sharp knives, integrated systems (the majestic monolith), progress over stability, and a big tent. It explains why Rails trusts programmers, favors shared defaults, and resists premature distribution.

principles.text: Optimize for programmer happiness; Rails was built first to make DHH smile, and utility served that.
principles.quote: I created Rails for me. To make me smile, first and foremost. Its utility was to many degrees subservient to its ability to make me enjoy my life more.

principles.text: Convention over configuration frees you from recurring mundane decisions and lowers the barrier for beginners.
principles.quote: Part of the Rails’ mission is to swing its machete at the thick, and ever growing, jungle of recurring decisions that face developers creating information systems for the web.

principles.text: Let experts curate the stack (omakase); give up individual tool choice for a better shared toolbox.
principles.quote: So with Rails we decided to diminish one good, a programmer’s individual privilege to choose each tool in their box, for a greater one: A better tool box for all.

principles.text: Provide sharp knives: trust programmers with powerful tools and teach them, rather than paternalistically restricting them.
principles.quote: I’ve yet to hear a single programmer put up their hand and say “I can’t trust myself with this power, please take it away from me!”. It’s always “I think other programmers would abuse this”. That line of paternalism has never appealed to me.

principles.text: Favor integrated systems and avoid distributing (microservices) until you absolutely must.
principles.quote: avoid distributing our system before we absolutely, positively have to.

principles.text: Mix paradigms pragmatically instead of following a single pure idea to its conclusion.
principles.quote: It isn’t a single, perfect cut of cloth. It’s a quilt. A composite of many different ideas and even paradigms.

sources.title: DHH on why test-first TDD is dead: rebalancing toward system tests
sources.originalTitle: TDD is dead. Long live testing.
sources.summary: DHH explains why he abandoned test-first TDD as a design practice while keeping automated regression testing. He argues that driving design from isolated unit tests produces over-engineered architecture, and that the testing mix should shift from unit tests toward slower, higher-level system tests. He also warns against replacing one testing dogma with another.

principles.text: Test-first was useful training wheels for learning to test, not a permanent design discipline to follow forever.
principles.quote: The test-first part was a wonderful set of training wheels that taught me how to think about testing at a deeper level, but also some I quickly left behind.

principles.text: Test-first fundamentalism breeds shame and gatekeeping; don't use it as a litmus test of professionalism.
principles.quote: Used as a hammer to beat down the nonbelievers, declare them unprofessional and unfit for writing software. A litmus test.

principles.text: Driving design from isolated unit tests creates complex indirection and architectural monstrosities to avoid anything 'slow'.
principles.quote: Test-first units leads to an overly complex web of intermediary objects and indirection in order to avoid doing anything that's "slow". Like hitting the database.

principles.text: Skip mock-everything unit tests in Rails; test models directly against the database with fixtures.
principles.quote: I test active record models directly, letting them hit the database, and through the use of fixtures.

principles.text: Shift emphasis from unit tests to full system tests, which are no longer so slow thanks to parallelization and cloud runners.
principles.quote: Less emphasis on unit tests, because we're no longer doing test-first as a design practice, and more emphasis on, yes, slow, system tests.

principles.text: Don't swap one testing religion for another; avoid 'system tests only' dogma.
principles.quote: The worst thing we can do is just rush into another testing religion.

sources.title: Test-induced design damage: why DHH rejects bending code to fit TDD and unit isolation
sources.originalTitle: Test-induced design damage
sources.summary: DHH argues that the maxim "code hard to unit test is poorly designed" causes test-induced design damage: needless indirection added only for fast, isolated, test-first tests. Using Jim Weirich's hexagonal Rails demo as the example, he prescribes model tests with the database, integration-tested controllers, system-tested views, and design driving tests.

principles.text: Hard-to-unit-test code is not always badly designed; bending code for testability damages clarity.
principles.quote: Such damage is defined as changes to your code that either facilitates a) easier test-first, b) speedy tests, or c) unit tests, but does so by harming the clarity of the code through — usually through needless indirection and conceptual overhead.

principles.text: Hexagonal, repository and command patterns applied to Rails for testing's sake make the design worse.
principles.quote: The hexagonal pattern is being misapplied to Rails applications, alongside it companions of boundaries and ports'n'adapter-like patterns, for the purpose of testing. This is test-driven pattern application.

principles.text: Test controllers as integration tests and views as system tests, not as mocked units.
principles.quote: Controllers are meant to be integration tested, not unit tested.

principles.text: Let model tests hit the database; fixtures and transactions make it fast enough, so isolation isn't worth it.
principles.quote: Finally, the fear of letting model tests talk to the database is outdated. This decoupling is simply not worth it any more, even if it may once have been.

principles.text: Put test emphasis where the app's complexity lives; system-test heavy is fine for a complex UI.
principles.quote: If you have a very simple model layer, but your UI is complex, then you should indeed be system-test heavy, and model-test light! This is not a sin.

principles.text: Design drives tests, not the reverse; pursue clarity over testability and backfill tests once happy with the design.
principles.quote: Above all, you do not let your tests drive your design, you let your design drive your tests!

sources.title: Slow database test fallacy: why hitting the database in unit tests is fine in 2014
sources.originalTitle: Slow database test fallacy
sources.summary: DHH argues the TDD rule that unit tests must not touch the database is a relic of 1990s hardware. With SSDs, local databases, Spring preloading and transactional fixtures, Basecamp's model tests run in seconds, so abstracting away the database only causes test-induced design damage.

principles.text: Don't avoid the database in tests; the "unit tests must not touch the DB" rule is obsolete.
principles.quote: That was probably true in 1997 when you were connecting to a mainframe database or some Oracle abomination. It's not true in 2014 where you can run your MySQL or PostgreSQL database locally off a super-fast SSD.

principles.text: Revisit any heuristic built on a definition of "slow" regularly, because hardware progress invalidates it.
principles.quote: Heuristics and principles we adopt in one era of computing do not necessarily apply tomorrow. In fact, anything that's based on a definition of "slow" should be revisited frequently.

principles.text: Abstracting away the database in MVC systems adds indirection that scars the code base and hurts clarity.
principles.quote: The amount of indirection and additional layers needed end up scarring the code base and hurting the clarity of the system.

principles.text: Run only the tests for the code you changed; a needing-everything-rerun urge signals high coupling.
principles.quote: If you have so little confidence in the locality of your changes, the tests are indeed telling you that the system has overly high coupling.

principles.text: Two modes of testing give confidence: fast per-model runs while working, the full suite before check-in.
principles.quote: Between the two modes of testing, you'll have great confidence in your ability to make changes and develop new functionality, without the anxiety of breaking stuff left and right.

principles.text: Don't warp your architecture to optimize for the performance of the mid-nineties.
principles.quote: Don't pervert your architecture in order to prematurely optimize for the performance characteristics of the mid-nineties.

sources.title: Testing like the TSA: why DHH says over-testing is coverage theater
sources.originalTitle: Testing like the TSA
sources.summary: DHH argues tests have real costs, so developers must learn what not to test. He gives seven blunt rules for a typical Rails app (no 100% coverage, watch test ratios and time spent, skip testing framework basics, mostly test-after) and calls blanket coverage "TSA-style testing". He backs it with Kent Beck's "test as little as possible to reach a given level of confidence".

principles.text: Tests are code and cost time to write, update and read, so their benefit must exceed that cost.
principles.quote: Every line of code you write has a cost. It takes time to write it, it takes time to update it, and it takes time to read and understand it.

principles.text: Over-testing is a bad trade: the cost of catching a trivial bug can far exceed the value of catching it.
principles.quote: If it takes you 1,000 lines of validation testing to catch the one time Bob accidentally removed the `validates_presence_of :name` declaration, was it worth it? Of course not

principles.text: Don't chase 100% coverage; keep test-to-code ratios and time spent testing in check.
principles.quote: Code-to-test ratios above 1:2 is a smell, above 1:3 is a stink.

principles.text: Don't test what the framework already guarantees, and don't integration test what a unit test can cover.
principles.quote: Don't test standard Active Record associations, validations, or scopes.

principles.text: Don't force test-first everywhere; most of DHH's tests are written after the code.
principles.quote: Don't force yourself to test-first every controller, model, and view (my ratio is typically 20% test-first, 80% test-after).

principles.text: Blanket coverage is quality theater; very few apps are critical enough to justify testing everything.
principles.quote: We must collectively decide that the TSA-style of testing, the coverage theater of quality, is discredited before we can move forward. Very few applications operate at a level of criticality that warrant testing everything.

sources.title: Rails is omakase: why a framework should be one curated menu, not à la carte
sources.originalTitle: Rails is omakase
sources.summary: DHH frames Rails as an omakase meal: a small team of chefs picks the ingredients and APIs into one opinionated, personal full-stack framework. Substitutions are allowed within reason, but loud demands from people who haven't contributed carry little weight; influence is earned by showing up with code.

principles.text: A framework should be a curated, opinionated whole, not an à la carte pile of choices.
principles.quote: Rails is not that. Rails is omakase. A team of chefs picked out the ingredients, designed the APIs, and arranged the order of consumption on your behalf according to their idea of what would make for a tasty full-stack framework.

principles.text: Defaults can be personal and quirky; they don't need to please everyone.
principles.quote: The menu can be both personal and quirky. It isn't designed to appeal to the taste of everyone, everywhere.

principles.text: Opinionated defaults don't trap you: substitutions are allowed, so swap out the pieces you dislike.
principles.quote: Substitutions are allowed, within reason. So you don't like test/unit? No problem, bring your own rspec.

principles.text: Experience shapes taste; the maintainers' well-formed opinions set the design direction.
principles.quote: This doesn't make my tastes right for you, but it certainly means that they're well formed.

principles.text: Influence over a project is earned by contributing code, not by complaining loudly.
principles.quote: Nobody ever got to have a meaningful impact on the direction of Rails by contributing no code and just showing up in a Github comment thread and yelling about the evils of CoffeeScript.

principles.text: If you mostly like the defaults, express differences as exceptions and extend the chefs good faith.
principles.quote: Can I express my differences as exceptions or substitutions to the few things I don't care for? If so, then maybe I should give the chefs in the kitchen the benefit of assuming that they are working on what they truly think is the best way to go.

sources.title: The Majestic Monolith: why small teams should embrace one integrated system, not microservices
sources.originalTitle: The Majestic Monolith
sources.summary: DHH argues microservices/SOA suit organizations with thousands of developers, and copying them is cargo culting. Small teams should build an integrated "majestic monolith" that removes needless abstraction and stays understandable by individuals, as Basecamp does with about 12 programmers across six platforms.

principles.text: Microservices fit very large orgs; copying Amazon or Google at small scale is cargo culting.
principles.quote: The patterns that make sense for organizations orders of magnitude larger than yours, are often the exact opposite ones that’ll make sense for you. It’s the essence of cargo culting.

principles.text: Don't distribute your computing unless you truly have no choice.
principles.quote: The problem with prematurely turning your application into a range of services is chiefly that it violates the #1 rule of distribute computing: Don’t distribute your computing!

principles.text: Extracting services trades object collaboration for failure states, migrations and operational pain.
principles.quote: Every time you extract a collaboration between objects to a collaboration between systems, you’re accepting a world of hurt with a myriad of liabilities and failure states.

principles.text: A majestic monolith is an intentionally integrated system that eliminates needless abstraction and conceptual models.
principles.quote: It’s an integrated system that collapses as many unnecessary conceptual models as possible. Eliminates as much needless abstraction as you can swing a hammer at.

principles.text: A small team can run a large, multi-platform product by committing to the monolith plus a hybrid app model.
principles.quote: I believe the only possible way to do so with a small team of ~12 programmers is do explicitly choose and commit to The Majestic Monolith, in all its controversial glory.

principles.text: Integrate systems until no single person can hold it all in their head; tooling hasn't changed that.
principles.quote: Integrate your systems until it’s impossible for one person to hold it all in their head. We still haven’t gotten there with Basecamp or any of our apps.

sources.title: The Majestic Monolith can become The Citadel: extract Outposts only when the monolith can't cope
sources.originalTitle: The Majestic Monolith can become The Citadel
sources.summary: DHH argues most web apps should start and stay as a Majestic Monolith, whose limits are far higher than architects imagine. If scale or team size ever demands it, extend into a Citadel: the monolith stays at the center, supported by a few small Outposts for divergent slices. Basecamp's Campfire poller is the example.

principles.text: Start almost every web app as a single codebase that does everything; most will never outgrow it.
principles.quote: The vast majority of web applications should start life as a Majestic Monolith: A single codebase that does everything the application needs to do.

principles.text: A monolith's limits are much higher than architect-minded developers like to imagine.
principles.quote: The limits upon which this pattern is constrained are high. Much higher than most people like to imagine when they fantasize about being capital-a Architects.

principles.text: Exhaust improvements to the monolith before reaching for the next architectural step.
principles.quote: Your first instinct should be to improve the Majestic Monolith until it can cope, but, having done that and failed, you may look to the next step.

principles.text: If you must split, keep the monolith central and extract only small Outposts for divergent behavior, not the whole app.
principles.quote: The Outposts are there to allow the Majestic Monolith to offload a particular slice of divergent behavior, either for organizational or performance or implementation reasons.

principles.text: Good Outpost candidates are simple services with very different performance profiles, like Campfire's polling endpoint.
principles.quote: We didn’t try to carve the entire app up into little services, each written in a different language. No, we just extracted a single Outpost. That’s a Citadel setup.

principles.text: The microservice chase is a blind alley; the monolith is waiting for refugees and the Citadel shows it can stretch.
principles.quote: As more and more people come to realize that the chase for microservices ended in a blind alley, the pendulum is going to swing back.

sources.title: Clarity over brevity: why DHH favors long, intention-revealing method names
sources.originalTitle: Clarity over brevity in variable and method names
sources.summary: DHH argues programmers should trade brevity for clarity in variable and method names, citing long Basecamp method names as examples. Names should express intention rather than implementation, which removes most need for comments. In replies he credits Kent Beck's Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns as the bible on this.

principles.text: Prefer clarity over brevity when naming variables and methods; don't abbreviate.
principles.quote: Many programmers have a natural preference for short variable and method names. I doubt many would recognize this preference as a trade of brevity for clarity, but that’s often exactly the result.

principles.text: Modern expressive languages save enough boilerplate that you can spend it on spelling things out.
principles.quote: Modern programming languages are expressive enough that what you save in laborious boilerplate can be spent on clarity

principles.text: Avoid abbreviations, especially app-specific ones that will be forgotten within months.
principles.quote: I cringe when I see ext for extension, cp for copy, or worse, application-specific abbreviations sure to be forgotten two months after you left the project.

principles.text: A name longer than its operation looks silly at first but pays off when you return to the code.
principles.quote: The name of the method or variable can be longer than the operation being performed! But the silliness quickly dissipates the first time you return to a piece of code and know exactly what it does.

principles.text: Treat comments as a code smell; clear naming should make them rarely necessary.
principles.quote: If you work hard at being clear in your naming, you’ll also rarely need to write comments for the code. Comments are generally only needed when you failed to be clear enough in naming. Treat them as a code smell.

principles.text: Method names state intention, the body states implementation, so name length needn't track code length.
principles.quote: The method name explains the intention, the code the implementation. I’ve on many a occasion had longer names than implementation.

sources.title: Conceptual compression: why beginners no longer need SQL (DHH, 2018)
sources.originalTitle: Conceptual compression means beginners don't need to know SQL, hallelujah!
sources.summary: DHH argues that abstractions like Active Record have compressed the database into an appliance, so beginners can build database-backed apps without learning SQL. Progress means making yesterday's fundamentals optional, unpackable on demand, and lowering barriers to entry. Experienced programmers shouldn't cling to hardships the next generation doesn't have to endure.

principles.text: Good abstractions let beginners skip fundamentals; unpack a concept later, only when you need it.
principles.quote: SQL, like memory management, is a concept you can unpack when you need to. Further down the line of your career.

principles.text: The ORM is a proven abstraction: Basecamp 3 serves millions without a hand-written SQL statement in app logic.
principles.quote: Basecamp 3 has about 42,000 lines of code, and not a single fully formed SQL statement as part of application logic! It serves millions of people.

principles.text: The database should be an appliance, a commodity; being relegated to appliance status is an honor.
principles.quote: The relegation to “appliance status” isn’t a dig, but an honor.

principles.text: Don't romanticize your own learning struggles; rejoice that the next generation doesn't have to endure them.
principles.quote: Falling in love with the trials and tribulations you had to suffer, rather than rejoicing in the fact that the next generation doesn’t have to endure them.

principles.text: Conceptual compression lowers barriers to entry and preserves the individual generalist who can build complete applications.
principles.quote: And we need such conceptual compression more than ever to starve off specialization, and to preserve the power of individual generalists to make complete applications.

principles.text: Don't fight conceptual compression; help make it happen, and don't try to hold every concept expanded in your head.
principles.quote: You can’t learn everything. You can’t hold every concept fully expanded in your head. And moreover, you shouldn’t.

sources.title: Turbo 8 is dropping TypeScript: DHH on JavaScript, typing, and joy
sources.originalTitle: Turbo 8 is dropping TypeScript
sources.summary: DHH announces Turbo 8 is dropping TypeScript. He explains he likes modern JavaScript, dislikes the compile step and type gymnastics, and argues programmers pick a typing camp early and rationalize it. He still respects TypeScript users and values compatibility.

principles.text: TypeScript's type gymnastics add little joy and often grief, making easy things hard and hard things 'any'.
principles.quote: it pollutes the code with type gymnastics that add ever so little joy to my development experience, and quite frequently considerable grief. Things that should be easy become hard, and things that are hard become `any`.

principles.text: Modern JavaScript is a joy to write, and running in browsers without a compiler is a real benefit.
principles.quote: it's simply our good fortune that we now have such a capable JavaScript, which browsers are able to interpret without any need for a compiler at all.

principles.text: Programmers pick a side on typing early in their careers and then rationalize that choice for the rest of it.
principles.quote: Most programmers find themselves drawn strongly to typing or not quite early in their career, and then spend the rest of it rationalizing The Correct Choice to themselves and others.

principles.text: Writing JavaScript free of tooling and strong typing is a blessing, since the browser forces JavaScript on you anyway.
principles.quote: JavaScript is a language of necessity when it comes to the client side.

principles.text: He respects that others prefer TypeScript; dropping it from Turbo doesn't stop anyone using it in their own code.
principles.quote: Just because Turbo 8 is dropping TypeScript won't mean you can't write your client code in it, or use any other library that employs it. We get to mix and match, which is wonderful.

sources.title: DHH on the TypeScript meltdown: dogmatic crusading and open source hooliganism
sources.originalTitle: Open source hooliganism and the TypeScript meltdown
sources.summary: DHH responds to the backlash after Turbo 8 dropped TypeScript. He separates good-faith technical objections from pile-ons by outsiders, argues a project may choose its own tools without being attacked, and notes TypeScript is still JavaScript, a superset that adds an appearance of type safety to a weakly, dynamically typed language.

principles.text: Passion for your tools is fine, but evangelism should not turn into dogmatic crusading.
principles.quote: there's also a fine line between being a passionate evangelist and becoming a dogmatic crusader.

principles.text: A project may drop a tool for its own reasons and let others reach different conclusions; that is no cause for attack.
principles.quote: This was one project, mostly overseen by one company, that removed TypeScript from their own project, and explained why, while allowing amble room and spirit for others to reach different conclusions for their own work.

principles.text: Good-faith technical discussion with real contributors and users is welcome; drive-by crusaders are not.
principles.quote: I'm always happy to have technical discussions in good faith with such individuals

principles.text: TypeScript is JavaScript: a superset that sprinkles an appearance of type safety on a weakly, dynamically typed language.
principles.quote: TypeScript is JavaScript! It's a superset that sprinkles an appearance of type safety on top of a weakly- and dynamically-typed language.
