principles.text: Whether to use compiler-based type checking is ultimately unresolvable, and low stakes make debates nastier (bikeshedding).
principles.quote: That's the eternal wisdom of bikeshed parable. That when the stakes are low, the debate more easily becomes nasty.

principles.text: Defacing a project's collaboration spaces or accusing differing developers of incompetence or malice is unbecoming of the profession.
principles.quote: find another way to express your enthusiasm than by defacing collaboration organs or slandering those who JavaScript differently with accusations of incompetence or malice.

sources.title: Programming types and mindsets: why DHH accepts both static and dynamic typing camps
sources.originalTitle: Programming types and mindsets
sources.summary: DHH says he is a dynamic typing person who loves Ruby for its poetic syntax, and he dislikes static typing. He used to evangelize dynamic typing as a mark of better education or competence. He now sees typing preferences as matters of faith and personality, and values multiplicity in programming paradigms.

principles.text: DHH is unashamedly a dynamic typing person, and Ruby's poetic syntax depends on dynamic typing.
principles.quote: Personally, I'm unashamedly a dynamic typing kind of guy. That's why I love Ruby so very much. It takes full advantage of dynamic typing to allow the poetic syntax that results in such beautiful code.

principles.text: Static typing clashes with Ruby's nature; typed Ruby would be an unnatural mix.
principles.quote: To me, Ruby with explicit, static typing would be like a salad with a scoop of ice cream. They just don't go together.

principles.text: Typing debates are matters of faith; rationalizations rarely convince anyone.
principles.quote: As rationalizations masquerading as reason rarely do in matters of faith. The rider will always justify the way of the elephant.

principles.text: Treating dislike of dynamic typing as lack of education or competence is folly; people differ in temperament.
principles.quote: Seeing the lack of enthusiasm for dynamic typing as a reflection of missing education, experience, or perhaps even competence. Oh what folly.

principles.text: Multiplicity of paradigms keeps programming creative; one paradigm for everyone would ruin it.
principles.quote: Programming would be an awful endeavor if we were all confined to the same paradigm. Human nature is much too varied to accept such constraint on its creativity.

principles.text: He can coexist with typed-language fans as long as Ruby stays free of type hints and the front end isn't forced into TypeScript.
principles.quote: As long as I never have to soil my Ruby with type hints or write all front-end code in TypeScript, I can so happily coexist with those who adore Go or can't stand JavaScript.

sources.title: System tests have failed: why DHH is cutting most browser-driven tests
sources.originalTitle: System tests have failed
sources.summary: DHH argues that Rails system tests, despite high hopes in 2016, remain slow, brittle and full of false negatives. He keeps a small top-level smoke test, relies on model and controller tests for business logic, and prefers human exploratory testing for UI logic and feel. HEY is cutting its roughly 300 system tests way down.

principles.text: System tests have been slow, brittle and full of false negatives for a decade; the time spent making them reliable outweighs the bugs they catch.
principles.quote: System tests remain as slow, brittle, and full of false negatives as they did a decade ago.

principles.text: Automate testing for fast feedback, regression catching and confidence, but system testing isn't automatically the best way to meet those goals.
principles.quote: These are all valid goals, but that doesn't mean system testing is the best way to fulfill them.

principles.text: Keep system tests only as a top-level smoke test that cheaply catches configuration or loading failures.
principles.quote: System tests work well for the top-level smoke test.

principles.text: Test business logic with model and controller tests, which do it better and cheaper than end-to-end tests.
principles.quote: The stickiest point, however, is not testing business logic, which model and controller tests do better and cheaper, but testing UI logic.

principles.text: Human testing in a real browser gives the most confidence in UI logic because it judges how it feels, which automation can't.
principles.quote: Because half the time UI testing is not just about "does it work" but also "does it feel right". No automation can tell you that.

principles.text: Don't let sunk cost keep a brittle suite alive; cut it down, as HEY is doing with its ~300 system tests.
principles.quote: The sunk cost fallacy has kept us running this brittle, cumbersome suite for too long.

sources.title: Why Basecamp lets pull requests run large and long: reviewing features in full context
sources.originalTitle: The advantages of large, long-running pull requests
sources.summary: DHH argues against chopping features into tiny, short-lived pull requests. Letting a PR run as long as a complete feature needs (weeks, up to six under Shape Up) lets reviewers see trade-offs and design decisions in context, protecting design standards and cohesive architecture. Merge-conflict costs are real but manageable for most teams.

principles.text: Review a feature as a whole, with all trade-offs and design decisions in context, not as fragments.
principles.quote: My favorite part of doing code reviews is to see all the trade-offs, design decisions, and changes in context together.

principles.text: Let pull requests run as long as a complete feature or fix needs, not to an arbitrary time limit.
principles.quote: at Basecamp, we let pull requests run as long as they need to encompass a complete feature or fix.

principles.text: Mitigate merge conflicts by frequently merging main into the long-running PR; most teams aren't big enough for it to be a real problem.
principles.quote: you can mitigate much of this by ensuring you keep your pull request up to date with main by frequently merging main into the pull request.

principles.text: The debate over PR size focuses on cost and ignores the value of high design standards and cohesive architecture.
principles.quote: It focuses mostly on the cost, not on the value. And the value is tremendous to any organization that seeks to keep high design standards and a cohesive architecture.

principles.text: Partial, disjointed PRs pollute the codebase and skip cleanup and whole-picture simplification that never happens later.
principles.quote: Code that doesn't leave the campsite in a better condition than it found it, because doing the cleanup is something for another pull request, on another day (by no one ever).

principles.text: Self-review of the full diff is a powerful way to see the shape of the code and catch bad smells.
principles.quote: It's in this dance you see the shape of the code, pick up on bad smells, and ultimately decide whether you're happy with the whole.

sources.title: The premise trap: treat AI like a junior programmer
sources.originalTitle: The premise trap
sources.summary: DHH says the hardest part of working with juniors, and with AI, is the premise trap: flawed assumptions in a first draft go unquestioned until too much time is sunk into polishing. Current AI is a superb junior that writes overcomplicated, subtly defective code, so seniors shouldn't delegate whole systems to it.

principles.text: Question a first draft's baked-in assumptions before investing in improving the implementation.
principles.quote: That's where the fundamental assumptions baked into the first draft of the code aren't questioned until you've already spent far too long improving the implementation.

principles.text: Today's AI is like a superb junior programmer: great syntax and API knowledge, same tendency toward overcomplicated, subtly defective code.
principles.quote: Because AI at the moment is like a superb junior programmer. One with an encyclopedic knowledge about syntax and APIs, but also one saddled with the same propensities to produce overly-complicated, subtly-defective solutions.

principles.text: AI code habitually pulls in needless dependencies, is verbose, and hits architectural dead ends.
principles.quote: But the propensity to pull in needless dependencies, the overly-verbose presentation, and the architectural dead ends are there all the time.

principles.text: Seniors master trade-offs by working on proprietary code bases, which tutorial-trained models lack.
principles.quote: Senior human programmers all got started on the same information diet, but eventually graduated to higher levels of understanding and mastery by working on proprietary code bases.

principles.text: Don't ask AI to produce whole systems if you care about quality; verifying its assumptions costs as much as doing the work.
principles.quote: It's rarely going to save you time asking it to produce an entire system, or even subsystem, if you care about the final quality of the architecture or implementation.

principles.text: Stay bullish on AI but guard against signing off on slop and letting leaning on AI sap your own learning.
principles.quote: As well as alert to the danger of luring more senior programmers, including myself, into signing off on slop, while it saps our stamina for continued learning, as we lean too much on AI writing for us rather than teaching how.

sources.title: How to recover from microservices: DHH on returning to the majestic monolith
sources.originalTitle: How to recover from microservices
sources.summary: DHH argues microservices-first is rarely justified and that most systems should start and stay as a majestic monolith. For teams already in the mess, he gives a five-step recovery plan: stop adding services, consolidate critical flows, keep true performance hotspots, prune esoteric languages, and partition with modules rather than networks.

principles.text: Start and stay with a majestic monolith; microservices-first suits very few systems.
principles.quote: The vast majority of systems are much better served by starting and staying with a majestic monolith.

principles.text: GitHub and Shopify run monoliths with millions of lines and thousands of programmers; you likely need less.
principles.quote: even the likes of GitHub and Shopify run their main applications as monoliths with millions of lines of code and have thousands of programmers collaborating on them.

principles.text: Recovery begins by not creating more microservices, then picking one as the center that absorbs the rest.
principles.quote: You can't clean up a mess before you stop making more of it.

principles.text: Consolidate first the services that splinter a single coherent flow like signup or checkout.
principles.quote: The worst form of microservice madness is when you splinter a single, coherent flow across multiple systems.

principles.text: Limit backend languages to two: a productive general one and a fast one for rare hotspots.
principles.quote: The vast majority of systems should have no more than two backend languages in play at any one time

principles.text: Partition large systems with modules and namespaces, not network boundaries; complex systems must evolve from simple ones.
principles.quote: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that works.

sources.title: Why DHH sees Kubernetes as the next Death Star of complexity (J2EE, WS-*, now containers)
sources.originalTitle: They're rebuilding the Death Star of complexity
sources.summary: DHH traces a recurring pattern: vendors profit from complexity, so each time a wave (J2EE, WS-*) is flattened by simpler tools like Rails and JSON over HTTPS, the merchants of complexity regroup around the next frontier. He argues Kubernetes and its ecosystem are the current iteration, with the ratio of good ideas to bullshit out of whack.

principles.text: Rails was created to extract the good ideas from enterprise complexity and discard the bullshit.
principles.quote: To liberate the good ideas from the bullshit. To flush out all the nonsense, and to compress the remaining intrinsic complexity, so mere mortals without an advanced degree in enterprisey gibberish could employ the hidden gems of ingenuity that really were present.

principles.text: Plain, simple technology wins: JSON over HTTPS beat WS-* regardless of RESTful purity debates.
principles.quote: The internet voted with its web requests, and simple JSON over HTTPS once again beat back the merchants of complexity to save the human race of programmers from a regrouping empire.

principles.text: Complexity is profitable and simplicity is not, so expect vendors to rebuild complexity wherever things get too easy.
principles.quote: The struggle between profitless simplicity and profitable complexity is eternal in the world of software. When things become too easy, too approachable, there just isn't room for all the enterprisey services, sales, and solutions to prosper.

principles.text: Kubernetes may hold good ideas, but its bullshit ratio is out of whack compared with Docker's original simplicity.
principles.quote: Again, I'm certain that there are good ideas hidden inside the advancement of Kubernetes, and the mushrooming of tools, services, and standards that are following in its wake, but the ratio of bullshit is also already completely out of whack.

principles.text: Start from the simple job: run an app on some hardware efficiently and redeploy it easily; don't accept complexity far beyond that.
principles.quote: What we're trying to do here? We're trying to run an application on some hardware in a reasonably efficient manner, where we can easily redeploy it when it changes.

principles.text: Complexity looks silly in hindsight but feels excusable in the thick of it; keep a skeptical mind and distance from it.
principles.quote: Beware carnies dressed as storm troopers. The circus empire is always coming to town. Keep a safe distance, a skeptical mind, and one hand on your wallet.

sources.title: The simplest thing that could possibly work: Beck's mottos as DHH's programming engine
sources.originalTitle: The simplest thing that could possibly work
sources.summary: DHH credits Kent Beck's XP mottos, "the simplest thing that could possibly work" and "you aren't gonna need it", as the drivers of all his programming work. He pairs them with a cultivated outsider's ignorance to break paradigms (Rails, Hotwire, Kamal) and get from nothing to working software in days.

principles.text: Beck's two mottos, simplest thing that could work and YAGNI, drive all of DHH's programming.
principles.quote: To this day, these are the mottos that move all my programming work forward.

principles.text: Pithy mantras are needed as antidotes to speculative 'wouldn't it be nice' and 'we'll probably also need' thinking.
principles.quote: It's so easy to get lost in sentiments like "but wouldn't it be nice if..." and "we'll probably also need...". You need pithy mental antidotes at the ready to provide a counter.

principles.text: Cultivated ignorance as an outsider helps you tackle problems from first principles and break paradigms.
principles.quote: It's easier to break the paradigms if you're not enmeshed in them on the daily.

principles.text: Cutting straight to the epicenter of the solution gets you from nothing to working software in days, not weeks or months.
principles.quote: It's how you go from nothing to working software in days, not weeks or months. By cutting straight to the chase for the epicenter of the solution.

principles.text: Human nature dwells on potentialities instead of acting, so sticking with simplicity takes constant effort.
principles.quote: Like human nature is primed to dwell on all potentialities vs the activating the instinct for action.

principles.text: Whether or not you adopt XP wholesale, its audacious prescriptions train you to look for the simplest thing, a huge productivity unlock.
principles.quote: Few changes in perspective will unlock that hallowed 10x potential like this.

sources.title: Try hard not to solve hard problems: reframe the problem, keep teams tiny
sources.originalTitle: Try hard not to solve hard problems
sources.summary: DHH argues most hard problems in business, design, or programming can be restated as easy ones by questioning assumptions, reweighing trade-offs, and abandoning sunk costs. He names this as 37signals' key principle for making big things with tiny teams, taught through constraints like 6-week cycles and two-person teams.

principles.text: Most hard problems can be restated as easy ones by questioning assumptions, reweighing trade-offs, and dropping sunk cost.
principles.quote: Almost all of them can be restated as an easy problem, if you dare question the assumptions, reweigh the trade-offs, and stop diving after sunk cost.

principles.text: Refusing to solve hard problems is the key to pace and big results with tiny teams.
principles.quote: Above all the other principles at 37signals, this is our key to keeping the pace, making big things happen with tiny teams, and avoid getting bogged down in motivation-killing slogs.

principles.text: Cultivate an allergy to hard problems and park the ego that takes pride in doing hard things.
principles.quote: To do this well, you have to cultivate an allergy to hard problems. Develop a higher sensitivity to the cumbersome, and park the part of the ego that thrives on doing hard things as a point of pride.

principles.text: Bootstrapped founders learn this naturally from constraints; everyone else can learn it via artificial constraints like 6-week cycles.
principles.quote: Like by embracing artificial constraints tight enough to require an aversion to hard problems. See the 6-week cycles we run in Shape Up, for example.

principles.text: Keep teams deliberately small: most 37signals work is built by one designer and one programmer.
principles.quote: virtually everything at 37signals is built by two people: one designer, one programmer

principles.text: When pushed, the answer is to do less, not throw more resources at the problem.
principles.quote: the right answer is not to throw more at the problem when push comes to shove, but to do just the opposite.

sources.title: A writer's Ruby: why linting should enforce your style, not a universal one
sources.originalTitle: A writer's Ruby
sources.summary: DHH argues that style is an integral part of code as expression, and that Ruby's many ways to do things make it a language for writers. Linters are good when authors and teams enforce their own style, which is why Rails ships RuboCop with his omakase defaults as a starting point, not an edict.

principles.text: Style and aesthetics in code matter; the best code is its own form of poetry.
principles.quote: The best code to me is indeed its own form of poetry, and style is an integral part of such expression.

principles.text: Ruby's many ways to do things is a feature; it delights programmers who write code as authors.
principles.quote: Whereas Python’s motto has long been “there should be one – and preferably only one – obvious way to do it”, Ruby is the exact opposite.

principles.text: A universal, language-mandated style (like gofmt) is totalitarian and flattens expression.
principles.quote: That’s the most totalitarian approach. A decree on what a program should look like that’s barely two feet removed from a compile error. I don’t like that one bit.

principles.text: Linters are for authors and teams to enforce their own style on their own codebases, not to mandate style on others.
principles.quote: I think they’re excellent tools for authors and teams to enforce _their_ style with consistency on _their_ codebases.

principles.text: Rails ships a default omakase linter config as a starting point to develop your own sensibilities.
principles.quote: But it really is just a starting point for Rails programmers and teams to develop their own sensibilities, not a permanent edict on what those should be.

principles.text: Style is invariably idiosyncratic; narrowing Ruby to one pre-approved path would be a shame.
principles.quote: Ruby affords us such rich and expressive syntax that it would be a damn shame if we narrowed all possible paths down to a single, pre-approved trail.

sources.title: Why we're leaving the cloud: renting computers is a bad deal for stable, medium-sized companies
sources.originalTitle: Why we're leaving the cloud
sources.summary: DHH explains why 37signals is leaving AWS and Google Cloud after years of running Basecamp and HEY there. The cloud only pays off for tiny apps or wildly irregular load, the promised ops savings never materialized, and owning hardware is cheaper and better for a decentralized internet.

principles.text: Renting computers is mostly a bad deal for medium-sized companies with stable growth.
principles.quote: Renting computers is (mostly) a bad deal for medium-sized companies like ours with stable growth. The savings promised in reduced complexity never materialized.

principles.text: The cloud shines only at two ends: very simple low-traffic apps, and wildly irregular load.
principles.quote: The cloud excels at two ends of the spectrum, where only one end was ever relevant for us.

principles.text: Paying cloud premiums for hypothetical spikes is like buying earthquake insurance far from any fault line.
principles.quote: we're paying an at times almost absurd premium for the possibility that it could. It's like paying a quarter of your house's value for earthquake insurance when you don't live anywhere near a fault line.

principles.text: Moving to the cloud doesn't materially shrink the ops team; some things get simpler, others more complex.
principles.quote: Some things are simpler, others more complex, but on the whole, I've yet to hear of organizations at our scale being able to materially shrink their operations team, just because they moved to the cloud.

principles.text: The cloud is marketing-packaged renting, with obscene margins; don't be dazzled by 'run your own powerplant' analogies.
principles.quote: The cloud is sold as computing on demand, which sounds futuristic and cool, and very much not like something as mundane as "renting computers", even though that's mostly what it is.

principles.text: Running your own servers isn't too complicated; tooling progress from the cloud era is available for your own machines.
principles.quote: Don't let the entrenched cloud interests dazzle you into believing that running your own setup is too complicated. Everyone and their dog did it to get the internet off the ground, and it's only gotten easier since.

sources.title: The Big Cloud Exit FAQ: how 37signals answered every objection to leaving the cloud
sources.originalTitle: The Big Cloud Exit FAQ
sources.summary: DHH answers the recurring objections to 37signals' cloud exit: team size, security, reliability, scaling, and cost. His core claim is that the cloud's promised savings and ease of use never materialized, and that owning hardware is mostly the same operational work done cheaper, with the same team and open source tooling.

principles.text: The cloud doesn't reduce operations headcount; the same team runs the apps on owned hardware.
principles.quote: This is the central deceit of the cloud marketing, that it’s all going to be so much easier that you hardly need anyone to operate it. I’ve never seen it.

principles.text: Running your own hardware isn't arcane knowledge; the internet ran on it for twenty years before cloud became the default.
principles.quote: The internet got going in 1995. Cloud as the default choice didn’t happen until maybe 2015. So for well over twenty years, companies have been operating hardware to run their applications.

principles.text: Security work is about your application and dependencies, so it's the same whether you rent or own the machines.
principles.quote: The work that needs to happen to properly secure your custom-built application is not any materially different whether you own the computers it runs on or rent them from a cloud provider.

principles.text: Overprovision cheap, powerful hardware for headroom; only large, regular spikes justify renting cloud capacity.
principles.quote: That’s all to say that you can afford to dramatically over provision your own hardware to give you ample headroom to deal with spikes, and it’ll barely make a difference in the long-run budget.

principles.text: Everything needed to run internet apps is open source, so skip enterprise service contracts and licensing fees.
principles.quote: Everything you need to run applications on the internet is generally available as open source. We run open source versions of everything we were running in the cloud.

principles.text: Cloud promised cheaper, easier, faster, but only faster delivered; managed services still needed management and Moore's Law savings weren't passed on.
principles.quote: Because we bought the marketing pitch. That it was going to be cheaper, easier, and faster. Only the last promise ever really came through for us.

sources.title: How 37signals runs with no full-time managers: managers of one and distributed mentoring
sources.originalTitle: We once more have no full-time managers at 37signals
sources.summary: DHH explains why 37signals dropped its experiment with full-time managers and went back to none. Management is spread across senior individual contributors, which keeps it minimal, avoids Parkinson's Law, and depends on hiring "managers of one". He also names the limit: poor-performance cases must bubble up to the top.

principles.text: Spread managerial duties across senior ICs instead of hiring full-time managers.
principles.quote: Everyone doing management here does so on the side, next to their primary work as an individual contributor. Including Jason and me. And it works.

principles.text: Distributed management stays minimal because it can't expand to fill a fixed forty hours (Parkinson's Law).
principles.quote: With this distribution, there's no longer a fixed forty hours for managerial duties to expand into, and so we dodge Parkinson's Law.

principles.text: Replace recurring one-on-ones with automated check-ins, and give each lead one mentee rather than many reports.
principles.quote: Instead of lining up a recurring schedule of weekly one-on-ones, we drive status updates and check-ins by automated questions.

principles.text: Hire and promote autonomous 'managers of one' who set their own agenda and thrive on uninterrupted time.
principles.quote: People with both the competence and drive to set their own agenda and follow it autonomously.

principles.text: A manager who is also your professional superior is easier to learn from and respect.
principles.quote: I find that it's easier to steer that development when someone's primary manager is also their professional superior.

principles.text: Recurring poor performance is a root-cause problem for the top to fix, not something to manage around.
principles.quote: If cases of poor performance keeps bubbling up, there's a fundamental problem somewhere in the process anyway, and that can usually only be definitively addressed by the top.

sources.title: Programmers should stop celebrating incompetence: why DHH rejects the "I have no idea what I'm doing" identity
sources.originalTitle: Programmers should stop celebrating incompetence
sources.summary: DHH argues that well-meant efforts to fight imposter syndrome have drifted into celebrating incompetence and copy-paste programming. He says programmers should treat lookups as part of learning, accept that the craft has depth and uneven talent, and aim to become the wizard rather than the bedazzled audience.

principles.text: Don't make 'I have no idea what I'm doing' a professional identity; the programming world must stop celebrating incompetence.
principles.quote: You can't become the I HAVE NO IDEA WHAT I'M DOING dog as a professional identity.

principles.text: Looking things up is fine as part of learning, but dig deeper to understand, or competence stays at the surface.
principles.quote: Treat it as part of a learning process to actually understand what's going on. Not merely as a shortcut to solve today's problems. If you never dig deeper, your competence will be stuck at the surface.

principles.text: Experienced programmers should not fake being clueless; relatability has a cost in making deep learning seem futile.
principles.quote: Whatever gains you derive from being relatable to someone struggling must be weighed against infusing this industry with a sense of futility of deep learning.

principles.text: Programming magic is just things you don't know yet; the goal is to become the wizard.
principles.quote: The magic of programming is largely just things you don't know yet.

principles.text: Accept that programming has depth and talent varies, as in chess; you can't master everything but should be on some path to mastery.
principles.quote: But it's not fine to think you shouldn't be on _some_ paths towards mastery, if you intend to make programming your career.

principles.text: The world needs more competent programmers, so embrace your capacity to become good rather than self-deprecating nonsense.
principles.quote: It's never had a greater need for _competent_ programmers than it does today.

sources.title: Coding should be a vibe: why DHH won't hand AI the keyboard
sources.originalTitle: Coding should be a vibe!
sources.summary: DHH argues "vibe coding" appeals mostly to programmers stuck in unpleasant languages, and that Ruby's programmer-happiness premise makes writing code itself the enjoyable part. He uses AI as a pair programmer for lookups and questions but refuses to permanently give it the keyboard.

principles.text: Vibe coding's appeal comes from unpleasant development environments, not from coding being inherently a chore.
principles.quote: The appeal of "vibe coding" — where programmers lean back and prompt their way through an entire project with AI — appears partly to be based on the fact that so many development environments are deeply unpleasant to work with.

principles.text: Programmer happiness is Ruby's core premise: writing code should be a joy, even at some cost to machine efficiency.
principles.quote: Ruby's entire premise is "programmer happiness": that writing code should be a joy.

principles.text: Hiding bad syntax and boilerplate behind AI doesn't remove the mess; fix the language and ecosystem instead.
principles.quote: Only it's like cleaning your room by stuffing the mess under the bed — it doesn't make it go away!

principles.text: Code should read close to English and favor the human reader over the machine's strictness.
principles.quote: It should allow a richness of expression that serves the human reader instead of favoring the strictness preferred by the computer.

principles.text: Writing code is the enjoyable part of the job; he won't give it up to manage AI agents.
principles.quote: I've had the option to retreat up the manager ladder for most of my career, but I've steadily refused, because I really like writing Ruby! It's the most enjoyable part of the job!

principles.text: AI is a superb pair programmer for lookups and questions, but the human keeps the keyboard.
principles.quote: AI is a superb pair programmer, but I'd retire before permanently handing it the keyboard to drive the code.

sources.title: Paranoia and desperation in the AI gold rush: Slack training on private messages
sources.originalTitle: Paranoia and desperation in the AI gold rush
sources.summary: DHH reacts to Salesforce announcing it will train Slack AI models on customers' private messages and files by default, with opt-out only via a special email. He reads it as a symptom of companies so afraid of missing the AI wave that they will trample trust and privacy for any edge in the chatbot race.

principles.text: Fear of missing out on AI is driving companies to desperation, more than excitement about the opportunity.
principles.quote: I've never seen so much paranoia in technology about missing out on The Next Big Thing as with AI. Companies seem less excited about the prospects than they are petrified that its going to kill them.

principles.text: AI-race desperation justifies nothing; training on private customer data by default is a breach of trust.
principles.quote: Things are moving fast enough that we'll probably see more such flagrant transgressions of trust and privacy, if there's even a sliver of a chance that it can provide an edge in the race for a better chatbot.

principles.text: Opt-out-by-obscure-email is a hostile default for consent over private data.
principles.quote: And they're going to do so by default, lest you send them a specially formatted email to feedback@slack.com.

principles.text: Scanning confidential company conversations to catch up in AI is a bad trade, and AI-autocompleted corporate text is slop.
principles.quote: All you have to do is edit out, say, Asana in your layoff completion, and voila, you'll have saved at least 8 minutes typing out the corporate slop yourself.

principles.text: Product decisions driven by AI KPIs at acquired products can pull teams away from their ethical compass.
principles.quote: Whether the vision of that gleams bright or dystopian probably depends on how well your inner compass is tuned to the kind of AI KPIs pushing product managers in charge of acquired chat products at large tech companies.

sources.title: DHH on promoting AI agents: from autocomplete to supervised autonomous teammates
sources.originalTitle: Promoting AI agents
sources.summary: DHH explains why terminal-based coding agents finally won him over after autocomplete left him cold. He treats agents as a team whose finished work he reviews, not a pair programmer, while staying skeptical of pure vibe coding and of claims that agents write 90% of code.

principles.text: Autocomplete-style AI left DHH cold; he wants to finish his own thoughts when coding.
principles.quote: When I code, I want to finish my own thoughts and sentences.

principles.text: Autonomous agents feel like a team: they work on their own, he reviews the outcome and guides when asked.
principles.quote: With a team of agents, they're doing their work autonomously, and I just review the final outcome, offer guidance when asked, and marvel at how this is possible at all.

principles.text: Agents became capable mainly because they were given tools beyond reasoning.
principles.quote: Partly because the models got better, but more so because we gave them the tools to take their capacity beyond pure reasoning.

principles.text: Pure vibe coding is still aspirational for professional work; supervised collaboration works today.
principles.quote: Yet pure vibe coding remains an aspirational dream for professional work for me, for now. Supervised collaboration, though, is here today.

principles.text: Claims of agents writing 90%+ of code don't hold up if you hold the line on quality and cohesion.
principles.quote: I'm nowhere close to the claims of having agents write 90%+ of the code, as I see some boast about online.

principles.text: Try current agents yourself on real work rather than tuning out the hype.
principles.quote: You gotta get in there. See where we're at now for yourself.

sources.title: Over my dead pencil: DHH on putting down the pencils and embracing coding agents
sources.originalTitle: Over my dead pencil
sources.summary: DHH follows up his Rails World keynote claim that programmers should stop writing most code by hand. He frames AI agents as fast, capable new coworkers rather than a threat, expects a boom in software as development costs fall, and says only those who refuse to collaborate with agents should worry.

principles.text: Hand-writing the vast majority of code is no longer economically viable; coding agents are good enough.
principles.quote: We're not going to write the vast majority of code by hand any longer. Coding agents have gotten so good that it's simply not an economically viable enterprise going forward to have humans typing out lines of Ruby, Rust, or C++.

principles.text: Treat AI as new coworkers who are fast and capable but still need help and sometimes make choices you disagree with.
principles.quote: It's far more like gaining some new coworkers who are exceptionally good and fast at a wide range of tasks, but still need a bit of help with some, and whose choices you might occasionally disagree with.

principles.text: Falling development costs will cause a bloom in software, so programmers who adapt have little to fear.
principles.quote: We're about to see an absolute bloom in software development as the price of development plummets and everyone realizes how much automation we still have left to do in this world.

principles.text: Skepticism about agent mistakes is fine, but refusing to collaborate with agents is not a viable career.
principles.quote: It's fine to be skeptical about the areas where our new clanker colleagues still occasionally get it wrong, but refusing collaboration is not a viable career path for almost anyone.

principles.text: Programmers who drag their feet on agents are the ones at risk; those who lean in and apply their skills to what comes next are fine.
principles.quote: I think the only programmers who have to worry about this change are those who refuse to embrace, or drag their feet on, the progress brought by the age of agents.

sources.title: The One Person Framework: Rails 7 and conceptual compression
sources.originalTitle: The One Person Framework
sources.summary: DHH presents Rails 7 as the closest realization of "The One Person Framework": a toolkit powerful enough for one individual to build a modern app and a competitive business. Conceptual compression and integrated defaults (Hotwire, import maps) let a single developer avoid the sprawling big-tech toolchain.

principles.text: A framework should be powerful enough that one person can build a modern app and a competitive business on it.
principles.quote: A toolkit so powerful that it allows a single individual to create modern applications upon which they might build a competitive business. The way it used to be.

principles.text: Conceptual compression is the engine: throw away irrelevant details so you can ship without mastering all the underlying physics.
principles.quote: The key engine powering this assault is conceptual compression. Like a video codec that throws away irrelevant details such that you might download the film in real-time rather than buffer for an hour.

principles.text: The conventional big-tech toolchain path is a trek you may not survive; don't adopt it by default.
principles.quote: The conventional path, as paved by solutions extracted from giant tech companies, is a journey akin to The Oregon Trail. You might well die of dysentery before you ever get to your destination!

principles.text: Ship integrated defaults so you don't need the whole JavaScript ecosystem inside your app.
principles.quote: which means you no longer need to run the whole JavaScript ecosystem enchilada in your Ruby app.

principles.text: Small teams and individuals can't beat giants by playing by the giants' rules.
principles.quote: You simply can't play by the same rules against an opponent exponentially stronger than you.

principles.text: The industry's drift toward ever-narrower specialisms runs opposite to the generalist, one-person ideal.
principles.quote: There are so many vested interests in the subdivision of expertise now. Specialisms are getting ever more narrow. And this is trying to go in the opposite direction.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains his shift from hand-chiseled Ruby to running parallel agents, shipping Omarchy Quattro without hand-writing its code. He covers vague prompts over specs, the shrinking payoff of beautiful code, AI pull requests in open source, Linux as the agentic OS, and fast installs as pursuit of excellence.

chunks.heading: AI as a step change: Opus 4.5 to agents that pick the route
chunks.text:
- DHH says his view changed in emotion and practice, not in principle. A year earlier he disliked autocomplete and chatbot-style AI, though he liked chat as a tutor and lookup tool. His feeling now is "100% pure unadulterated joy and optimism and amazement."
- He dates the break to Opus 4.5 in late November 2025. He tried it around the 26th and found the output "uncannily close to what I would have written." He credits the agent harness more than raw intelligence: using tools, checking its own work, and producing real output.
- Early 2026 brought sub-agents. These split a task across parallel workers, so work took a fraction of the time. He still had to drive, specifying what he wanted and auditing the result.
- By summer 2026 (Opus 5, Fable, GPT Sol), he says he describes a problem or a fuzzy idea and the model picks the route. He compares this to GPS: early GPS had people driving into harbors, and now it is trusted.
- He says that unless you can see this, you are not recognizing the gravity of the moment. In his view the real "psychosis" is believing the world is barely different. He quotes the line "decades where nothing happens and weeks where decades happen."

chunks.heading: Where agents work best: Omarchy at 100%, Basecamp harder
chunks.text:
- On Omarchy "Quattro" (shipped late August 2026) he wrote none of the shipped code by hand over roughly the last two months. He reviewed the shape of everything and the individual lines of anything critical in the model layer. He skipped much of the UI and auxiliary code.
- He calls this the black box experiment. His Typora replacement, "Omarkdown" (his name for it, a C++/Qt app), was built in about 20 minutes. He stopped using Typora within two days and has written all his essays in it since. He never looked at its C++.
- Basecamp 5 was the first 37signals product accelerated by agents, and it was harder:
  - Designers vibe-coded features around February.
  - Individually acceptable PRs, taken together, "destroyed the architecture."
  - The team had to mop it up by hand to get back to a coherent system.
- His take is that vibe coding on an existing, substantial codebase still requires a programmer if you want to keep the architecture. He adds that the average human programmer's output is also slop, with 3,000 humans through a codebase making it awful.
- He gives three reasons large established products have not visibly sped up:
  - The bottleneck is human bandwidth and communication, not implementation.
  - Many orgs are bottlenecked on ideas, vision and taste, not implementation capacity.
  - It has only been about six months. Microsoft had endless programmers for decades and still shipped mediocre software.
- To get the 10x to 100x gain, he says you must interact with agents directly, because a human intermediary is "too slow."
- He sees the innovator's dilemma at work. Big companies are tuned for a world that no longer exists, so new entrants and individuals win. His example is rewriting your own 5% of Photoshop or Premiere. He says everyone uses a different 5% of Office, and "what if we all just built our own 5%."

chunks.heading: Specification, taste and prompting: stay vague, then interact
chunks.text:
- He argues that being a programmer can be a handicap in the agent era. Prescribing the path made sense in the first agentic moment. Describing the outcome or problem now beats prescribing a solution.
- Many programmers are poor product managers, and he says "software is product management": what it should do, for whom, how it looks, what version one includes.
- On `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, he cites Boris at Anthropic: the system prompt for Opus 5 shrank by about 80%. Overly prescriptive humans actively damage the output, and he compares it to a pointy-haired boss telling programmers how to code.
- He ties this to the Agile Manifesto. People do not know what they want until they receive it, so "be as vague as you can to manifest something, then interact with the something."
- Humans are good at snap judgments. Give them three options and they pick quickly. They fall off a cliff with 22 options.
- He likes using ambiguity deliberately, as in poetry. Over-specifying makes the model follow instructions too literally. He says "if there is one programming language more beautiful than Ruby, it is the English language."
- He embraces non-determinism. The same prompt will not give the same result twice, and he finds that part of the appeal. He also sees his own writing as resembling next-token prediction with some temperature.

chunks.heading: Craft, code quality and what still matters
chunks.text:
- In Ruby he still sweats the details, but he thinks the economic payoff is "diminishing rapidly." The case for beautiful code was that humans would modify it. He calls it an open question how much that matters now.
- It still matters for the moment because tokens are scarce. A coherent architecture lets agents make the next change as cheaply as the last. Without it you get a ball of mud.
- He uses a Commodore 64 analogy: a programmer from that era teleported to 2026 would have heuristics that no longer apply.
- He is not sad about losing hand-chiseled code. He wrote it for 25 years, he does not romanticize it, and he compares the nostalgia to people who still ride horses for pleasure. He notes people still write new Game Boy games for the love of the constraints, and he mentions the Analogue/Chromatic Tetris reimplementation.
- He frames his own transition through programming having never been about `if` statements: "I became a programmer because I wanted programs." AI returned him to that.
- Agents' bash is now very good. His one complaint is early exits (precondition-or-exit chains) instead of fully expanded conditionals, which he corrects each time.
- He still acts as an editor on code shape:
  - He looks at proportions and complexity.
  - He says "it looks a little too complicated," and the agent usually simplifies. He sees this as human intuition still being needed, and compares his role to a master like da Vinci directing a studio of students.
  - Agents will say work is done, a second agent will agree, and a human nudge toward simplicity still halves the code.

chunks.heading: Workflow, tooling and model comparisons
chunks.text:
- His setup is shifting from single-threaded flow to parallel work:
  - Terminal-first, running agents in tmux-style panes, then a tool he calls "Herder" (tmux plus agent notifications).
  - Tailscale and GL.iNet Comet KVMs to put idle mini PCs in a closet onto his network.
  - He maxes out at about 16 concurrent threads, with agents producing hundreds of lines an hour versus his own roughly 20-30 lines an hour by hand.
  - He calls lines of code a stupid metric, only a shorthand for output volume.
- He still uses Neovim, mostly as a project browser and to view changes. He also tries Hunk for diffs but wants surrounding context, not just the change set.
- He types prompts rather than dictating them. He uses Omarchy's built-in Voxtype for short commands (hold F9). Lex disagrees and prefers long voice monologues.
- Model views, as of this episode:
  - Fable is best overall. Opus 5 is second.
  - GPT Sol and Grok 4.6 are strong. Grok 4.6 surprised him.
  - Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro (a smaller open-weight model) also completed the task.
- His benchmark was translating the Python `terminal-text-effects` library into Rust as a single dependency-free executable that is pixel- and frame-perfect:
  - Fable finished in under 45 minutes, plan included.
  - Startup went from 86 ms to 2 ms, execution became about 9.6x faster, and the binary is 3 MB.
  - It was later pushed to about a 46x speedup with auto-research loops.
  - Fable's per-token cost would have been about $550. Sol took about 1.5 hours at roughly $46. Grok 4.6 cost roughly $55 and DeepSeek Pro 2 hours 45 minutes at about $23. Luna and DeepSeek Flash failed.
  - It was released as the TTFX package.
- He uses Fable for planning and review and Opus for implementation. His standard process is to have one model do the work and another, such as Codex at extra-high effort, review it. GitHub Copilot review has also become useful after previously generating noise.
- He prefers Claude Code's harness (agent view, multi-agent), uses Open Code for open-weight models through Fireworks, and runs four Max subscriptions. He is annoyed that Claude reads only `CLAUDE.md` and not `AGENTS.md`, so he points each `CLAUDE.md` at `AGENTS.md`.
- Shopify's CTO ran a study tracing production incidents back to PRs. PRs reviewed by agents caused fewer production issues than human-reviewed ones, using models from about six months earlier.
- At 37signals he is experimenting with agents as co-workers inside Basecamp, assigned to-dos and cards, since asynchronous collaboration suits agents better than chat.

chunks.heading: Open source, contributions and the Omarchy plugin economy
chunks.text:
- He rejects maintainer complaints about AI pull requests. His line is that it is like complaining your "steak is too juicy and lobster too buttery."
- Most human contributors do not write tests, fill in context or double-check work. Agents do if told to, so the median agent PR beats the median human PR.
- You can say "no thank you" to an agent-written PR without hurting a human's feelings. Agents also review PRs for him, sort chaff from pearls and validate bug fixes in a VM.
- On Omarchy he has merged over 1,000 PRs in three months, with about 400 open. Many came from non-Linux-distribution programmers whose ideas would otherwise have stayed in their heads.
- Omarchy ships skills that teach any agent how to extend the OS. In about three days the plugin marketplace reached 330 plugins, which he says is faster participation than any project he has run. The calendar plugin is one example, with about 17 implementations.
- Ideas now come from models as well as humans. He says he has seen model-originated ideas so good they make him humble.
- He built Quattro to diagnose its own crashes. When an app crashes, an optional popup asks the configured agent to diagnose it, and agents have traced bugs to source lines. In one case an agent found a race condition in a package manager (mise) and emailed the maintainer a bug report on unreleased code that was already fixed in source.

chunks.heading: Omarchy Quattro: speed obsession, Linux for agents
chunks.text:
- Omarchy is a Linux distro on Arch with Hyprland. The Quattro release (version 4) is, in his words, among the best software releases of his career, despite him having hand-written the least code of any release.
- He explains the sub-60-second install:
  - His first target was 15 minutes, then 2 minutes, then 1 minute. The record is now 45 seconds.
  - He contrasts this with a Mac that needed 42 minutes of updates and a Windows Panther Lake PC that took 1 hour 35 minutes.
  - The NVMe drive tests at about 7 GB/s, so he argues there is no reason an installer should not approach hardware limits. A turbo image for the Dell XPS could install in about 12 seconds.
  - Tricks used: preloading while the user types the five setup answers, shrinking the ISO from 7.5 GB to about 5.85 GB (a slim JetBrains Mono package saved about 180 MB, and heavier ZSTD compression on the Nvidia drivers saved about 200 MB), and auto-research loops by agents.
- He compares this to McLaren shaving grams and to the W126 Mercedes: over-building for its own sake pushes a field forward, and pursuing a frivolous number can produce unexpected innovation.
- Omarchy is "opinionated" and pre-installs software (OBS, Kdenlive, Neovim, Herder, tmux, themes) by design. The name comes from "omakase," meaning the chef's choice, and he is the chef.
- Why Linux fits agents:
  - Everything is a config file or a CLI tool, and agents love the Unix philosophy.
  - Agents know the Linux source and can diagnose cryptic errors.
  - Mac is hostile to automation (for example, Raycast has no config file, and settings cannot be set up by script). Windows Subsystem for Linux is a sandbox.
- He sees an opening for the first time in roughly 40 years. Computing platforms are in play, Linus Torvalds has welcomed AI contributions, and he thinks Linux desktop growth is the most probable outcome. Dell now makes an XPS that finally competes with MacBooks. Lex received an Omarchy-loaded Dell XPS 14.
- On compatibility, he says Linux used to fail on drivers, and that persistence and a patient maintainer eventually fix this. Malleability is what makes people switch, not mimicking Windows or Mac.

chunks.heading: Employment, anxiety and advice for programmers
chunks.text:
- On job fears, he separates people who loved the mechanical act of coding from people who love building. The first group faces more risk. He says he can see more builders being needed, citing the Jevons paradox and the ATM and bank-teller example.
- He accepts that productivity means fewer people for the same job and real pain for individuals, but argues it is good for the economy and for growth. He notes it is fine to grieve for a moment.
- He thinks much of the layoff wave is overhiring from the pandemic and AI used as a convenient excuse. He also says AI will expose roles that were not productive, as in David Graeber's "Bullshit Jobs."
- His advice to young programmers:
  - Do not try to predict two model generations ahead, because that leads to "AI psychosis."
  - Focus on right now and lean in. Catching up takes about two weeks, because the frontier churns and what survives is sorted ruthlessly.
  - Seek community (open source) to counter isolation and existential dread.
- He is using the 80s as a mental anchor for optimism. He keeps a memento mori Easter egg in the Omarchy calendar showing percentage of life elapsed, and he declares he wants a normal finite life, around 90 to 100 years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A long conversation where DHH explains why Ruby's focus on programmer happiness shaped Rails, and why he defends dynamic typing, the majestic monolith and tiny teams without managers. He also covers leaving the cloud, writing code by hand versus vibe coding with AI, and open source as a gift exchange.

chunks.heading: DHH's path into programming and the Ruby aesthetic
chunks.text:
- DHH failed to learn programming twice as a kid. First try at age 6-7 was typing in magazine source code on an Amstrad 464. He didn't understand the purpose of a variable. Second try at 11-12 was EasyAMOS on the Amiga 500, where he got as far as conditionals and loops and concluded "maybe I'm not smart enough."
- It clicked on the third attempt, around age 19-20, through the web: HTML first, then ASP, then PHP. PHP gave him the first working web applications.
- He says late-'90s PHP set the bar for web developer ergonomics: write a script, FTP it to a server, and it's live. Change the file and reload. No build, no setup. He says he has chased that feeling for the rest of his career.
- Ruby was the first language he thought of as a calling. He found it through Dave Thomas and Martin Fowler, who used Ruby to explain patterns in IEEE-style magazine articles because it read like pseudo code. A proof of concept (talk to a database, pull records, format them, show an HTML page) took one weekend. He had budgeted two weeks.
- He describes Ruby as "made for my brain like a perfect tailored glove."
- He considers the web mostly forms writing to databases. Many developers are uncomfortable being "CRUD monkeys" and compensate by overcomplicating things.

chunks.heading: Why Ruby is beautiful: aesthetics over machine convenience
chunks.text:
- DHH says Ruby is built for human readers and writers even when that makes the interpreter harder to write. Its goal is programmer happiness, and none of this affects what the computer does.
- Examples he gives:
  - `5.times { ... }` iterates five times, with primitives being objects.
  - No semicolons and optional parentheses. "If the human doesn't need the additional characters, we're not just gonna put them in."
  - Predicate methods like `user.admin?`. The question mark means nothing to the computer and everything to the human.
  - Statement-first conditionals: `user.upgrade if user.admin?`, and `unless` instead of `if !`.
  - A readable initializer, `def initialize`, versus Python's `def __init__(self, ...)`, which he says offends his sensibilities.
- He says Ruby is not abbreviation-minded: `initialize` is longer than `init` but reads better, and you don't type it often.
- He contrasts Matz with James Gosling. In his reading, Gosling's Java assumes average programmers can't be trusted with sophisticated features. Matz believes in humanity's capacity to learn, trusting even a stranger to extend his classes.
- Open classes: DHH added `5.days` (returns seconds) to Number in Active Support so he can write cache expiry as `expires_in 5.days`. "A reader of Ruby could not tell the difference between the code Matz wrote and the code that I wrote."
- Ruby philosophy shows in the interactive shell, where both `exit` and `quit` work because humans pick either. Python's `exit` gives a lesson instead. Ruby accepts ambiguity; Python wants one obvious way.
- He says Ruby's first draft was about 90% of what's still used 30 years later, and no other language has copied its essence. Early Ruby was very slow, and getting it fast took hundreds of person-years.

chunks.heading: Metaprogramming, dynamic typing, and why he rejects static typing
chunks.text:
- Metaprogramming in Rails means the framework adds keywords to the language. `has_many :comments` and `belongs_to :account` look like part of Ruby but are Rails domain-specific languages. He says you can't tell his metaprogramming from Matz's keywords, with zero line noise.
- He defends dynamic typing as the essence of Ruby: "Why would you wanna turn one of the most beautiful languages into something far uglier?"
- His objections to static typing:
  - It makes metaprogramming harder. Trying to write metaprogramming in TypeScript infuriated him, and the team pulled TypeScript out of Turbo.
  - It repeats itself. `User user = new User` states "user" three times.
  - The usual benefits (autocomplete, catching calls to missing methods, fewer null errors) don't matter to him. He writes in a text editor, not an IDE, and catches logic bugs with unit and integration tests.
  - He says great tooling raises a language's tolerance for boilerplate because "you're not typing it anyway." He doesn't want that.
  - Duck typing: ask whether an object responds to a method, not whether its class has it. That underpins runtime method adding and metaprogramming.
- He says he hates TypeScript "as much as I like JavaScript" and sees only costs: extra typing, type gymnastics, people falling back to `any`. He says he's not willing to turn a dynamic language into a pretend statically typed language. He doesn't want to take TypeScript away from people who enjoy it, and tells anyone using it only because they think professionals should that "you don't have to."
- He distinguishes contexts. What's right for 10 million lines and 100,000 programmers isn't right "in my bedroom to create Basecamp." He compares using one tool for both to using a Pagani to pick up groceries at Costco.
- He says it's idiotic to claim static typing is the only way to build reliable systems, "in the face of mountains of evidence to the contrary."
- Evidence: Shopify runs on Rails, with roughly 1 million dynamic requests per second on Black Friday and about 5 million lines in a monolith. Its YJIT compiler contribution makes Ruby faster. He notes the monolith is 5 million lines; in Go or Java it could have been 25 million or more, which he says would be harder to understand.
- He says he has mellowed from the old evangelism. Programmers' brains are configured differently, so his brain suits dynamic duck-typed Ruby while others want the security of an IDE.
- He ranks his languages: Ruby first, JavaScript a distant second (he likes modern ES6 with proper classes), TypeScript nowhere. For a beginner who wants the web, he recommends Ruby (with Rails for something real), JavaScript, and Go. He uses Go for HTTP proxies and recommends writing business logic in Ruby instead.
- He identifies as a "software writer," not a software engineer. He says it fits high-level business software and that the engineer label flattens different levels of abstraction.

chunks.heading: The Rails doctrine
chunks.text:
- He wrote the Rails doctrine down (nine points, 2012) because a community that doesn't record its values drifts as new people arrive. His analogy is Chesterton's Fence.
- **Optimize for programmer happiness.** Accept trade-offs against runtime or performance in favor of beautiful code.
- **Convention over configuration.** It came from hundreds or thousands of lines of Java XML config. Foreign key naming (`post_id` vs `postID` vs `PID`) doesn't matter, so pick one and it becomes a convention. Rails hands you a finished toy, not a box of Lego for the Millennium Falcon. Programmers love the Lego box and make many decisions that don't matter.
- **The menu is omakase.** Someone chef-like decided the whole menu. He points to the JavaScript ecosystem, where about 25 ways to do the controller layer multiplied by the data layer means "no retained wisdom" and no durable skills.
- **Integrated systems / the monolith.** Rails tries to solve the whole web problem. He's been against microservices since the term appeared. Microservices solve a Netflix-scale problem; applying them to 20 programmers and 500,000 lines is "idiotic." The first rule of distributed programming is "do not distribute your programming." He hates "premature decomposition."
- Basecamp and HEY are each roughly 100,000 lines of Ruby, and Basecamp has about 420 screens. He says a single human can understand a system at that scale, and it starts breaking down beyond roughly 500,000 lines.
- He also decries splitting front end and back end as "one of the great crimes against web development." HEY shipped about 40 KB of JavaScript, versus Gmail's roughly 28 MB uncompressed (about 6 MB compressed).
- **No one paradigm.** Ruby is object-oriented at its core but borrows functional ideas (blocks, immutable strings). He says Rails is a remix of ideas from many camps. He notes functional languages struggle on the roughly 10% of problems that need mutation, and he's an "object oriented guy."
- **Exalt beautiful code.** **Provide sharp knives.** He trusts developers, like Matz does, and says "maybe you cut off a finger... you're not gonna do that again."
- **Value integrated systems.**
- **Progress over stability.** He says this is the point he'd rewrite today. Rails has been very stable (Rails 8 was nearly a no-upgrade from 7, which was nearly a no-upgrade from 6). The 2010s JavaScript churn showed him that stability matters. He says Basecamp from 2003 still runs and looks like today's Rails code.
- Active Record is the crown jewel. It follows Martin Fowler's pattern from "Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture," which he has reread many times. It turns tables into classes and rows into objects. He accepts SQL rather than hiding it, calling SQL "very humanly readable" and still worth learning ("SQL was a good thing to invest your time in learning"). Rails provides a "soft ramp that goes to infinity."
- He accepts Worse Is Better. He releases open source slightly broken to invite contributors, because people join a project they know how to fix.

chunks.heading: Rails 8, no build, and the JavaScript dark ages
chunks.text:
- No build is his rejection of the JavaScript tooling of the 2010s. He says he doesn't hate JavaScript but hated pipelines like webpack, which wouldn't compile after sitting for five minutes.
- His view of the cause:
  - Browsers had stagnated since IE5's freeze, so everyone pre-compiled their JavaScript into a dialect they wanted.
  - Huge companies like Facebook sliced web development into 15 niche roles, which injected complexity.
  - Some complexity was a necessary bridge, in his view. Browsers are now strong enough that you can write text files and serve them with no pre-processing.
- He wants to combine the '90s ease (FTP a PHP file) with modern progress. Pieter Levels (PHP, jQuery, SQLite) proves it's not nostalgia.
- He gives Chrome credit as a gift to web developers and opposes the DOJ's push to split it up. Google's Chrome kept the open web viable as a development platform, he says. He praises Ladybird as a rare independent browser engine.
- He calls GDPR cookie banners "a monument to good intentions leading straight to hell." They made the internet ugly, helped no one's privacy, and benefit only lawyers, accountants, and bureaucrats.

chunks.heading: AI, vibe coding, and learning to program
chunks.text:
- DHH uses AI in a separate window, not an agent driving his editor. He tried Cursor and Windsurf and disliked it: "I can literally feel competence draining out of my fingers."
- When he wrote Omakub's Bash with AI doing the typing, he kept asking for the same conditional syntax and wasn't learning it. His fix: type the code yourself, because "you learn with your fingers" (the guitar analogy). He prefers Claude Code in the terminal but finds it too slow and impatient-making.
- He says AI makes him a bit smarter each day when he uses it for explanations: ELI5 answers to things he'd be embarrassed to Google. Estimate: about half a percent a day, compounding. He treats it as a pair programmer, which he wouldn't tolerate from humans for more than five minutes as an introvert.
- On Ruby specifically, AI impresses him occasionally but would be told to shape up if it were a junior programmer. He is skeptical of Dario Amodei's claim that 90% of code will be AI-written by year end. He notes Tobi's Shopify memo asking teams whether a task could be done by AI before hiring.
- Ruby's high bandwidth (lots of concept per character) matters for human-AI collaboration, because both sides can read compact human-readable code.
- Programming might become like horses, a recreational skill. He says he'd feel gratitude, not regret, after decades of an economically valuable career. His own motive: the joy is in typing the code, like playing "Stairway to Heaven" yourself rather than playing a recording. If he stopped programming to manage AI he'd become "a project manager of a murder of AI crows."
- On learning: write more from scratch than you vibe code. "You're not gonna get fit by watching fitness videos." Vibe coding gives "empty calories." If you can only vibe code, you're not a programmer. He compares it to Excel making accountants into model builders, which he finds wonderful but not programming.
- On skill: he rejects the idea that you can be a good editor without being a good doer. Editing is the reward of being a good writer. He doesn't buy prompt-engineering wizards, and thinks the real promise of AI is that messy natural language works. Today, vibe coding falls apart on real products, creating a whack-a-mole where fixing one thing breaks five (the same mistake junior programmers make).
- On the future: "nobody fucking knows anything." He cites VR (Lawnmower Man in '95, still not here), airplanes (huge progress to the 747, then flat), and COBOL still running Social Security. He advises being content with all outcomes.

chunks.heading: Small teams, no managers, and 37signals' way of working
chunks.text:
- Default team size at 37signals is two: one programmer, one designer, one feature. Small teams "just do." No roadmap argument, no 18-month plan, just build something and see if it's good. He says you know more about the next step when you're one step behind than when you plan ahead.
- The first version of Basecamp took him about 400 hours in 2004. At the time Jason paid him $15 then $25 an hour. The whole company was four people. He says you can't build Basecamp with a thousand-person team. "You will build the kind of software that a thousand people builds."
- Managers: he tried hiring engineering managers for a couple of years, concluded he was right, and went back. He argues feedback on work needs someone better at your craft than you, which middle managers aren't. Programmers who become managers lose touch fast. Meetings are toxic and he'd rather leave people alone for long uninterrupted blocks. He calls manager, lawyer and similar roles services to call in occasionally.
- He cites Quake II (id Software): about eight designers and programmers, no managers.
- The company stayed bootstrapped. No venture capital because once you take other people's money, they want a huge return and the enterprise-sales playbook follows. Jeff Bezos bought secondary shares from Jason and DHH, with 100% going to them personally and nothing to the company. DHH says it acted as "a vaccine" against taking VC and a vote of confidence. He now regrets having taken that vote of confidence for granted.
- Finance: 37signals went almost 19 years without a head of finance. A sales-tax nexus mistake across US states cost about two years and $5 million in settlements before they hired one. They once had a full-time data analytics person for 10 years, then chose an accountant over analytics.
- Work rhythm: 40 hours a week is "a ton if you don't piss it away." Remote work lets him close the door for six hours. Kids made his schedule stricter (roughly 9 to 5:30) without changing his total hours. He says overwork claims of 80 to 100 hours are padded with fluff.
- His partnership with Jason Fried lasts because each trusts the other's area (technology vs design/product). They argue about ideas, not people, spend little direct time together (maybe two hours a week), and follow "disagree and commit," which he credits to Bezos.
- He says small is not a stepping stone. "Mojito Island is a mirage"; flow research (Csikszentmihalyi) shows peak happiness comes from stretching your skills, not retiring. He doesn't want to be the best in the world at one thing, just the top 5% at several.

chunks.heading: Cloud exit, owning hardware, and home labbing
chunks.text:
- 37signals left the cloud. The AWS bill peaked at about $3.2-3.4 million a year. Realization in early 2023: servers had gotten much faster, so costs should fall, but his bills rose.
- The cloud pitch of easier, cheaper, faster he judged mostly false. AWS isn't easier now (IAM is "hella complicated"), isn't cheaper, and only speed held true. AWS runs at roughly 40% margins, which undercuts the "competitor's margin is my opportunity" idea.
- The move: in just over six months, seven major applications (compute, caching, databases, workers) went onto new Dell servers in a professionally managed colocation data center. They hired no extra staff. White-glove remote hands (Summit, previously Deft) swap parts, so "it's not that different" from the cloud's view.
- Savings: cut infrastructure spend by half to two-thirds. They projected about $10 million over five years. They kept S3 on a four-year contract for petabytes of files because discounts require long commitments.
- His reasoning: it's cheaper to own what you use for years than rent it. He cites the internet's distributed design (DARPA) and notes outages like US-East-1 take down large parts of the net. Modern CPUs jumped again after TSMC and Apple pushed process technology, so servers are exciting again.
- His next experiment is home labbing: running server hardware in his apartment with a 5-gigabit connection. He notes that when Basecamp ran on a single box in 2004, a 100 Mbps link sufficed.
- He admits the argument against it: someone said "imagine losing to Jira but boasting that you have a couple million dollars per year." His reply: saving $2 million a year matters, an inefficient business is "a splinter in my brain," and opportunity cost isn't ignored but doesn't justify indifference to cost.

chunks.heading: Open source, WordPress, and Apple's 30%
chunks.text:
- Open source philosophy: build it primarily for yourself; users aren't customers. Early on he put a slide saying "fuck you" in answer to demands like "unless you implement an Oracle adapter this is always a toy." Open source is a gift exchange, not a vendor relationship, and walking away is allowed. He argues there's no funding crisis and that people wanting money should sell software or get hired by a company that does open source.
- He prefers the MIT license for being short and clear, and dislikes GPL's demand for code.
- WordPress: he criticized Matt Mullenweg's conflict with WP Engine. You can't give away a gift and then demand a share once the user succeeds, he says. Licenses define the obligations on both sides, and violating them "upends decades of open source licensees and the essential de facto case law." He says Matt should drop it, and that the grab destroyed value (trust) rather than capturing "easy money."
- Apple: when HEY launched in 2020 (one week before WWDC), Apple blocked updates unless HEY used in-app payment with a 30% cut. DHH refused: "I will burn this business down before I hand over 30% of it to Apple." Public pressure produced a truce with a dummy-account workaround.
- He credits Epic and Tim Sweeney (over $100 million in legal fees, by DHH's account) for the ruling that lets apps link out to web payments. 37signals plans new HEY apps that take payment on the web, giving a direct billing relationship that works across platforms.
- He says Apple's toll booth soured his 20 years of evangelism, and that he lost Apple partly over the Vision Pro, whose lack of developer goodwill hurt. He now runs Linux (Ubuntu with his Omakub setup), Neovim with LazyVim, and a Lofree Flow84 keyboard. He keeps his Apple 6K XDR monitor and a Logitech MX3 mouse. He says Linux is closer to what he deploys on and a fresh machine takes about 30 minutes to set up. Switching virtual desktops on Linux is nearly instant, unlike macOS's animation.

chunks.heading: Priorities, flow, hiring, and racing
chunks.text:
- Hiring: he judges work, not resumes. Candidates need a good cover letter (he works remotely, so writing matters) and a real programming test that mimics how the team works. He says the capacity to evaluate work products is a superpower, which he compares to Elon Musk and Steve Jobs pushing for simplification while knowing enough to be credible.
- Gut over analytics: the upcoming book with Jason Fried is about trusting your gut when you don't know what you're doing upfront. "Inspiration is perishable" (the last essay in "Rework").
- Family: he says his three boys and wife matter more than all his work. He has logged over 1,000 hours of Fortnite with his kids, and is taking up go-karting with his oldest. He thinks the Coco Chanel line applies: the best things in life are free, the second best are very expensive. He wants to be content with all outcomes and recommends people treat inspiration as a thing to follow.
- Racing: he got his license at 25 (Danish car taxes were over 200%). A friend took him to a track in Chicago in about 2007, he drove a single-seat Mazda race car, and he got hooked. He raced seriously from 2009, reached Le Mans in 2012, and won his class at Le Mans in 2014. He drives in LMP2 as a gentleman driver alongside a professional co-driver. Flow is nearly guaranteed in a race car because it takes 100% of his brain, unlike programming flow, which is a lottery. Driving at the edge of adhesion balances danger and skill. A key mistake at the 2024 Le Mans came in the rain.
- His car is a Pagani Zonda HH, which he says he'll never sell. His fastest speed was about 340 km/h (just over 200 mph) at Le Mans.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues Opus 4.5 on Nov 24, 2025 was the Kodak Brownie moment for programming, and that 37signals has gone "pencils down" on handwritten code. He covers native apps with Rust backends driven by agents, rethinking abstractions, CLIs over embedded chatbots, and choosing optimism.

chunks.heading: DHH's view of the AI inflection point and how it changes programming
chunks.text:
- DHH calls November 24, 2025 (Opus 4.5) "the Kodak Brownie of our era": the point where AI became accessible enough in a usable harness for many people to build software alongside a new form of intelligence. He says history books will mark it as the inflection point of the Age of Agents. For him there is "everything before November 24 and then everything after."
- He compares it to photography. Portrait painters spent months or years on a single painting, then the Brownie (c. 1900, about a dollar) democratized photography. Painters pivoted to new art (cubism, impressionism) once depicting reality perfectly was no longer economically viable. He notes his great-great-grandfather, the painter Laurits Tuxen, embraced photography himself.
- Technology advances in fits and starts. Photography barely changed for roughly 80 years, then went frictionless and reached about 2 trillion photos a year in 2026.
- He describes a trough of disillusionment from February to May 2026, when new models seemed worse and people said the exponential had stalled. It ended in June with Fable 5 and Mythos, which he says is where his AI delirium/euphoria set in. Then GPT-6 Astra arrived in September, and Deep Seek 4.1 Flash showed frontier intelligence would not stay with a few large American companies.
- His practical test of the shift: with Opus he went from "I can tell an agent to do something" to code he wanted to merge. With Fable he could hand over problems or ideas and have them solved with no direction on implementation.
- He argues no one can predict the final state, since any prediction is out of date within about 20 minutes. His recommendation is to lean in rather than take the "black pill."

chunks.heading: Productivity numbers and the 10x debate
chunks.text:
- The 10x programmer idea traces to a 1968 ACM study showing the best and worst programmers varied 5x to 30x, about 10x on average. The industry then argued about it for roughly 45 years.
- He says it is now uncontroversial that the best programmer with AI tools is about 100x the worst programmer without them. He adds, less controversially in his view, that the figure may be about 1,000x.
- His own numbers:
  - In the past 20 months he wrote half as much code as in the previous 21 years.
  - Over 21 years he wrote about 30,000 lines of production Ruby per year.
  - In August 2026 he produced 150,000 lines in one month, about 60 times his long-term average.
  - Over half his past work was Ruby; this year about 3%. He caveats that much of the new output is verbose Rust he would never tolerate in Ruby.
- He frames the bottleneck as a single question: "how do you get the most out of this intelligence explosion". Every other question sits below it.
- He compares it to his 2005 Rails demo in Brazil, where he was excited about "all the code I wasn't writing." In his view the same feeling applies now, at far larger scale.

chunks.heading: 37signals stops writing code by hand
chunks.text:
- At 37signals, about a few weeks before the talk, the team decided they are "pencils down" on handwritten code. Writing code by hand is now an exceptional state, treated like seeing a bug in Sentry: something went wrong, so fix the machine or "the factory."
- He polled the room: only about five people still wrote material amounts of code by hand weekly. He says a similar claim three months earlier would have sounded crazy, and that the claim only recognizes what is already happening.
