- A failed attempt in spring 2026 during Basecamp 5: designers vibe-coded final features and each PR looked reasonable, but 20 to 30 together left the architecture like Swiss cheese. The team reverted to manual review with programmers using agents. DHH now calls that "the wrong conclusion," because the models (Fable) were about five minutes from making it work.
- Basecamp 5 shipped agent-accelerated but still with a lot of handwritten code.
- He says he retired as a professional programmer around March 2026. He asks people to look back on 25 years of handwriting code with joy, not regret, and says handwriting code is no longer economically productive for most programmers at most companies, and by the end of 2026 will not be for virtually any.
- The new career he describes is a professional maker of things who steers intelligence. He calls English "a better programming language than Ruby": more expressive, a bit vaguer and less deterministic, but a joy.

chunks.heading: Native apps and Rust: rethinking the web-app default
chunks.text:
- 37signals is starting a new version of Hey and will stop making it a web app. His reasoning: Hey was a web app only because that was how small teams stayed productive. Maintaining six native apps was previously preposterous, which is why React Native and Hotwire Native existed, accepting a fidelity hit.
- Six native applications were kicked off about a week before the talk, and he demoed them already running. A first Windows prompt produced something not shippable; a redirected version landed 20 minutes later.
- He predicts that web apps that exist out of necessity, convenience, programmer preference, team size or resources will become native apps, because the cost of building them has fallen to nearly zero. Shopify's recent rewrite of the Shop app from React Native to native, done by about six people over a short time, is his example.
- On the backend he dislikes Rust ("the ugliest programming language invented in probably the last 40 years") but loves it if he never has to read it. Agents like Rust.
- With the frontend native and no HTML rendering, the Hey server becomes the mail server it is at its core, written in Rust. Claimed results:
  - 99% less CPU.
  - 95% less memory.
  - 10 hosts needed only for redundancy.
  - By back-of-the-envelope calculation, Hey's peak traffic could be served on a single Raspberry Pi.
- He treats Rust and C++ as black boxes he evaluates from the outside, like any business owner who commissions programmers. He says not knowing Rust is "a feature and a privilege," and warns programmers who know too much about how computers work not to be overly prescriptive. A beginner's mindset, with higher-level prompts, works better.

chunks.heading: Where Rails and Ruby still fit
chunks.text:
- The web remains valuable because it asks no one to install anything, which suits ephemeral customers. Basecamp is his example: strangers who need a file or short-term collaboration. He says Rails is well positioned for those apps and admits he does not have the answer for exactly where to draw the native versus web line.
- Rails' 25 years of convention over configuration pay off in token efficiency. The one-developer-framework focus fits the agent era, where single developers can go much further.
- Evil Martians built agent evals for the Rails Foundation, measuring implementation of features against reference apps. Agents saturated the first version at about 95% completion, so the evals were made harder. He says this elevation of tasks will keep recurring.
- He says agents also work best asynchronously: hand an agent a task like a coworker, leave, and review later, rather than waiting on a chat interface. 37signals is experimenting with directing agents from inside Basecamp (via its agent, Marie).
- He stresses that models can now be assigned outcomes or problems rather than tasks, and that this capability is only a couple of months old.

chunks.heading: Software architecture and abstractions need re-evaluation
chunks.text:
- DHH says everything we think we know about structuring codebases will have to be revisited. Abstractions, his long-time favorite tool (including naming things), "don't make quite the same sense in the age of agents."
- Reasoning: abstractions existed partly to avoid repetition. With hundreds or thousands of conscious processes mutating an app, abstractions become choke points, and the price of repetition and of keeping things in sync has dropped to near zero.
- He calls these fundamental re-evaluations of computer science with no blueprint yet, and says things like methodology, cycle length and who specifies what are all open. He compares being present now to being there when object orientation first appeared.
- Optimization is another payoff: with programmer time no longer the scarce resource, every optimization becomes affordable. His examples: his Hype presentation app is half a megabyte, while Spotify's player is 1.2 GB.

chunks.heading: CLIs over embedded chatbots, and concept search
chunks.text:
- He rejects bolting a chatbot concierge into every app: "I have my own personal butler" that can use CLIs to connect Basecamp, Hey and many other apps. His request to software makers: "If your app doesn't have a CLI, I want to see it by next Friday," and let users bring their own agent.
- The Hey CLI changed his experience of search. Elasticsearch, which Hey uses, is serviceable but does not find things when he doesn't know the keywords. Through an agent he can search by concept: he found a five-year-old email about sneakers and a podcast without remembering the company or the year.

chunks.heading: Building with agents: Omarchy and small apps
chunks.text:
- The "we can just fix everything" feeling extends to the whole computer. He credits it for Omarchy, a Linux setup he says is far superior to any computer he's used, with about $20 million raised for the effort.
- Install time progress: 3 min 33 s at last year's Rails World, 35 seconds on an AMD Strix Halo laptop (installed by Anush from AMD), and 9 seconds in the lab. He quotes Mitchell Hashimoto: "The pursuit of excellence does not need justification."
- He built several apps in C++ and Qt without knowing either well, never reading the generated code:
  - A calculator, one-shot from a single screenshot, working about 7 minutes after the prompt and pushed to the public repo about 15 minutes later, then included in a new ISO.
  - A writing app replacing iA Writer.
  - A video trimmer, now included in Omarchy.
  - Hype, a Markdown-based presentation tool, started Thursday before the keynote, built while preparing the talk, with a binary of about half a megabyte.

chunks.heading: Optimism, security and uncertainty about the future
chunks.text:
- He argues predictions about the economy and society are consistently wrong. His example: when ATMs arrived in the US in the 1950s, there was panic that about 30,000 bank tellers would lose their jobs; instead banks opened more branches and employed more tellers (about 40,000 by 2010). He cites Jevons paradox for the pattern.
- He criticizes AI researchers who see scary things in the lab and extrapolate to societal doom, comparing it to Oppenheimer being unable to predict the Cold War outcome. He asks for more optimism and less "P doom."
- He accepts that real risks exist, especially security (an agent might try bad things), but says tools can be invented in response. The example is a recent Rails CVE involving a C image library, with a quarantine/sandbox effort ("Hot Cell") presented by Mike at the conference. His line: "You have agency."
- His game-theory argument: since no one knows the future, optimism is the rational stance; if it turns out well, sadness was a waste, and if it turns out badly, you should have spent your last day cheerful.
- He expects competition as more people can program, but says Rails programmers are "the best of the best." He closes by saying kids are not weighed down by things to unlearn, and tells people to take "the optimism pill."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH rants that web development has regressed (deploys slower than 1999 FTP, brittle stacks) because we embrace complexity instead of proudly being CRUD monkeys. He argues for maximalist, end-to-end frameworks, then shows what 37signals pruned (system tests, cloud CI, Puma-dev, Docker-for-everything) and demos Omarchy, local CI and cloud exit.

chunks.heading: Rails as a "mega framework" built on the crud monkey
chunks.text:
- DHH argues the industry has regressed: in 1999 he deployed a PHP/HTML change by dragging a file via FTP, live in 5 seconds. Today teams take 30 minutes, an hour, three hours, even 8 days to deploy.
- Modern apps do the same job as in 1999 ("reading from a database and writing to a database and then formatting that output into some HTML tables") with far more moving parts, and three nines of uptime was common in '99 but is now hard despite Kubernetes, AWS and Datadog.
- Cause: big problems sliced into tiny isolated ones, so progress on each slice adds up to going backwards overall.
- Merchants of complexity exist, but they only profit because developers buy. The root cause is a psychological need to be seen as more than a crud monkey. DHH: "We have to get back to embracing happily, proudly the monkey."
- Embracing CRUD frees you to solve problems end to end. This is maximalism, not minimalism: Rails covers HTML templates, database access, routing, email, background jobs and more.
- He criticizes new frameworks for not trying to address the whole problem.
- He frames Rails as a philosophy modeled on the Pax Romana: libertas (freedom, e.g. `bundle open`, monkey patching), proprietas (ownership, sharp tools, no one dictating how), and pax duty (contributing back to the framework and open source).

chunks.heading: New in the framework: Rails 8.1 and beyond
chunks.text:
- **Markdown:** `format.md` and `render markdown:` duck-type any object to `to_markdown`, because AI prefers Markdown. A pending Writebook PR would let you download an entire book as one markdown file.
- **Lexxy editor:** Action Text's new default replaces Trix. Trix got little outside help and sat on 37signals' back burner. The new editor is built on Meta's Lexical (used by WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook; about 1.7 billion people daily). It has live syntax highlighting, pastes Markdown into WYSIWYG, and exports Markdown. It is used in Fizzy. DHH likes that Meta's team does the maintenance work.
- **House dropped:** House, the Markdown editor from last year, is not being invested in further. In Fizzy and another unannounced product they found most people don't want Markdown; they switched to Lexical.
- **Action Job continuations:** jobs can be interrupted and resumed without losing progress. Needed since leaving the cloud for Kamal: old containers are shut down within 30 seconds of a deploy, but jobs like exporting a big Basecamp account can take hours.

chunks.heading: Native frontier: offline, push and Hotwire Native
chunks.text:
- DHH says teams can't pretend native apps aren't needed. When Hey launched about four years ago, Apple "unceremoniously tried to murder us". He holds a grudge but still builds native apps because customers want them.
- **Turbo offline:** coming soon, built by Rosa. It is solved at the Turbo layer, so it helps all web apps, not just native. V1 is "cache as you go" (a visited Hey email is cached for offline). V2 is "cache as I say so" (preemptively cache, e.g. a travel folder).
- **Action Push Native:** replaces AWS Pinpoint, sending directly to Apple and Google. It is configured via a new `config/push.yml` with keys for each platform, supports silent notifications, and has run in production for a few weeks, sending millions of notifications.
- **Action Web Push:** used in Campfire, not yet extracted, and clunkier (a JavaScript dance for keys). Native push still has advantages: notifications can be pulled back, and deliverability is slightly better.
- **Campfire now free:** instead of $2.99, Campfire is free with an asterisk. He wants a community member to extract Action Web Push.
- Hotwire Native 1.3 is covered in a later keynote.

chunks.heading: Pruning: localhost, Docker for databases only, no system tests
chunks.text:
- **Localhost instead of Puma-dev:** since 2017 localhost is a secure context, so no local SSL setup or extra process is needed. Puma-dev took about six steps on Linux. 37signals now uses explicit ports (e.g. 3010 for Queen Bee). He argues each port maps to a process, so writing them down is fine and the convoluted fix isn't worth it.
- **Docker only for databases:** Docker is great for versioned services like MySQL or Redis, since apps may need different versions, but painful for development. The setup: native Ruby managed by `mise`, plus shared versioned Docker databases on set ports.
- **System tests nuked:** DHH said 10 years ago on stage that system tests were the future. Now: "It never worked. It never works. It's always brittle. It's always broken. It's always slow and it's totally not worth it." Hey had many and fought their stability. They deleted them and kept about 10 as a smoke path. He knows of no production bug they would have caught. Rails 8.1 no longer generates system tests for new controllers.

chunks.heading: Run CI locally instead of on cloud runners
chunks.text:
- The BCX (Basecamp 2) cloud test run took 10 minutes across 8 parallel projects. Hey's suite (30,000 assertions) took well over 15 minutes in a cloud run. Basecamp 3's has 13,000 assertions.
- Claim: Intel stagnated, then TSMC (via Apple and others) made local CPUs faster than rented cloud ones. Hey's suite runs in 1 minute 12 seconds on the fastest AMD chip, under 4 minutes on an M4, 2:22 on an M4 Max, 2:05 on his Framework laptop and 2:23 on the Framework desktop. Linux is about twice as fast as Mac.
- Shopify-scale suites are an exception (about 0.001% of Rails apps); most apps can run everything locally.
- "Works on my machine" is answered by pinning Ruby with `mise` and database versions with Docker.
- PRs are gated by a GitHub required sign-off: a human attests they ran the tests and they passed. DHH says trust works: programmers want to ship working software and know lying could get them fired.
- Rails 8.1 adds a DSL for declaring a local CI run (RuboCop, gem audit, tests, then sign-off).
- Fortnite renders a scene in about 8 milliseconds, yet tests take 15 minutes in the cloud. He proposes a "frame budget" for everything.

chunks.heading: Bootstrap budget and Omarchy
chunks.text:
- 37signals' bootstrap budget: from a cold machine to a change deployed in production in 15 minutes.
- Live demo: installing Omarchy (his Arch/Hyprland-based Linux distro) from a USB key on a new Framework desktop took 4:44, and a Rails blog scaffold was running in about 6.5 minutes.
- He switched to Linux about 18 months ago via Ubuntu, then fell into tiling window managers and Hyprland after a YouTube video by TJ DeVries (Typecraft). He argues computers should be fun and look like a hacker movie.
- Omarchy ships with git, mise, Docker, databases, Neovim, lazygit, Starship prompt, short aliases (`r` for rails), and git username/email pre-set from the signup form.
- 37signals also built a tailoring script so a new machine is ready quickly. Fizzy deploys in 58 seconds; Basecamp 4 takes about 4 minutes, and he promises to cut it to 3.
- His reasoning for owning the OS: "I should not have to ask Apple for permission about anything at all."

chunks.heading: Cloud exit, mini PCs and micro data centers
chunks.text:
- Campfire for the conference ran on a roughly $300 mini PC in DHH's closet. He estimates the same performance would cost $300 a month on DigitalOcean droplets and upwards of $1,200 a month on Heroku.
- 37signals runs two main data centers and added an outpost in Amsterdam for Hey.
- Plan for Fizzy: many small outposts instead of mega data centers, to cut latency. Light lag math: Earth's circumference is 40 million meters, light in fiber is about 300 million m/s, so a full circle is 137 ms in theory.
- Measured RTT: New York to LA 70 ms, New York to Sydney 220 ms. A POST needs a TLS handshake, the POST and a redirected GET, so roughly 660 to 700 ms of pure latency to Sydney. From Copenhagen: 2 ms local, 8 ms across Denmark, 17 ms to Falkenstein (Hetzner), 25 ms to Amsterdam.
- With a 150 ms POST and 75 ms GET, New York to Sydney is almost a second; Copenhagen to Copenhagen is about 200 ms. The goal is to not exceed a Formula 1 driver's reaction time (about 200 ms).
- He concedes edge computing has been "all [ __ ]" so far, but sees it as a fun challenge.

chunks.heading: Active Record Tenanting, Beamer and geo routing
chunks.text:
- Cost is in the data, not compute, so each outpost should store all data but serve only a fraction of queries. This requires splitting the single database into one database per customer.
- **Active Record Tenanting:** Mike's work, one tenant per customer database. It also helps isolation, backup and privacy.
- **Beamer:** Kevin's replicator for SQLite databases, built for tens of thousands of databases and tens of thousands of transactions per second (unlike LiteFS in scale). DHH thinks SQLite suits one database per customer.
- **Kamal Proxy geo routing:** readers are served from the nearest app server; writes go to the single dominant writer (distributed writes are not solved).
- Design rule from RFC 2616: GET should have no side effects. All writes happen on POST (other methods piggyback on it), so routing works.
- Session affinity uses a transaction ID instead of a guessed delay: after a write, the reader serves the user only once it has that transaction, otherwise a header redirects them.

chunks.heading: Closing principles
chunks.text:
- Do more end-to-end problem solving and open source; own the whole stack (computer, server, framework) so you can change anything.
- "I want libertas. I want proprietas. I want pax. I want freedom, ownership, and duty."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH launches Rails 8 as the bridge from Hello World to IPO: no build, no PaaS, and a one-person framework. He argues for invalidating stale patterns, deploying your own servers on cheap hardware, and collapsing queues, cache and cable into one SQLite/database stack.

chunks.heading: Rails 8 and the no build, no PaaS mission
chunks.text:
- DHH calls Rails 8 one of the most exciting releases since Rails 7. Its mission is a one-person framework with an on-ramp "on the freaking floor": a single developer can take a Rails app from Hello World to IPO.
- Rails 7 delivered Hello World (no build, Hotwire). Rails 8 builds the bridge to the IPO, and the first step is deployment.
- He says the goal is that Rails does not require "a commercial vendor to go to production in a way that feels reasonable and approachable". PaaS offerings become optional extras for minor use cases.
- Teams should deploy to any hardware in any configuration: cloud VM, their own computer, or "a Pi in the closet".
- Rails stays a "big tent". Apps built with React or other stacks are fine, and people can opt out of any part. The Rails 7 and 8 path is not a dictate.
- He lists the Rails 8 pieces: generated authentication, Propshaft, the Solid trifecta (Cable, Cache, Queue), Thruster, Kamal 2, and SQLite as a production database.
- He says all of it is shipping that day: Rails 8 beta, Kamal 2 final, and Solid Queue 1.0.

chunks.heading: Pattern language, context change, and cache invalidation of mental models
chunks.text:
- DHH uses the pattern-language template to judge technology: a problem, a context, a solution, and consequences. When the context changes, the pattern is invalidated.
- Before Rails 7, he felt unease about following the rest of the industry on the front end and in the cloud. He could not yet articulate why.
- Rails 7's context change was ES6 JavaScript working in the browser with no transpilation, HTTP/2 making bundling unnecessary, and import maps allowing modern code directly in the browser.
- Old patterns such as browsers only open four connections, so bundle everything and browsers are bad at JavaScript, so transpile no longer hold.
- He says developers are historically bad at naming things and cache invalidation. The cache invalidation of mental models is what he cares about most: ES6, HTTP/2 and import maps arrived years before people took advantage of them.
- Hotwire is "a pattern fit for 2024", not 2012. It was reachable only after "the necessary jungle of complexity" had been crossed.
- His haiku: "Progress is our path / Complexity builds the bridge / Simplicity waits." Complexity is a necessary ingredient of progress, but "we're done by the time we've made it simple", not by the time we've solved it.

chunks.heading: Extraction, shipping proof, and no-build at 37signals
chunks.text:
- Rails does not build speculative frameworks. It takes solutions proven in real applications "with real customers under real production pressures", packages them, and shares them.
- Hey, which he started in 2018, was where he discovered the new patterns. The launch in 2020 still used webpack, and it took about another year to move fully off it.
- DHH says Hey went 100% no-build the day before the keynote, with no JavaScript build step and no CSS pipeline. Every application 37signals has made since Hey is no-build.
- The industry argument says heavy build pipelines, bundling and tree shaking are required. His answer is "everyone must be wrong" on that premise.
- He does not want to win it by arguing. Shipping working software creates "a monument to the argument that is simply immovable". He can't say no-build doesn't work for you, but he can say "you can't claim that it doesn't work".
- His example is Tobi's yearly tweet about one million requests per second on the largest Rails app in the world, answering 20 years of Rails doesn't scale. He says: "This argument has been settled."
- Hey serves JavaScript with no source maps and no bundling, exactly as written.
- He argues minification is "one of the absolute atrocities inflicted on the open web". Saving 2-5% of overhead is not worth destroying view source as a learning platform. Adding source maps layers complexity on complexity, and "the tower will fall".
- The trigger for his interest in no-build was returning to a JavaScript project left alone for about five minutes. He could not compile it, lost half a day to Webpacker (an integration he had himself made for Rails), and concluded the model was fundamentally broken.
- He says "only the browser is forever". It runs markup and styling from 30 years ago without modification. Craigslist's 1995 design, essentially unchanged, is his example of longevity worth aspiring to.
- His rule: the more intermediaries between you and the browser you remove, the more likely your code still runs five minutes from now.
- Rails 8 assumes a modern browser. Some apps must support a longer tail of browsers, but for a new application he says you should do this.

chunks.heading: Optimizing for limited brain budget and the zero-to-one problem
chunks.text:
- DHH says "our limited monkey brains" cannot hold much. If they are spent learning a complicated build pipeline, there's little room for anything else.
- The goal is the full-stack developer who can see the whole problem and the whole solution, and keep it in their head as long as possible. Eventually that stops working. He doubts anyone can hold Shopify's five-million-line monolith in their head, but Tobi did for a long time, and that enabled the growth.
- To the objection great for the beginning, but what about when you're making billions a day, he answers that by then you can do whatever it takes because you have all the money in the world. The problem to optimize for is "how do we get to the billions".
- Rails' headline mission is to compress the complexity of modern web apps. Compressing each part into small units lets them all fit side by side, without splitting the industry into tiny slices of expertise. That kind of specialization is a billion-dollar problem, not a zero-to-one problem.
- He uses relearning Vim as his own example of something that takes brain space and has to be compressed.
- Competence is also a pleasure: "it's more fun to be competent", and it's more fun to know Linux because that's where your applications live.

chunks.heading: Leaving the cloud: pink elephants, AWS margins, and Heroku pricing
chunks.text:
- DHH says the industry cultivated a fear of touching a server, and developers became "pink elephants tied with a tiny rope of learned helplessness". The rope is tiny compared with the elephant's mass.
- He grants AWS a good origin: Amazon had huge usage spikes on certain days and idle capacity on others, so renting it out made sense for their context. Most applications don't have that context, and the insurance premium is high both in money and in complexity.
- He argues AWS's incentive is to keep developers petrified of servers. He cites roughly 40% margins for AWS against about 5% for Dell, which actually makes the computers, and calls this "a failed market" with unchallenged super-profits.
- He gives Heroku "endless accolades". It reduced deployment to git push in 2007, before most people understood containers. Rails developers owe it for getting from "Hello World" to online.
- His price comparison, said with the caveat that he's talking about software:
  - Heroku Performance-M dyno: one core, three threads, 2.5 GB RAM, $250 a month.
  - A Hetzner box he signed up for a couple of weeks earlier: 40 cores, 96 threads, 256 GB RAM, 2 TB of NVMe RAID storage, $220 a month.
  - He calls $250 for the Heroku spec "preposterous" and "offensive" in 2024, and says it implies paying about 100x more for RAM and 50x more for compute.
- On the business model: if you convince programmers they can't touch a computer, you can charge 100x. VCs see "the insecurity of developers" as a mass market.
- He uses drug patents as an analogy. He hates software patents but accepts medical patents, which pay for roughly a billion dollars of trials. Those expire after 20 years and generics arrive. He says deployment is well overdue for generics, and open source is the generic.
- He ties this to his claim that if a market opportunity is egregious enough, a Martin Shkreli-style figure appears, so the industry should fix itself first.

chunks.heading: Linux as the cure for server phobia, and Omakub
chunks.text:
- DHH's prescription for server phobia is Linux, which "runs all of our servers" and also runs on your laptop. He frames it as cognitive behavioral therapy: one small exposure at a time.
- He demoed a Framework 13 laptop running Linux. He had not used a non-Apple computer for about 20 years before this.
- He built Omakub, a "comfortable, productive, great looking" Linux setup, to lower the barrier. He says it may lead people to other discoveries, such as finally finding Vim just right.
- On the fear of hackers, he says to ignore "the pink elephant talking". Basic server security covers about 90% of the problem:
  - Put an SSH key on the box and make it the only way to authenticate.
  - Turn on the firewall with a simple UI.
  - His analogy is a locked door: attackers can jiggle the handle but can't get in.
- He wants people to level up from beginner to competent, not stay at the beginner stage forever.

chunks.heading: Rails 8 features: generated auth, Propshaft, and the Solid trifecta on SQLite
chunks.text:
- **Authentication by generation:** Rails 8 won't ship Devise or a black box. It generates the code so you must look at it and understand it. He says authenticating a user isn't worth being a pink elephant over, let alone paying someone else for. The generator gives a roughly "90% authentication system" from handcrafted templates he extracted from 37signals applications.
- **Propshaft:** a replacement for Sprockets (the asset pipeline since 2009), written on a clean sheet of paper for the modern browser context. With JavaScript shipping directly to the browser, what remains is a load path and digesting assets for far-future caching. The code is small enough to read via `bundle open propshaft`, and he says you will understand it, unlike Sprockets.
- **One database instead of many stores:** a modern app used to need separate stores for queues, caches and WebSocket routing. Databases and NVMe drives are now fast enough that RAM is not needed for most operations. NVMe drives jumped two orders of magnitude, which wasn't possible in 2009.
- **Solid trifecta:** database-backed adapters for Action Cable (Solid Cable), caching (Solid Cache) and jobs (Solid Queue), all running on one database. A new Rails 8 app gets four SQLite files: primary, cache, queue and cable. SQLite means no database process to run, just files.
- **Solid Cable:** extracted about two weeks before the talk, when his demo still needed Redis. It was built by Nick Pezza, and he says it reaches within 50% of the performance of Redis pub/sub while writing to a file.
- **Solid Cache** (from Basecamp's needs):
  - Basecamp stores 10 TB of cache for 60 days, with a 96% hit ratio. Cache lifetime was previously 17 hours.
  - Switching to it cut P95 request time from about 400 ms to about 200 ms.
  - It supports Active Record encryption, which was designed for Hey, so cached data stays encrypted.
  - Hey promises that deleted data is gone from logs, database and cache within 60 days. A 60-day cache cap backs that retention warranty. He criticizes the common "little Boolean" soft-delete.
  - Being built on Active Record means it can be sharded beyond one machine.
- **Solid Queue:** built because a new application needed "one, two, three, four, five, six, seven gems" just to process jobs, some of them private forks.
  - It works on SQLite, Postgres and MySQL, and is full-featured, so it needs no extra gems.
  - It can run attached to Puma in the default setup, or as separate job hosts via `bin/jobs` at larger scale.
  - Recurring jobs are built in, replacing cron inside containers.
  - Hey runs about 20 million jobs per day on it. Basecamp and other apps add about 80 million, for roughly 100 million a day total.
  - He says it lets you kick Redis out of the stack.

chunks.heading: Thruster and Kamal 2: container to the internet with no configuration
chunks.text:
- **Thruster:** a Go proxy in the default Rails 8 Docker image, run in front of Puma. The goal is that the container image should be directly exposable to the internet, fast and secure, with no expertise required. It provides:
  - X-Sendfile acceleration, so large file sends don't tie up Puma.
  - Caching of anything marked public via cache control.
  - Gzip compression, with Brotli planned.
  - Zero configuration by default.
  - Go was chosen because it is "better at that part", and he's happy to use it for it. In Kevin's testing on his laptop it handled 60,000 requests per second, and he says it will not be your bottleneck.
- **Kamal 2:** the missing step in his "leave the cloud" plan. Features:
  - Automatic SSL via Let's Encrypt, with no certificate knowledge needed.
  - Multiple applications on one server, so it scales down as well as up.
  - A minimal deploy YAML.
  - A new Go proxy replacing Traefik, to be faster and need zero configuration.
  - Aliases such as running a console against production.
- **The demo:** he pointed two domains (alpha and bravo) at one Hetzner server and deployed two Rails apps to it.
  - He generated a scaffold and tested it in development.
  - For production he filled in only the registry user, the server IP, and the hostname, committed to git, and ran `kamal setup`.
  - Kamal builds the Docker image, includes Thruster, runs an entry point that prepares the databases, and pushes to a registry (he is working to remove the Docker Hub step).
  - The second app used a Rails template and Tailwind.
  - The server needed only a fresh Ubuntu box, with no pre-cooking.
  - Both apps ran on the same server with auto SSL, Action Cable live updates, caching and queuing, all on SQLite.
  - He viewed logs, ran the production console and changed a record, then ran `kamal remove`. A removed app returned a 502 from the built-in proxy.
- **Compression claim:** the original Rails video took 15 minutes and didn't reach production (2005). He took two apps to production in five minutes, which he calls a compression of complexity "six times over".

chunks.heading: Next up: Action Notifier, Active Record Search, and Markdown in Action Text
chunks.text:
- **Action Notifier:** a new framework for web push notifications, so apps can avoid native clients. Campfire already uses an early version for conference chat. It handles the awkward parts: service workers, subscriptions, and reliable sending.
- **Active Record Search:** built on the same premise as the Solid libraries. He says Elasticsearch is "wonderful" but a torture for developers and operators, and most people only need to search their Active Record models. The API he showed declares searchable attributes, then calls something like `Post.search("announcement")`. The name changed from Solid Search because it isn't an adapter for another database.
- **Markdown in Action Text:** a markdown option for people who prefer it over a WYSIWYG editor, called House MD. It already powers Writebook, a free-to-download book-publishing app from 37signals.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH opens Rails World on the 20th anniversary, arguing the zero-interest era bred a productivity dark age of over-specialisation and complexity. He tours seven tools (Propshaft, Turbo 8, Strada, Solid Cache, Solid Queue, Mission Control, Kamal) that push toward simplicity and a one-person framework, with no-build JavaScript/CSS and cloud exit as through-lines.

chunks.heading: Rails World 2023 keynote: why Rails and the 20-year mindset
chunks.text:
- DHH says he has spent about half his life (he is 44) working on Rails, and the 20th anniversary leaves him "this fired up" to keep improving it.
- He treats the Rails community as a gift-swapping environment built on the ethos of the MIT license: no transactional I give you X, you owe me Y, just gifts with no strings attached.
- Code is foundational but not enough. Without understandable documentation and flattering marketing "no one's going to care."
- Rails 7.1 shipped that day. About 700 people contributed code to it (roughly 4,000 commits since Rails 7.0, almost two years earlier). Almost 7,000 people have contributed over 20 years.
- The Rails Foundation was set up as a new institution. Eight founding companies put in a million dollars: Cookpad, Fleet, GitHub, Intercom, Procore, Shopify and 37signals. Contributing members include AppSignal, Big Binary, CedarCode and Planet Argon.
- He argues the industry is young: 2003 is as far from 2023 as 1983 was from 2003. He prefers looking forward over nostalgia.

chunks.heading: Interest rates, the "productivity Dark Ages" and the pendulum swinging back
chunks.text:
- DHH ties the last decade-plus of tech to the US Federal Reserve rate, which hit zero around 2009 and stayed there about six years. In his view this produced "a sloth," an indifference to productivity and to how capable individual programmers needed to be.
- He calls the period from 2009 onward a "productivity Dark Ages": primitive tools that demanded far more labor for slightly better versions of the same things. "The low productivity tolerance was a zero interest phenomenon."
- He welcomes the pressure of rising rates (5.5% at the time), and of AI, because pressure forces people to stay productive. That was the original pitch of Rails.
- Evidence he cites: Basecamp was built in about six months by one developer and two designers part-time, and went on to generate hundreds of millions of dollars. If that was possible in 2003-2004, 2023 should allow far more, yet startup team sizes and specialization show the opposite.
- Twitter example: a former employee's account says they left Rails because of a badly designed Rails app, moved to a constellation of Java microservices, and then "nothing happened for 10 years" while thousands of people were hired. He says Airbnb followed a similar trend.
- He expects the pendulum to swing back as economic forces demand it.

chunks.heading: Full-stack and Renaissance developers versus specialization
chunks.text:
- DHH argues against ever-smaller specialization. Developers should design, install, maintain and know how to do all of it themselves.
- He cites an anecdote from the Elon Musk biography: solar panel installation was unprofitable because designers were not present during installation. Every split between who has the ideas, who implements them and who maintains them "created just inefficiencies" and cumbersome products.
- This is the same as the split between specialized developers and full-stack developers. Unless you both design and implement and feel "the pressures of all the little bolts," you get it wrong.
- He recommends Joel Spolsky's 2001 article "Don't Let Architecture Astronauts Scare You": architects solve problems they think they can solve, not useful ones. His test for the last 10 years: what new things could we do that we couldn't before?
- His ideal is Leonardo da Vinci, who merged art and engineering. He says "full stack" has aged a bit and prefers "Renaissance developers": interested in design, implementation, maintenance and deployment. Developers are writers and artists, "code poets."
- Ruby's openness supports this: `bundle open active_support` shows you that framework code is the same Ruby you write, so there is no divide between framework makers and users, and you can level up over a decade.
- "Progress is not synonymous with complexity. Complexity is a bridge we use to get to simplicity."

chunks.heading: Front end: no-build JavaScript and CSS, and Propshaft
chunks.text:
- Webpacker was added in 2019 as a bridge he hoped would not last, and it is now gone. He likes JavaScript as a "wonderful second language" but likes Ruby much more.
- esbuild was 40x to 80x faster than webpack, and he integrated it via `jsbundling-rails`. Bun is a further marginal gain and a sign of weariness with splitting everything into billions of packages.
- Import maps were a gamble in Rails 7 (experimental in Chrome in 2020, now supported everywhere). Combined with HTTP/2, there is no longer a penalty for loading many individual scripts, so bundling is unnecessary. "What is even better than esbuild, what is even better than Bun? No build... literally infinitely faster."
- HEY ships plain-text, uncompiled JavaScript with zero build, and you can view source with no source maps. This answers the old claim that you couldn't build something like Gmail as a multi-page app: HEY is an email client written that way.
- CSS is catching up. Nesting and custom properties (variables) are supported in all browsers. 37signals' new applications (the "ONCE" line) use no build step for JavaScript or CSS, with nesting and variables.
- He still recommends Tailwind CSS for those who build CSS, and praises Tailwind's standalone executable that needs no Node or Bun. 37signals does not use it because its designers prefer working directly in CSS.
- Propshaft is a clean-sheet replacement for Sprockets (introduced around 2009), built with Breno. Sprockets carries a "graveyard of experiments" (Bower, a 2011-era compressor) and roughly 35,000-40,000 lines of code. Propshaft is under 3,000 lines.
- Propshaft does two things: a load path for assets (including gems) and digest stamps for far-future expiration and caching. It has no compression and no CoffeeScript. His point: fewer lines mean far fewer issues and code people can actually understand.
- He cites the Rails Doctrine: when choosing between momentary disruption and progress, choose progress. Rails adopted WebSockets (Action Cable) on that principle.

chunks.heading: Hotwire: Turbo 8 morphing, view transitions, local storage and Strada
chunks.text:
- He says the pendulum has swung from sending JSON everywhere back to HTML. HTML is good, needs no translation step, and search engines can reach it. HTMX shares this idea.
- Turbo's layers: Turbo Drive (full body replacement, the speed win with no changes needed, "peak of developer happiness"), Turbo Frames (segments, simpler back end) and Turbo Streams (updating individual page pieces most efficiently). More responsiveness the further up the chain you go.
- Turbo 8 adds morphing, borrowed in spirit from React's virtual DOM diffing: compare the two DOMs and update only what changed. It keeps scroll position and reduces flicker, giving Turbo Drive ergonomics for cases where you'd reach for Frames or Streams. Demo: the Basecamp card table with horizontal and vertical scroll.
- He is also integrating the View Transitions API (Chrome only at the time) to make web apps feel native, "skating where the puck is going to be."
- Local storage work would let Turbo Drive cache across tabs and open a path to offline support, avoiding the pain of service workers.
- Strada, announced around late 2020 and finally shipped, is the last piece of Hotwire. It drives native controls from web markup so more work stays on the web side, and it sidesteps App Store and Google review for many updates.

chunks.heading: Back end: Solid Cache, Solid Queue and Mission Control
chunks.text:
- Storage transfer rates went from about 100 MB/s in 2009 to two orders of magnitude faster with Gen 5 SSDs. "Two orders of magnitude is the kind of change that should reset all your fundamental assumptions."
- Redis was born in 2009. He loves it (and found the right Rails abstraction in Kredis) but says he doesn't need it for as many things now.
- Solid Cache uses the database as a cache backend, since RAM is 5 to 10 times as expensive as storage. Longer cache life (months instead of days or hours) makes apps faster.
- HEY measured 0.8 ms per cache request on Redis versus 1.2 ms on Solid Cache, 50% slower on a scale that doesn't matter. Basecamp's 95th percentile dropped from about 350 ms to 250 ms after switching.
- Cache trimming is set by data retention policy, not storage limit: 60 days of fragment caching for Basecamp, matching what 37signals promises customers about deletion after cancellation. It includes encryption and built-in sharding. It was available the day before the talk.
- Solid Queue is a new job backend for Rails, built on the same idea (why use RAM for queuing?). 37signals had used Resque for 10 to 12 years and needed six gems to make it work. Sidekiq is excellent but commercial, and he says that should exist but never be required in Rails.
- Delayed Job (Toby, 15 years ago) pioneered database-backed jobs but is hard to scale. GoodJob inspired Solid Queue but is Postgres-only and built on Delayed Job. 37signals uses MySQL, and MySQL 8 gained the needed query features.
- Goal: install Rails, add a database, and get excellent caching and jobs with no further changes. It was running in production for some workloads and he hoped to release it within months and possibly make it a Rails 8 default.
- Mission Control, built for Resque and then targeting Active Job, shows and controls queues so any backend works (including Solid Queue). It came out of a Basecamp outage where they couldn't pause expensive jobs while the database needed less load.

chunks.heading: Kamal, leaving the cloud and ONCE
chunks.text:
- Rails should be free, open source and not owned by any commercial entity, end to end. Commercial vendors can offer alternatives but must not be required. He praises Heroku (2009, four years before Docker in 2013) as a pioneer whose developer economics stayed ahead for 10 years.
- Kamal was built to get 37signals off AWS and onto their own hardware (cutting an "exorbitant" cloud bill). It aims to make deploying Rails to any vanilla VM anywhere as easy as Heroku, and he says it is pretty close.
- ONCE: after 20 years of all SaaS all the time, he is "sick of it" because you don't control your data and pay recurring fees for everything. He wants software people can own and run themselves, but it must be Heroku easy to install, not 15 pages of manual.
- This has given him new love for SQLite: if the whole app runs in one process, he calls it the best database, simplifying setup, maintenance and backup. It's not just a development tool.
- Goal: Rails as a one-person framework, where one individual can make everything happen from start to end.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why his opinions on AI didn't change but the tools did: agent harnesses plus Opus 4.5 crossed his quality bar. He covers his tmux/Neovim agent workflow, senior-vs-junior leverage, small teams, designers as product people, beauty in code, and avoiding burnout.

chunks.heading: Aesthetics as a signal of correctness
chunks.text:
- DHH holds that "aesthetics is truth." When something is beautiful, it's likely to be correct, and he sees this in mathematics, physics and many other domains.
- He believes being surrounded by beautiful, well-functioning objects is a key part of human happiness. Laggy systems, touch interfaces that don't register and old COBOL systems that block simple tasks are a source of anxiety and "malaise for civilization."
- The aesthetic applies inside as well as outside. He says Steve Jobs cared about the inside of the box because people who care about the circuit board layout also sweat the user interface and the ergonomics of opening the case.
- Ruby is "the house I want to live in" because it produces the most beautiful code in his book while not being rigid about its ideology. He finds Smalltalk beautiful in its minimalism, but it is not where he wants to live.
- He wants programmers to see themselves as craftspeople who polish "until there are no splinters left."
- His favorite book on tactical programming patterns is Kent Beck's Smalltalk Best Practices (mid-1990s). He recommends it as the top book for structuring a method and a class.

chunks.heading: Why he went agent-first (and why his opinions did not change)
chunks.text:
- DHH says his opinions did not change; the circumstances and facts did. He saw early that ChatGPT's launch was an obvious marker on the timeline.
- He disliked the early tools: autocomplete and Copilot-style completion in the editor kept interrupting a thought ("Was this what you meant?"). He gave a "tap tap tap" image of that future, tied to the Homer Simpson mechanical bird that hits Enter, and did not want to be the bird.
- What he did like in that period was ChatGPT as a tutor and pair programmer that doesn't drive: paste in code or an error and ask why it works or what is wrong.
- Two things changed his view:
  - Agent harnesses (Claude Code, which got traction over the summer and fall), where the AI has tools such as bash, the terminal and the internet.
  - Opus 4.5, released around late November, which he calls the inflection point. It was the first model that "continuously and consistently" shocked him with the quality of its analysis from vague input and its output. It produced code he wanted to merge with little or no alteration, and it remembered corrections.
- His bar is high: agent code must look as good as his own, or he won't merge it, just as he wouldn't merge a junior's sloppy work. Early models could not meet that.
- He thinks the winter break is when many developers had the same shock with side projects, then returned in January and started mandating the tools.
- He calls the you're left behind unless you know everything FOMO on X nonsense. You could pick it up in about three weeks, and you can skip steps. Instead of MCPs, you can go straight to CLIs and skills.
- Toby Lutke at Shopify saw this earlier than DHH and kept sending him examples. He finds it helpful to be near people whose gaze is further up the road.
- His advice to skeptics is to sit down with a harness (he names OpenCode) and a frontier model, start with Opus, and try one of your unfinished hobby projects.

chunks.heading: His current agent workflow
chunks.text:
- Day to day he is "agent first on everything." In early November he was code-first and asked an AI for a second opinion when stuck. He now starts with the agent, reviews the draft, and edits if needed.
- Harnesses and models:
  - OpenCode is his main harness; he also uses Claude Code a little.
  - He is critical of Anthropic pulling subscription use from OpenCode and sees it as a mistake. He still says Opus is currently the best model and goes to it for hard problems.
  - He also uses Codex and Kimi K2.5.
- Layout in tmux, built into Omarchy: Neovim on the left. On the right, OpenCode running Kimi K2.5 on top and Opus in Claude Code below. A terminal strip sits at the bottom.
- Loop: he tells an agent what he wants, then jumps into Neovim and opens the lazygit diff with `space gg`. If it looks right, he commits. If not, he redirects the agent or edits the code himself.
- He does not call this being a project manager for agents. He compares it to stepping into a mech suit: "I don't just have two arms, I have 12." He has been hyper-accelerated as a programmer, with the same affinity for aesthetics when writing Ruby.
- For hard, risky changes he has Opus write a plan, then has Codex critique it, and ping-pongs the plan back and forth a couple of times before executing. He used this on dual-boot support for Omarchy (Linux next to Windows), where mistakes can corrupt partitions or boot records and where LUKS encryption on a partial drive is fiddly.
- Cheap exploration: he now gives vague, half-formed prompts to test a hunch and reverts if it isn't good, because 75 lines of code are no longer "precious." The cost of exploring a hunch has dropped "by a thousandfold."

chunks.heading: Agent-assisted PR review on Omarchy
chunks.text:
- Before the Omarchy 3.4 release he had about 250 pending PRs. He gave Claude a review URL per PR and processed 100 PRs in about 90 minutes, which he says would have been a week's work or at least days.
- Outcome breakdown:
  - About 10% merged as-is.
  - About 20% merged using Claude's own implementation, because the contributor had found a real issue but hand-rolled code he didn't want to keep. He asked Claude to "clean room" it: right problem, done right, in his style.
  - About 25% he decided he didn't want.
  - About 25% Claude flagged as maybe something here but without a good implementation.
- Claude's analysis on at least half the PRs covered areas he knew nothing about, where it was a better reviewer than he could be. The PRs had sat because he would not have put in the effort to learn the area.
- Most of Omarchy is bash, but he notes bash still has a shape and he wants it coherent with the rest of the project. Opus matched that.
- Omarchy facts: it started as a summer project during downtime at the 24 Hours of Le Mans week. It is built on Arch and Hyprland, has about 400 code contributors in just over six months, and tens of thousands of daily-driver installs. 37signals now runs Linux on most technical machines because it has its own distro.

chunks.heading: Agents, CLIs and the Unix philosophy
chunks.text:
- He installed OpenClaw on a VM and, with no tools, MCP or CLI, asked it to sign up for Fizzy. It asked for an email address, so he told it to sign up for Hey. It did both on its own. He then invited it to Basecamp, and it joined a project and introduced itself to the team. It took about seven minutes.
- He reads this as the end state: agents won't need accommodations or on-ramps. But he does not want to wait for AGI, so 37signals is building CLIs for Basecamp (releasing very soon), Hey, Fizzy and probably the legacy products.
- He sees the CLI as validating the Unix philosophy: small tools that interoperate through pipes. Basecamp, GitHub and Sentry can then be chained by an agent. His example: check errors in Sentry, write them up in Basecamp, open a GitHub PR, and comment back in Basecamp.
- Agents still need help. He says "we're not quite at AGI yet" and notes an agent-generated CLI is not right without human guidance. He is hand-tuning the Basecamp CLI.
- Token efficiency still matters for now. He argues Ruby on Rails is "one of the most token efficient ways of building web apps" and ideally suited to agent workflows, and that agents producing human-readable code still matters (he allows that may end).

chunks.heading: Small teams, designers, and how 37signals builds products
chunks.text:
- 37signals was founded in 1999. DHH joined in 2001, Basecamp was built from 2003 and released in 2004, and the company went full-time on software around a year later. Basecamp remains the biggest and best idea they have had. Hey launched in 2020 after almost two years of work and millions of dollars of R&D.
- Hey's screener: nothing reaches your inbox until you give a sender a thumbs up. A thumbs down means you never hear from them again. He says it keeps email from being a chore and removes sales drip campaigns. The screener takes a short daily pass.
- His method for major products: start with a tiny team, often one programmer and one or two designers. They find the shape and architecture first. Once something clicks, they add a few more people, and in the last ~20% everyone piles in. He says pouring people into an uncertain direction makes you slower, and "if you don't know what you want a million people is not going to build it for you."
- Designers at 37signals are not there to make a spec look pretty. They find what the spec should be, act as product managers, and also write the CSS and HTML and dabble in JavaScript and Ruby. He argues that knowing your material makes work cut "along the grain." He compares it to a jeweler knowing gold or an architect knowing load-bearing structures.
- He points to Apple's decline in native Mac craft as the same loss. Native apps now feel "synthetic" instead of "authentic." He thinks Electron gets too much hate; the problem is bad implementations, and it is just the web in a box.
- Agent acceleration is empowering designers to do the whole thing. He expects the industry to move toward 37signals' stance: smaller teams where one person builds something valuable, because communication costs shrink. He recalls that people said Basecamp with one programmer would be a toy.
- Team size: about 60 people, roughly 20 programmers, about 10 designers, 14 in customer support, 10 on operations running servers, plus HR and finance.
- Shape Up's two-month cycles no longer make sense at this pace, and he says no company has rewritten those scripts yet.

chunks.heading: What agents do to productivity, seniority and hiring
chunks.text:
- The pie is exploding: work that would never have been started is now done. His example is Jeremy's "P1" project, which optimized the fastest 1% of requests. It took the floor from about 4 ms to under 0.5 ms (a 10x gain) across about 12 PRs and 2,500 lines of code over a couple of days, as a side effort.
- On his team the same people can do much more. They already had headroom, so he plans to plow the extra capacity into more and more ambitious work, not cut staff.
- Senior vs junior:
  - Most successful agent acceleration at 37signals has come from the most senior people, who can judge whether output is safe to ship to millions of users and can run many agents in parallel.
  - He cites Amazon's reported internal conclusion that junior programmers can no longer ship agent-generated code without review, and says juniors' roles are more tenuous than six to nine months ago.
  - A 5x to 10x senior's hour is worth far more, so the trade-off between spending it with agents or teaching a junior has changed. He says it is not clear how this plays out.
- His bet is that agents eventually stop making mistakes, as self-driving did. He cites Tesla FSD going from version 13.1 to 14.2 in about 18 months. He also notes Musk's 2017 claim relied on handcoded C++ and a different approach than today's AI.
- He thinks "peak programmer" has probably passed in terms of the number needed for the same work, even though more software than ever will be produced (Jevons paradox does not rescue every programmer). Cost centers, where software is not the product, will face the most pressure.
- Value moves to figuring out what to build and for whom. He used to have a low opinion of product management, partly because implementation was the constraint. That is flipping. He says "you have to be John Carmack levels of good" to just sit and code, and you must beat what agents offer off the shelf.
- He is cautious about timing predictions and advises not planning life around a 12-month forecast. He also says he can't rule out implementation being solved by next summer.

chunks.heading: Hiring at 37signals and career advice
chunks.text:
- They have looked at tens of thousands of candidates and hired roughly 100 programmers over the company's life. He thinks the batting average is only slightly better than 50/50, even after a long process. He cites a Google paper concluding they could not predict employee outcomes from GPA, Ivy League background or LeetCode.
- Process: they discard roughly half to two-thirds of applications up front (people not addressing the job or ignoring instructions). About 20 people get a take-home test, which he defends and says is not free labor, and that the submission is not used. He says the odds are not a lottery and not equally distributed; he is often surprised how little effort most submissions put into being presentable.
- He says long-term success has been higher from people the team had worked with for two years than from open calls. Warm referral is the best path.
- His advice: be as good as you can and put in effort, even at a place you think is bad. People who worked next to you remember whether you showed up and learned. He calls the my workplace isn't worthy of my best idea cope.
- He says the 2010s notion that you can be a great programmer without caring about computers outside work hours is over, if it was ever true. He works a roughly 40-hour rolling average at 37signals but plays with computers in his free time. He expects reference checks to become more important.

chunks.heading: Staying sane and why he keeps building
chunks.text:
- He is enjoying programming more than at any time since early 2000s when he discovered Ruby ("I just discovered Ruby feel"), and sees the same in the most AI-forward programmers at 37signals.
- The risk is overwork: he says the dopamine loop from shipping is hyperactive, and the people furthest along are working harder than ever. His reminder to himself is that this is "not a limited sale" and AI will be here next month.
- His health rules:
  - He gets eight hours of sleep and doesn't use an alarm, and calls cutting sleep "such a poor trade."
  - Don't trade away exercise or diet for more agent work; it doesn't help even over three weeks.
- His drive is a love of computers. He says wealth as a "checkpoint" followed by leisure is misery, and that selling a business typically leads to three weeks on a beach and then back in the game. He is also trying not to open X first thing in the morning.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why AI isn't writing his code yet: he still cares about how code looks, uses AI mostly to learn faster, and sees no proof yet that AI lets companies cut half their programmers. He also covers cloud exit savings, small-team leverage, and open-sourcing Fizzy as marketing.

chunks.heading: Why AI isn't writing DHH's code yet
chunks.text:
- DHH says AI is not writing Basecamp or anything from scratch for him. He uses it for one-shot experiments, and they "usually stay on one shot" because once he gets into evolving something, he decides he "could have done it quicker" himself.
- At 37signals, every developer uses AI to some extent, but the Ruby code is mostly not AI-written. Where it is used for code, it is mechanical translation: "Here's something that we know exists. Can you write that in a Ruby version" gives a first draft.
- AI helps a bit more with Go code that is more boilerplate-heavy, but he says even there "it hasn't changed the game".
- He says 95% of Basecamp was typed by humans. He is skeptical of claims that "in five minutes we're not going to need any programmers", and asks which model those claims are based on (he mentions Opus 4.5 as the current one).
- He calls the quality a flickering light bulb: sometimes the AI pieces everything together in a way that astonishes him, and two seconds later it produces code he wouldn't maintain, below what a junior programmer would deliver.
- He stays open to change. He says it "could change in three months", and he is prepared to be in a mode where AI writes the majority of his code at some point. He compares his hand-written code to a modern saddle maker: a luxury, but still competitive.
- He does not enjoy being a project manager for "a gaggle of AI agents". He prefers writing code himself.

chunks.heading: Using AI to learn instead of to write
chunks.text:
- The real productivity gain for him is becoming better and smarter: getting up to speed on new APIs, techniques and concepts, and finding leads on why a bug happens.
- Omarchy, his Linux distribution, "would not have existed without AI". He would not have had the patience to trawl Linux forums to decode obscure error messages. Pasting them into an AI beat a condescending, three-year-old Stack Overflow post.
- Example: Rails switched its CSRF protection from tokens stored in cookies to a newer browser header-based feature. He asked AI which header it is and when it became available. He could have gotten this from caniuse.com or the RFCs, but the AI served it combined on a platter.
- He says the point is "using the AI to make me smarter", not just making it do things for him.
- He worries about competence draining. While writing a lot of bash for Omarchy, he caught himself asking the AI for the umpteenth time how to write an if conditional, and noticed he had not internalized it. He asks whether that is like teachers who thought calculators meant students no longer needed their times tables.
- His rule: his "moving average" of knowledge must go up and to the right. He does not need to know everything, but he should know more things in more domains at the end of each year. If not, he gets bored, then unmotivated, then does "jack diddly".

chunks.heading: Where AI genuinely paid off at 37signals
chunks.text:
- **Security bug bounty triage (HackerOne):** The volume is brutal. About 300 submissions in a quarter, of which roughly 3 were legitimate, about a 1% ratio. Verifying and dismissing the other 99 was a big time sink.
- AI processes incoming reports, checks them against the codebase, gives a verdict on whether the report is legitimate, and writes the reply. He says compressing 100 reports to review down to 5, or 10, or 20, is real productivity.
- It also writes the replies in a calm tone. He notes that human programmers find it hard not to shout obscenities at entitled, impatient researchers demanding a $5,000 bounty for a bad report, while AI calmly explains why the report is wrong.
- **Customer support:** this is harder because 90% correctness is "actually pretty bad". A wrong answer to 10% of customers can cause churn, and the lifetime value lost erases any savings. The last full test was about 18 months earlier and "didn't pan out so well". He says it is time to retry, and notes Intercom's Fin AI agent is seeing great adoption.
- **AI features inside products:** 37signals experimented with an AI command line for Fizzy cards and AI summarization, and tried several features in Basecamp. None "made the cut" as clearly better, so none shipped.
- **Shopify Sidekick:** as a Shopify board member, he calls its AI agent that helps merchants set up and optimize shops "truly incredible", with undisputable tangible benefits.
- He understands pushback against AI features, citing Apple's news and text summarization as hilariously bad. If a company of Apple's size cannot get it right, others probably cannot either.

chunks.heading: The productivity test: more with fewer people for less money
chunks.text:
- He applied the same test to AI that he applied to the cloud. 37signals left the cloud because "can we do more with fewer people for less money" never panned out. Going to the cloud often doubled team size and quadrupled invoices.
- The exit saves about $2 million a year. Cloud spend peaked at $3.4 million and is now just over $1 million in ongoing cost.
- He has not seen AI let a standard SaaS business fire half its programmers and still go faster. He is skeptical of claims that it already does.
- He uses an analogy: if one beer distributor uses a horse and buggy and another a truck, the market settles in five minutes. He has not seen that kind of gap yet with AI, though there may be a data lag.
- Even the AI companies are still hiring lots of programmers, and AGI has not arrived.
- He says people are sometimes busy with AI and feeling productive while shipping less, making less and understanding even less.
- He explains that developer productivity has always been the premise of Ruby and Rails. A single developer can build a product. Lowering the cost of experimentation gives more shots on goal, whether via Rails, AI, or both together.

chunks.heading: Launching and marketing in the age of algorithms
chunks.text:
- Launching a product has never been easier, so the market is flooded with launches. Fizzy's launch was good, but smaller than earlier ones. He attributes that partly to social algorithms: he has 500,000+ followers on X, but they work for a sharp take that goes viral, not for a "right hook" call to action. He no longer even sees his business partner Jason's tweets unless they go viral.
- Gary Vee's "jab, jab, jab, right hook" playbook no longer works, since people only see the jabs. His answer is to throw both punches at once: give something of developer value (a cool Fizzy feature, community work) and say "Fizzy, Fizzy, Fizzy" in the same post. Repetition is marketing and branding.
- Fizzy's open-source release served this strategy. It is a gift to developers wanting to learn from a production-grade Rails app, and it also gave 37signals a license to talk about Fizzy continuously.
- The blockbuster launch (teaser, trailer, big day) from "Getting Real" in 2006 is dead, because there is no shared culture of events anymore, only individualized feeds. A launch is now "a quarter or a year or even a decade", not a day.
- He now tweets more, because the algorithm handles volume, and more volume gives more seeds a chance to land.
- Omarchy's marketing: about 40 releases in the first month, which blasted feeds for around three months. People replied things like "FINE, I've heard about Omarchy for the 17th time, I'll install it." He cites the rule of thumb that you must hear a brand seven times, and Jason's "transfer of enthusiasm".
- Platforms ghost corporate accounts. Tweets from 37signals' and Basecamp's company accounts get "crickets", and even The Verge with millions of followers gets a handful of likes. Only personalities, or god-tier brands like Wendy's, get traction.
- He admits that he still does not fully know why Basecamp hit when nothing else he built has matched it, and that thousands of people still sign up every week despite many competitors. His takeaway is humility: try many things, take the hints, and do not expect a repeatable master formula.

chunks.heading: Opportunity for small teams and the open field of software
chunks.text:
- He argues competition is higher because more people can build, but attention has not left the system. He compares it to music, where complaints about Spotify coexist with an industry as big as ever.
- Opportunity is still large outside the over-picked categories. He has made about seven to-do lists in his career, and there are billions of others. He suggests software for hair salons, which often has terrible tools built decades ago.
- His own habit has been solving his own problems, since he immediately knows if the software is good. Building for other industries needs more customer interaction, which he says he is not personally cut out for, but others are.
- Fizzy is a fresh take on kanban, a concept Toyota created in the 1950s for its production line, turned into software in the early 2000s, and popularized by Trello. His point is that you can revisit a crowded domain to make something better, more fun, more lightweight, more colorful, with fewer features.
- Pricing for Fizzy: 1,000 cards free, then $20 a month. The full codebase is open source and free to self-host. It also acts as a lab for techniques going into Basecamp 5.

chunks.heading: Staying open as the market shifts
chunks.text:
- He compares this moment to the mid-to-late 90s internet and the 2007 iPhone. Unlike those, he says this shift is obvious in real time, since anyone who used the first ChatGPT could see it would rewrite the rules.
- He says you cannot roll these shifts back, and the best response is to accept uncertainty, stay curious and ride it.
- He loves computers themselves, not just as tools. He ranks this change as at least on par with going online with a modem on a Commodore 64 or Amiga.
- He tried local models again and was "shocked at how good" they have become, though not frontier level. He says the "halflife of truth" for statements about AI is now very short. He raises the possibility that open models become good enough that no one dominates, as open source did to backend software (Linux, databases, Ruby, Rails).
- On mobile, he sees Apple and Google as the two winners with full lockdown, and hopes the AI shift flips that board, though he does not trust that the outcome will be an open utopia.
- His advice for the anxiety: "your sense of wonder is your safety line".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why Rails' stable back end let Basecamp 5 evolve on a 2013 chassis, and how AI agents change his workflow. Agents produce code fast but bolt on rather than refactor, so architecture, taste and human review still matter. He sees agents opening Rails to non-programmers.

chunks.heading: Rails' backend stability and longevity
chunks.text:
- DHH calls Ruby "the most beautiful programming language that I've ever laid eyes on", and says it stays a delight whether he writes the code or watches an agent do it.
- He backs the internet as the best application platform software developers have had, because it allows distribution "without gatekeepers".
- Old Rails code looks much like today's. The 2005 "look at all the things I'm not doing" demo has controllers and models with a shape "eerily similar" to modern ones. Active Record has kept the core of its DSL since the start, with more power and polish added.
- The backend is where Rails got things right early. The front end is what changed (Hotwire, minimal build pipelines, no-build JavaScript).
- Learning Active Record was an investment he says can be "amortized over literally two decades". Most ecosystems churn so much that a 2009 JavaScript framework pays nothing back.
- The early years (about the first five or six) involved open-surgery changes, such as the Rails 2.3 to 3 transition. That is what gave the foundation its stability.
- Rails is now at the "99.999% of coverage" stage. Weekly commits mostly polish edge cases, and he sees that as an achievement.
- His stance on change: "whenever I know better, whenever I see better, I put it into Rails". He is willing to rip out legacy code if there is a better way.
- Contributions: about 6,000 to 7,000 contributors to the Rails codebase.

chunks.heading: Green-field and legacy codebases are nearly the same in Rails
chunks.text:
- 37signals maintains both. Basecamp 5 is built on the chassis of Basecamp 3, code that started in 2013.
- They still maintain the original 2003 Basecamp for thousands of customers, even though they stopped selling it to new customers in 2010.
- Fizzy is a green-field app built with their best current ideas, and its codebase is public. DHH says he compares Fizzy with the Basecamp 5 codebase and they "are not that different".
- A model file from today's Basecamp "would look absolutely right at home in Fizzy".
- Basecamp 5 probably has no complete SQL statements, because Active Record is now powerful enough that you don't drop down to SQL.
- The main architectural shift in Basecamp was "recordables" and delegated types. He says this is a nudge toward an architectural style and needs little Rails plumbing.
- Dating a Rails app: look at the front end, not the models. The tells are Webpacker, esbuild, no-build, jQuery, or which front-end framework it started with.

chunks.heading: Hardware and the front end: what modern Rails benefits from
chunks.text:
- The developer machine used to be the slow part and the server the fast part. That has flipped.
- Benchmark he ran just before the call: the entire Basecamp 5 test suite on his local AMD 395 machine, 16 physical cores, versus a fast cloud machine with 20 data-center-grade cores. Local was about twice as fast, and the suite ran in 60 seconds.
- He says this compresses auxiliary processes such as CI and build pipelines.
- The switch to no-build and real JavaScript modules ended the Webpacker era (about 2015 to 2019), when the front end was less enjoyable than the back end. He knew then it wasn't the final form.
- Passkeys are one of the modern web features Rails is working to support natively.
- Basecamp 5 has a new editor built on Meta's Lexical framework. Lexical underpins Facebook and WhatsApp. They wanted tables in the Basecamp editor for almost a decade, and the in-house Trix editor couldn't be extended for them.

chunks.heading: Likely Rails World features: Action Text with Lexxy and passkeys
chunks.text:
- Action Text will get a major upgrade. Lexxy (the Lexical-based editor) becomes the default, stays compatible with Trix, and supports migrating from Trix.
- Rich text input is "table stakes" for almost any modern web app. Trix lacked Markdown support and tables, which were deal breakers for some.
- A pull request is already open to add end-to-end passkey support to Rails.
- DHH changed his mind on passkeys. He first expected them to replace passwords entirely and saw usability problems, for example a passkey set up on an iPhone not working on a Windows PC.
- What won him over is the Fizzy approach of pairing passkeys with magic links, so you can always log in through email. His conclusion: most applications should simply have magic links and passkeys, ideally without social login.
- He finds it "crazy" that developers outsource login to a SaaS provider, and thinks this combination lowers the floor "so low that everyone can play".
- The framework should own the "delicate dance" of the passkey JavaScript behind an easy API.
- He hinted at more Rails World announcements in September.

chunks.heading: Why Rails isn't rushing to bake in agent features
chunks.text:
- On giving agents access to apps (MCP, CLIs, passkeys for agent accounts): "it's not figured out at all". MCPs were hot, then the "puck kind of skated to CLIs", and now both are discussed.
- He is not in a rush to put foundational framework concrete around agent features until the final shape is clearer.
- Example: a default AGENTS.md shipped in the last Rails version would be badly outdated after about three model jumps, and literally harmful.
- Studies of agent instruction files, as he describes them, show that telling an agent to do something it already knew how to do right makes it dumber. It fills the context window with distractions and produces worse code.
- Pace: he compares it to JavaScript churn "on turbo steroids", with a new way of working every six weeks or so. Many pin last December as the inflection point, when people started letting agents write the first code instead of using autocomplete.
- He describes GPT-5.5 as "one of those Opus 4.5 moments", with larger delegable tasks and better code.

chunks.heading: Working with agents: where they help and where they fail
chunks.text:
- Agent as explainer: while building keyboard accessibility for Basecamp 5 (sidebar navigation, a neovim-like interaction), he spent a lot of time with GPT-5.5 on JavaScript focus handling. It needed steering. When he challenged "too much code", it walked him through edge cases and timing problems, such as why a frame must be requested first.
- Designers and project managers can now write Rails code and test their hypotheses without a programmer mediating. Most of that code is not merged.
- The benefit is answering "is it good, is it fun, does it feel right" much earlier, without spending weeks of a programmer's time. He recalls writing code that Jason (Fried) rejected after a week or two of work, and says being relieved of that "coding in vain" is a big step forward.
- Process impact: Shape Up's six-week cycle was built on assumptions about implementation time that are "no longer valid". He can hardly imagine a Basecamp feature needing six weeks now.
- Quality risk, the monkey's paw curse: the agent gives you whatever you ask for. It happily writes 1,200 lines when an architectural twist could reduce it to 20.
- He quotes Kent Beck's "make the change easy, then make the easy change" and says agents aren't good at it yet. They are "eager to please as quickly as possible in as few tokens as possible", which leads to bolt-on code.
- Humans also turn codebases into a ball of mud when time pressure removes refactoring. His reservations are about development "without care towards architecture, without care towards style and beauty".
- Keep that care if you want a large system that isn't whack-a-mole where one feature creates three bugs.
- Caveat: his good experience is biased because 37signals codebases already have established patterns. He does not know how agents do in a ball of mud.
- On hallucination: it largely stopped mattering once models became agents with tools, because they run tests and linters, so hallucinations don't reach the pull request.

chunks.heading: AI adoption, ambition and cost of implementation
chunks.text:
- He calls it a "professional obligation" for every programmer to take AI seriously and spend time learning it. Skeptical stances like "it's just a parrot" are "distracting ideological dead ends".
- His own change: a year earlier he said he loved writing all his code by hand. He changed his mind once an agent could produce code of the same quality he would have written. He says AI-accelerated he is "so much more productive".
- He compares this to earlier shifts (the internet, script kiddies for PHP, early mobile apps) and says NFTs were an idea that didn't pan out. He calls AI "maybe even the biggest one".
- Cheap implementation: he wants to see many implementations (he needs about seven before he finds a shape he likes), comparing it to browsing art. He says he feels no guilt "flushing a thousand lines of code down the toilet" because agents will build another one.
- Level of ambition goes up. Example: Jeremy on the team started a project to speed up the fastest 1% of requests, lowering the floor from a couple of milliseconds to sub-millisecond. He says it matters for infrastructure spend at millions of requests, even if users can't perceive it.
- The keyboard accessibility sprint close to launch is another example. Before, he'd have scheduled it as a post-launch Shape Up cycle. Now "it's easier to let an idea turn into running code rather than a card for planning".
- Toby Lütke at Shopify saw it earlier and mandated paying attention to AI before the rest of the industry caught up.
