chunks.heading: Reliability, risk and vibe-coding with Rails
chunks.text:
- More pull requests means more incident opportunities. Analogy: self-driving cars crash at a much lower rate, but 100 times more cars still means more accidents. Going from 5 to 50 pull requests a week at half the defect rate still adds instability.
- He thinks the general feeling that systems got more unreliable with AI comes from volume and speed, not from agents being worse programmers.
- Basecamp 4 had literally 100% uptime over the last three months, with not a second of downtime. For startups he says aiming for 100% is wrong: "get to product market fit quicker" and tolerate some instability.
- Vibe-coding with Rails: he sees a class of apps (the Microsoft Access, FileMaker Pro or Excel kind) that non-programmers could build with Ruby and Rails and agents without ever looking at the code. He wouldn't do this at Basecamp scale or for "my next bank app".
- He changed the tagline on rubyonrails.org from "hello world to IPO" to "from prompt to IPO". He expects IPOs where the first app was vibe-coded to product-market fit and programmers were hired afterward.
- Rails has always flattened the curve for newcomers by handling things like security defaults, so mistakes aren't critical. He wants it "flat" rather than a "200 meter wall".
- Agent-written Rails features and contributions are welcome, but must be reviewed by qualified humans on the core and committer teams. AI slop in security reports is a nuisance that needs ways to be handled.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A panel with Matz and DHH on how agents are changing programming. DHH argues acceptance comes first, that human value is taste and joy rather than hand-typing code, and that the "slop" critique is cope. He says to trust agents the way you'd trust a senior hire, and that agents will speak Ruby to you if you ask.

chunks.heading: Matz and DHH on the AI transition and why programmers should accept it now
chunks.text:
- DHH expects that by the end of 2026 virtually all programmers will be working through agents, as Matz already does. He says Matz has coded almost entirely with Claude Code since the previous November.
- He frames the future as "probabilities, not certainties," and puts the odds on this shift as very high.
- He compares the reaction to the stages of grief. Anger is mostly past, and many people are now "bargaining with the future."
- The AI "will listen to you, but it will not change its trajectory," so the quicker people reach acceptance, the better.
- He says the other side is amazing, wonderful and fun in the same ways programming always was: you have ideas, you see them come to life, and with AI it happens much faster.
- He says there is room for nostalgia, as with every past paradigm shift (the internet, mobile), where some people chose to stay at the station.
- He argues the community has a "collective responsibility to lean in and help each other" get to acceptance.

chunks.heading: Software writer to software maker: identity, taste and what humans still add
chunks.text:
- DHH never saw himself as a "software engineer" because it sounded too serious and rigorous. He has long seen himself as a "software writer."
- He says people who never fit the engineering hat are better placed for the new role of "software maker," which is broader.
- He finds being a software maker more satisfying than being a software writer, and he loved writing: "the whole enchilada" is more satisfying than handwriting code.
- The human value added when working with agents is taste, a sense of proportion, a sense of beauty. These are the same things Rubyists cared about when writing Ruby.
- He says this makes the Ruby community "uniquely well tuned" for the moment, since what makes a good Ruby programmer makes a good agent driver.
- He says the shift is not about Rails or Ruby; it is "coming for everyone, for all domains, for all libraries, for all frameworks, for all languages." He calls the online focus on Ruby's fate "myopic."
- He rejects tribal attachment to the next language: he has no interest in becoming a Rust programmer because that role "has been abstracted away." Rust is just the most efficient tool today, and he would switch to a better one "with none of the grief" because he has no ego invested.
- He speculates agents may soon skip Rust and write machine code or assembler per platform, so portability stops mattering. "The camps are gone. We're not building new ones."

chunks.heading: Directing agents like a promoted lead: judgment, trust and egoless code
chunks.text:
- DHH compares agent work to what he did on Rails. The first version he wrote himself, the second about half, and by the sixth and seventh "barely any at all, just direction": where to go, what's in, what's out.
- He says this is a promotion into direction and judgment, and that it is "immensely satisfying" once you give it five minutes.
- He gives agents responsibility in proportion to their competence, "measured in your trust that the last pull request was handled correctly, just like you would any human."
- He judges an agent as he would a 37signals programmer: is this person ready for more responsibility, and how often do I need to check in? The more senior the agent, the less he checks in.
- If you stop reading every line, you rely on outputs and trust and accept some risk. "Who amongst us have not written poor code with bugs that could be faster?"
- He calls demanding perfection from the new intelligence while accepting it from humans "AI psychosis" and "AI delusion."
- He prefers pull requests and issues opened by agents. He says they are higher quality than any average human-produced PRs and issues he has handled on any repo he has managed.
- He treats a "slop grenade" PR as just a suggestion and does not have to catch it. If he likes the idea, his agent picks the implementation apart and returns "a beautiful implementation."
- Contributors who did not write the code feel no loss when he discards it. Past open source friction came from people attached to lines of code they had invested energy in, and he says there are few lines of his own left in the Rails codebase.
- He sees this as letting more people produce code without ego, with attachment only to ideas and better ideas.

chunks.heading: Cope versus real criticism: slop, meat proxies and the innovator's dilemma
chunks.text:
- DHH calls "90% cope" the contempt for AI shown in terms like "slop" and "meat proxy."
- He accepts the meat proxy as a real but temporary problem. If you copy and paste error messages between tools, you should let the agent read them directly: "Why are you in the loop?" The role is unfulfilling and ineffective.
- He calls the claim that agents cannot write original, high-quality, bug-free code "delusional," and "far more AI psychosis than the optimism." He says the slop label should be retired soon.
- He applies the innovator's dilemma. New technology first looks like a toy, and incumbents dismiss it. People once said Ruby "doesn't scale" and now say the same about AI, "wrong in exactly the same way."
- Whatever doesn't scale yet "is going to scale in five minutes from now," because the technology is improving at an "absolutely astronomical rate." He says not to sit as the incumbent who scoffs at toys.
- He compares the standards to self-driving cars. He cites a figure of roughly 45,000 US traffic deaths a year and says the technology he has seen is about eight times less likely to crash than the average human. Cutting deaths to an eighth would leave about 30,000 people alive.

chunks.heading: More software, not fewer jobs: against the fixed-pie view
chunks.text:
- DHH says people anxious about jobs assume a fixed number of applications and conclude fewer programmers are needed.
- He agrees that the applications that exist today will need "vastly, vastly fewer programmers" to maintain and evolve.
- He argues the world will make far more software: "That's the bloom." He points to GitHub falling over constantly as evidence of an explosion in software creation.
- He expects all those new applications to need tending, which is why he is optimistic for programmers who accept the future and take on the software maker role. He calls it "job security."
- He says this only works if you don't "hold on to the pencil so tight that you can't imagine the calculator helping you out."

chunks.heading: Languages, token efficiency and what agents are good at
chunks.text:
- DHH says current token cost and speed concerns reflect this moment only. He calls today's agents a "Commodore 64" at "1 megahertz," expecting them to run 10 times as fast next year and 100 times in two years.
- He says humans cannot intuit exponential growth, so you should watch your token bill now but treat it as short-term.
- He calls fears of being rug-pulled by Anthropic and OpenAI "economically illiterate." He cites strong open-weight models and says there is more competition than in any earlier computing shift, with leads measured "in months, if not weeks."
- On language choice, Matz cites a colleague's measurement across about 13 languages, including Ruby, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Kotlin and Go. Ruby, Python and plain JavaScript were the three best on token efficiency and time efficiency, and static typing helped neither. DHH's reaction was "told you."
- DHH says agents speak Python by default because the ML researchers who built them used it, which says nothing about what they do better. They are fluent in every language and will write Ruby if asked.
- He says the focus on pre-training and teaching labs more Ruby was a mistake. Models don't need to see much Ruby to write Ruby, because the principles of good software are universal.
- He rejects the idea that models are parrots. He calls them "incredibly creative thinkers," and says the creativity is why security is hard, since they string together attack combinations. He says defenders need agents of their own.
- He says to have agents write Ruby when you want to read code, because "Ruby is the best programming language for humans." They can then compile down to machine code for the CPU.

chunks.heading: Ruby's role going forward: readable explanation, rewrites and Spinel
chunks.text:
- DHH first took Ruby for pseudo code when reading Dave Thomas's articles in a magazine, and sees Ruby as the best language for explaining concepts. He says an agent explaining Rust code to him in Ruby would be "an amazing return to form."
- He plans to start all new web applications in Ruby on Rails. He says most Rails apps run on a single Raspberry Pi and need no more speed than that.
- If something becomes popular enough that a Rust or machine-code rewrite pays off, he would do the rewrite and can turn it back into Ruby afterwards. Code is malleable in both directions and you aren't "condemned" to Rust.
- He thinks future software may be generated on the fly, with operating systems, drivers, frameworks and languages produced like current generative game worlds. He says we need "more science fiction" to guide imagination, because our current mental models (HAL 9000, Terminator) are decades old.
- Matz describes Spinel, a Ruby compiler to native binaries he started in March (2026). It runs fast and uses much less memory, and in a realistic program he cites about 20 MB against 100 MB, roughly one fifth.
- Matz's concern is that as agents make components transparent, society will stop caring about open source foundations such as Ruby, Rails, Linux, the Rust compiler and databases. He says their sustainability still has to be worked on.

chunks.heading: What Ruby and Rails got right: agency, joy and motivation
chunks.text:
- DHH says Ruby and Rails' central contribution is agency: individual programmers going much further with efficient, pleasurable, beautiful tools.
- Ruby was for him both a practical tool for shaping web applications and an endless source of joy and motivation.
- He says the communities understand human psychology and productivity better than others, and motivation is a large part of it. Code that looks like "poetry" matters beyond whether it runs fast.
- He thanks Matz for letting the Rails community "finish the book he started," placing the application programmer on the same level as the language designer.
- Matz says Ruby's biggest contribution is showing the importance of joy, motivation and community in programming. He says joy, motivation and freedom will stay important even if Ruby does.
- DHH says humans need to find a tribe with a shared outlook but enough friction to learn from each other. He treats static versus dynamic typing, tabs versus spaces and Emacs versus Vim as disagreements that are not reasoned into or out of but come from near-bedrock presets in people's brains.
- He says we should celebrate such divisions and invent new ones, as agents write more code, to keep camaraderie.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why Ruby's aesthetics and metaprogramming made programming itself the reward, why competence and understanding beat copy-paste or AI crutches, and why open source is a meritocratic gift exchange. He defends plurality of languages, refuses static typing in Ruby, and defends no-build JavaScript.

chunks.heading: Why DHH picked Ruby and why programmer happiness drives his career
chunks.text:
- DHH first saw Ruby in articles by Martin Fowler and Dave Thomas, written in Ruby to explain programming concepts. He wondered "is this a programming language or are they just writing pseudo code because this looks too good", with no semicolons and none of the line noise of other languages.
- He had worked with PHP, Perl, some Python and a fair bit of Java before, all "fine in their own regard". Ruby gave him a desire for "Peak Aesthetics".
- Ruby taught him metaprogramming ("a program can program itself"). He says whoever teaches you that next tier of programming gets a bond with you.
- He did not care that Ruby had fewer libraries and frameworks, because he could write what he needed himself. It still had "just enough" to bootstrap from.
- Early Rails came fast: about two weeks to get HTML talking to a database, and a couple of months in "the shape of rails as it exists today was visible".
- Ruby's motto, from Matz, is "optimized for programmer happiness". DHH's analogy is photography: the best camera is the one that makes you want to go out and shoot. Ruby made him want to program, so programming itself became the reward.
- He spent years trying to persuade everyone to use Ruby for everything. He later concluded that the larger part of the superpower is helping programmers find the experience he found with Ruby, whether in PHP, Python, Elixir or something else.
- The world of web languages is small. Of all languages ever made, perhaps 50 were used seriously and 10-20 are real options for web work today. After sampling nearly all of them, he still picks Ruby. He compares other languages to a vacation: JavaScript is fine when he needs it, "then I come back to Ruby and I go like holy [ __ ] this is good to be home".
- He thinks the 2010s made it almost dirty to say you liked programming, as if passion were discriminatory against people who hate their jobs. He says it is easier if you like it, and that few programmers who built something notable lacked a passionate phase.

chunks.heading: Competence, the soft ramp, and why "I don't know anything" is a bad message
chunks.text:
- DHH rejects the "I don't know anything" dog meme and the idea that competence doesn't exist. He calls it a luxury belief: people who already have marketable skill pretend it doesn't matter, and juniors who embrace it are the ones who suffer.
- He agrees that getting started should be easy. In a Java shop he watched a new project wait a week for "XML situps" to configure a Spring web app server, and judged that a lack of sophistication, not a sign of mastery.
- The first-run experience matters most: "can you do a thing and then see a thing". Once you're in that loop you're well on the way to becoming a programmer.
- His principle is "the ramp needs to be soft but it needs to go to infinity". Day one can be knowing nothing, but a year later you shouldn't be a "copy pasta monkey" who doesn't know what you're inserting.
- He notes the JavaScript world has recreated some of the madness where early difficulty is mistaken for mastery, when it is just boilerplate.
- Pulling the thread is a transferable skill. He applies the same "I'm going to figure it out" mindset to a ventilation problem at home (identify the variables in a closed-loop system) and to race car driving (find the main levers, such as the brake trace).
- Bugs feel like magic only until you remember "there is no magic, there's just sand shoved together into silicon", so it will be logical once understood.
- He expects AI slop to make it easier to give up on understanding, and wants juniors to build stamina and perseverance to figure things out.

chunks.heading: How DHH struggled to learn programming and found the right level of abstraction
chunks.text:
- He failed to learn programming three times:
  - Around 1985-86, age five or six, he typed in code listings from a magazine and couldn't make them work.
  - Around 12 or 13 (Amos), he couldn't see the point of a variable.
  - Around 15-16, his friends were into assembler, and he balked at needing vector math for games.
- There was no Stack Overflow, Google or AI, and little help.
- It clicked around age 20 on the gaming site dailyrush.dk (around 2000), written in PHP. There were real programmers on the project to ask and code to read.
- He found his level of abstraction: concepts, words and domain models, not vector math. Ruby's English-like flexibility (such as `unless`) delighted him.
- He is "an object-oriented programmer through and through". He likes functional elements inside his objects but doesn't want to separate functions and data.
- He likes CRUD: "almost everything on the internet is some [ __ ] database getting inserts, updates, writes and deletes", and he embraces that.
- He tried Commodore 64 assembler about a year earlier and lasted about 45 minutes. He likens it to boats: he likes the image but wants to get back to shore.
- He deliberately flunked high school math by copying a friend's homework, then recognized math is unforgiving. He thinks that is fine because open source lets him trade: other contributors who love math made Rails fast. Roughly 7,000 people have contributed code to Rails.

chunks.heading: Open source is a gift exchange and a meritocracy, not a democracy
chunks.text:
- DHH says open source looks democratic but is "meritocratic". The person who does most of the work, in the best way, ends up with the most say, which is what you want.
- Every project he respects (Linux, SQLite, neovim, Ruby, Rails) has someone at the top who does the bulk of the work and sets the direction. Projects run as a "Kumbaya circle" go nowhere.
- Maintainers aren't vendors or employees. His slide at his first Rails conference talk (about three months after release) said "[ __ ] you", aimed at people demanding things like Oracle adapters. He later softened it to "PDI": please do investigate. If you want it, submit the patch, and if the code is good he'll take it and thank you.
- Users can be fired, and the fork button is always available. He is wrong often and changes his mind, but the power dynamics should still be accepted.
- Forks and tension are healthy. Git exists because Linus was evicted from BitKeeper and wrote his own.
- He wants plurality, not convergence: programmers are "weird and wonderful in very idiosyncratic ways that are incompatible", so there should be many languages and frameworks. The vim/neovim relationship (patches flow both ways) is an example.
- He doesn't want to be paid to do open source, so he has no need to "smash everything" or capture market share. He smiles when he sees Rails-isms in Elixir or Laravel.
- That plurality gives permission to be opinionated. Static typing is the hill he'll die on for Ruby: "we're not putting static typing into Ruby", since plenty of statically typed languages exist.
- The open internet lets you use any language, unlike iOS or Android, where you are a second- or third-tier citizen if you don't use the platform's language.

chunks.heading: No-build, TypeScript, and why DHH removed it from Turbo
chunks.text:
- DHH pulled TypeScript out of Turbo, a front-end library, "last year" (relative to 2024). He objects to people who show up to tell maintainers it was the wrong decision, and to PRs opened to put it back.
- He is fine with others using TypeScript but won't "ram it down my throat". He is working toward a TypeScript-free future.
- He is big on no-build, and TypeScript doesn't fit because it must be built. He would welcome browsers running TypeScript natively, which would let both camps coexist.
- Evidence he cites: hey.com runs as a million-dollar business, serving email to tens of thousands of customers, on a no-build setup for about four years. It serves roughly 120 individual JavaScript files.
- He argues it works better for caching. About 98% of code rarely changes, so small files live in cache forever. A single bundle turns over entirely when one semicolon changes, which hurts people on slow connections.
- He compares critics to someone insisting swans can't fly while watching one flap past, or noting that one black swan disproves "all swans are white".
- Cloud exit, no-build and "no thank you" to TypeScript are not trolling or engagement farming to him. They are how his company is run, and he will have to maintain them for years.

chunks.heading: Staying calm in online arguments
chunks.text:
- With age he stopped taking the bait. Discussions are public, and others are watching the "Coliseum".
- His approach is to plant seeds. People can't be convinced in real time because of the ego and community "barricades", but a good argument can land over the barricades. Months later people have said they tried it and it worked.
- He compares it to parenting: exposure to bodily fluids desensitizes you, and a trauma surgeon stays calm at a missing leg. Enough exposure makes Twitter's insults routine.
- He prefers open discourse to policed discourse, since over the past five years many "consensus" views turned out wrong. He tries to model good behavior publicly, including not calling people names even if he thinks them. He lets it run "four laps" in his head instead of tweeting it.
- He expects to hold views he thinks are idiotic today in a couple of years, and expects others to think the same of him.

chunks.heading: AI coding: a better Google, not an autocompleter
chunks.text:
- DHH enjoys AI as a superior Google, Stack Overflow and API doc, and as a pair programmer who doesn't drive. He says he enjoys projects slightly more since AI arrived.
- He doesn't want AI writing his code. While writing his Ubuntu setup project Omakub (he calls it a remix of Ubuntu as a programming environment) in bash, he used AI to translate Ruby into bash. He found himself asking the same question a fourth time and decided: "the training wheels are great when you're first learning to balance but if you keep them on forever you're never going to find balance".
- When it starts autocompleting his code he's "out". He likes the code part and likens it to wanting to move the joystick himself in Street Fighter, not watch a robot play.
- He distinguishes two phases of his career: first programming for outcomes, then, after Ruby, programming for its own sake. He is keeping the second phase.
- He is skeptical that AI will definitely get to the promised land. His analogies: Elon Musk's 2017 self-driving promises, and VR (he mentions The Lawnmower Man and Zuckerberg putting about $40 billion into it) that "five people in a dog showed up" for. He notes nobody can predict what will become reality, and even AI researchers say they don't fully understand why models work.
- He says "maybe there's five years left" of manual programming and he'll enjoy them. He'll keep programming afterward anyway, like people who program the 1 MHz Commodore 64 for the challenge.

chunks.heading: Metaprogramming moment, hiring juniors and open source as a cheat code
chunks.text:
- His decisive moment was discovering Ruby metaprogramming and building Active Record. Writing `class Person < ActiveRecord::Base` and `has_many :comments` showed that he could write DSLs at the same level of expression as the language designer. In his words, you couldn't tell his `has_many` apart from a keyword.
- He tries to scatter many "golden ticket" moments like this in Rails so people find their own early.
- Race driving as a parallel: a lap is a clock cycle, optimizing it is like micro-benchmarking, and a race team is a miniature company compressed into six months. He got a license at 25, bought an Audi S4 on arriving in the US for 37signals, and later set the goal of the 24 Hours of Le Mans. He wants "a little bit" of risk as seasoning.
- On hiring juniors: they are hired on promise, not accomplishments, so look for "sparkle".
  - Don't use AI for cover letters: he can tell, and the same phrases appear across about 50 other applicants. His company requires cover letters specific to the opening.
  - Commit to being good and to figuring things out ("not the dog that doesn't know"), and peel back the onion.
  - Good bug reports show analytical ability, especially reducing an issue to the smallest reproducible case.
  - He reads a candidate's code assuming he will maintain it in 5-10 years, so he hires people whose code he wants to look at again.
- At their last hiring round they received 1,500 applications. He notes feedback to all would take about three weeks of full-time work (5 minutes each), which is why detailed rejections aren't possible.
- Open source is "a cheat code" for juniors because he can read their actual lines of code. He looks at open source contributions before almost anything else and doesn't look at grades, though it isn't a requirement.
- He also recommends running Linux on your own laptop as a differentiator, since a Mac is now the vanilla AI wrapper of computing in web circles. He had switched to Linux full-time relatively recently.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH, Kent Beck and Martin Fowler discuss TDD after DHH's RailsConf critique. DHH separates self-testing code from TDD, objects to mock-heavy isolation that distorts architecture, and says red-green-refactor is a personal preference, not a mandate.

chunks.heading: DHH's definition of unit testing and why isolation is not required
chunks.text:
- DHH says that a lot of the trouble he saw in the Rails world around TDD came down to how people defined "unit test". The prevailing definition was: no collaborators, no database, no file system, and a whole suite fast enough to finish "in a blink of an eye".
- He cites arguments that if the entire suite takes more than 300 milliseconds it is "way too slow".
- That definition did not match what he found useful, and he says he "wasn't getting anything useful out of unit tests that weren't talking to any collaborators".
- He separates TDD from unit testing: TDD is often used to drive unit tests, but the two are not the same thing.
- His complaint is aimed at the prevailing, mock-heavy definition promoted by people currently speaking in the programming community. He says it did not come from Kent Beck or Martin Fowler.
- He describes that definition as "very moralistic" about one specific technique for reaching the shared goal.

chunks.heading: Test-induced damage: mocks and architecture
chunks.text:
- DHH argues that if you want everything in the suite to be extremely fast, you must talk to mocks and avoid touching many layers at once.
- This pushes you toward a mock-friendly architecture: repositories, hexagonal patterns, and other structures that make it easy to stub your way out of every dependency and turn every test into a unit test.
- Example in an MVC framework like Rails: stub out everything in the controller, talking to the view and the model, and call that great. He did not find it great.
- He calls this "test induced damage": the architecture suffers from the drive to unit test everything, and that drive arrives through the TDD pipe.
- Core fallacy he wants to take "a real big swing at": the idea that a system that is easier to unit test is a better-designed system. He says he saw a lot of code where this was not true. The code was not better, and it was full of "three streets of mock".
- Concrete casualty: people discarded productive patterns like Active Record because they did not fit unit tests that must run in 300 milliseconds, cannot talk to the database, and must be isolated. He says teams "had to throw out all this productive work" to worship at "the altar of a test driven design".
- Higher-priority principles than testability: is the system clear, is it understandable.
- Questions he flagged for the follow-up session: in what ways can a desire to TDD damage an architecture, and how do you evaluate whether hexagonal Rails code is really better than his approach.

chunks.heading: Red-green-refactor as a mandate rather than a preference
chunks.text:
- DHH's third concern is the red-green-refactor loop. His issue is personal: it felt "less optional more of a mandate", and he never used it for the bulk of his work.
- On some occasions the flow worked and was good. For a lot of the code he wrote, it "was just not an enjoyable way to do it" and he did not feel he got to a better place by going through it.
- He says writing the test first and watching it fail, for every piece of code before moving on, was not a natural or pleasurable flow, even after getting familiar with it.
- He contrasts brain styles. Some people think by stating the hypothesis first and filling in the implementation. He thinks by writing the code out: "it's a much more tactile experience". He has a hard time writing a test first "if I don't have to see it first".
- He compares this to why some people enjoy Python and others Ruby: people have different ways of looking at things and feeling good about them.
- When TDD flow works for him: work with "a very clear input and a very clear desired output", little environment or context, nearly algorithmic. In that case he actually likes the flow.
- Much of his work is not like that, and the question becomes what he is willing to sacrifice to get the flow. His answer is "I'm not willing to sacrifice that much". Forcing other kinds of programming into that mode leads to "nasty hacks" and "really bad tradeoffs" in code design and productivity.

chunks.heading: Confidence, programmer happiness and self-testing code
chunks.text:
- DHH ties programmer happiness (Ruby's mission) to feeling confident in your code, confident making changes, and confident it will work. He says confidence is only one part of that picture.
- He agrees with the early extreme programming rule that you are not done until you also have tests for a piece of functionality.
- The goal everyone shares: confidence about making changes and a self-tested system that runs from a single command.
- His objection is tying that goal to a single path. He is "not a fan of tying oh you deserve to be confident to TDD".
- He describes the community mistake: people believe you cannot have confidence or deliver incremental functionality with tests unless you take the "well-paved road of TDD".
- He objects to the framing in which self-testing code is just a "byproduct", "side benefit" or "leftovers" of driving design through tests. He says that framing is what made it moralistic: talks about whether you are "being professionals" turned on whether you write tests first or second.
- Martin Fowler's distinction, which DHH says he finds helpful: self-testing code (one command, whole system tested, in acceptable time, enabling refactoring with confidence) is the primary benefit, and TDD is one particular technique for reaching it. DHH says the two get conflated and need to be teased apart, and that most people "throw it all into one big pot" labeled TDD.
- He says the community needs "a reboot": TDD should not mean self-testing code plus red-green-refactor plus mocks plus unit testing everything.

chunks.heading: Mocks, trade-offs and the case against mock-heavy suites (Kent Beck and Martin Fowler's positions DHH agrees with)
chunks.text:
- DHH asks both guests how much they would sacrifice to stay in the TDD flow, including whether they use heavy mocking.
- He notes that you can reduce any work to pure input and output if you work hard enough at removing dependencies and environment. The mocking approach does exactly that. The question for him is whether the flow is worth that cost as a general case.
- He agrees with the guests' view that there are different schools of thought on isolation versus non-isolated unit tests, and that people have different preferences.
- Kent's and Martin's stated practice, which DHH accepts as consistent with his own: they use almost no mocks. If efficient testing with the real thing is hard, Kent finds another way to build a repeatable feedback loop.
- DHH did not offer his own detailed rule here beyond rejecting mock-heavy design and the unit-test-everything paradigm. His position is trade-offs: do not warp the design to make code testable.

chunks.heading: Mixed practice and where TDD fits for DHH
chunks.text:
- DHH is clear he is not against testing. He is against the claim that one flow and one style of unit test is the only legitimate way to get there.
- His stated positions across the discussion:
  - Tests alongside the code from the start are right. The early XP rule of not done until the tests exist and pass is something he is "completely on board with".
  - TDD is one path to confidence, not the path.
  - Use the TDD flow where the work is algorithmic and well specified. Do not impose it where the work is entangled with environment, data and framework.
  - Do not drive architecture from testability, since doing so produced worse code in the Rails examples he cites.
- He says the aim of the series was to clarify definitions. He did not want a "Duke out", and he found he and the guests were "at the same page" on much of the substance.
- Agenda for the next installment, as he framed it: how TDD can damage an architecture, and whether the hexagonal-style Rails code its advocates prefer is really better.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH debates Kent Beck and Martin Fowler over whether TDD pushes designs toward needless indirection. He argues that isolating every layer for fast unit tests (hexagonal, command and repository patterns) hurts clarity and cohesion, rejects internal mocking, and gives up on TDD as a universal path to good design.

chunks.heading: DHH's position: test-induced design damage from unit-test isolation
chunks.text:
- In the 2014 "Is TDD dead?" conversation with Kent Beck and Martin Fowler, DHH points to Jim Weirich's "decoupling from Rails" example as a representative case. It splits a Rails controller into a command-pattern runner, a repository for getting and saving models, and a business-model wrapper around the ActiveRecord object. Each slice can then be unit tested alone.
- He calls the damage "the creation of unnecessary indirection," meaning extra layers of complexity added so code can be unit tested without collaborators.
- Each of these patterns (command, repository, domain wrapper) is damage in his view. He says he sees applications that are worse by the end.
- He says he often sees people reach this design through mock-heavy TDD, where every collaborator is mocked out while testing one thing.
- Hello-world examples can look more complicated when wrapped like this, but he says that's not his point. His point is the unnecessary indirection and layers.

chunks.heading: Mocking rules: only externals, never internals
chunks.text:
- DHH's position is stricter than avoid three levels of mocking: he doesn't want even one degree of internal mocking.
- Mocking externals such as a payment gateway is fine.
- When testing a controller, he doesn't want to mock the model. When testing a model, he doesn't want to mock the database.
- He argues that even first-level mocking pushes a design toward injecting patterns, and that the end result is a layer between each of the other layers so each can be mocked.
- Looking at the full layered version, he says "the application is worse off for what you try to do to make it easy to unit test with mocks."

chunks.heading: The cost of more code and indirection
chunks.text:
- He argues there is a direct correlation between the size of a code base and the ease with which it can be changed: the larger it is, the harder it is to change.
- Layers of indirection must be kept in sync. In the repository-to-business-object-to-ActiveRecord chain, the repository must be updated every time there's a new interaction with the model, because every call goes through it.
- Before changing a system you must understand it. Code that fits in 10 lines is much easier to understand than 60 lines with three added layers of indirection.
- His general stance: "more code to do same things bad," unless it reflects inherent complexity in the domain. In the example, both versions accomplish the same business goal, so the extra code is pure cost.
- He says he sees a high price for every layer of indirection in understanding, maintenance and evolution.

chunks.heading: Why isolation, not architecture arguments, drives people there
chunks.text:
- DHH says tdd's red-green-refactor flow is addictive and gives a lot of dopamine. He thinks people want that feeling everywhere and apply it to all code, and unit testing works best in the traditional no-collaborator sense.
- He argues people end up with a "monstrosity" they never set out to build, reached one test at a time.
- Kent Beck argues the real driver is the desire for isolation, and DHH agrees that isolation is the driver but says people see it as a goal because of unit testing. Isolated code is easier to unit test.
- He rejects the other justifications for hexagonal-style isolation as "laughable" in the general case:
  - "I could turn this into a terminal application" is rarely going to happen, though it fits a narrow case like a flight booking system.
  - Swapping a repository for an in-memory store or a web service is a pipe dream, because the two have completely different characteristics, such as performance.
- In his view the real payoff people get is isolation for testability: mocks and fast unit tests.

chunks.heading: Coupling versus cohesion
chunks.text:
- DHH argues coupling and cohesion are often in opposition, not a pair that always go together. Getting very low coupling often damages cohesion.
- He is willing to trade high coupling for high cohesion. His example is a Rails controller that explicitly refers to the model, to authentication code and to a mailer object, with class names hardcoded.
- Those explicit dependencies aren't easily stubbed or swapped. His answer is that such code won't be easily unit testable in the fast, no-collaborator way, and he won't try.
- The payoff is a system that is easy to comprehend and that anyone can jump into and see what's going on.
- He says naming "test induced damage" points out that the drive for testability, with its pull toward isolation and low coupling, can harm other aspects of the trade-off, and he thinks that shouldn't be controversial.

chunks.heading: Testability does not always equal better design
chunks.text:
- DHH accepts that testing has sometimes told him something that improved his system, whether via test-first or test-after. He has also had the opposite happen.
- He rejects the equation easily testable, therefore better, calling it the fallacy behind many poor decisions.
- He rejects what he calls "faith-based TDD," the belief that TDD will eventually, with no evidence, lead to the right design. He says he was stuck in that loop and felt bad about himself when he couldn't reach those conclusions.
- He concludes there are cases with no answer. You can't always have both an easily testable design and a good, coherent one, and in many cases TDD takes you to the wrong place, not the better design.
- In his words, he's giving up faith in it as "a universal solution." That is why "tdd as a faith-based programming principle is dead" for him.
- He says people should stop assuming the only thing holding them back is not having thought about it long enough.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In the fourth Is TDD dead? hangout, DHH argues that TDD nudges teams toward over-testing, high test-to-code ratios and worship of testing infrastructure. He wants testing treated as a tradeoff: calibrate coverage to how much the code matters, keep the code as the top authority, and rank design clarity above measurable test metrics.

chunks.heading: Why TDD pressures lead to over-testing
chunks.text:
- DHH says TDD nudges rather than forces, and he is looking at the drawbacks because "nothing is free."
- The rule "never write a line of production code without a failing test first" sounded reasonable to him at first, but he disliked the results: teams chasing a ratio of four lines of test code per line of production code.
- He argues that large multiples of test code make behavior harder to change, because tests are still code that must be kept in sync.
- Behavior-driven style is an improvement over plain method tests. But tests only stay stable when you refactor. Most of his code changes alter behavior, and if every production line changed means four test lines changed, something's not right.
- He asks what the right ratio is, and ties it to "the nines": some code deserves five nines of coverage, other code maybe 80% or 60%. He says he hears little support for that view and a lot for "every line of production code should have a failing test."

chunks.heading: Over-testing declarative Rails code
chunks.text:
- DHH's example is ActiveRecord validations, where one declarative statement says an attribute must be present.
- He has seen people write about five lines of test code for that one statement, as a unit test, again in a functional test, and again in a system test. His reaction: "wait a minute, this is not worth it."
- The strict rule implies you cannot add an association or validation to a model without a failing test first. He is comfortable with significantly less than 100% coverage, and these declarations have not broken often enough to justify the effort.
- He wants more nuance than "every production line needs a failing test first," and thinks pressing on where the line sits for what "couldn't possibly break" is worth exploring.
- Martin Fowler's heuristics (which DHH engaged with): comment out a line, or flip an operator, and ask whether some test fails. Don't test simple getters. Assume the library works unless it is wonky.

chunks.heading: Test-to-code ratio depends on context, not a target
chunks.text:
- DHH's concern is that a test-to-code ratio is not a good goal. He sees Fowler's view as agreeing that calibration comes from experience.
- DHH says the right amount of testing differs by audience. A consulting team handing a codebase to unknown developers tends to be paranoid and bolt everything down. A product team with a stable, low-rotation team of known quality can be fine with 60% or 80% coverage that buys enough confidence to change code and catch errors.
- He says people who have handed over ten codebases and seen the results will think this is crazy, and that introducing this nuance would be a vast improvement on the staple "every line needs a failing test" claims.
- He did not defend the "every line" rule as a general discipline.

chunks.heading: Tests versus code as the authority
chunks.text:
- Documentation used to be the top of the chain of authority, and the industry rejected that. DHH hears from some quarters that tests are now at the top: read the tests first, and the code is secondary.
- He finds this as spurious as the documentation version.
- He says the code should always be the top level of authority. That is what has helped him understand systems, and it is the pressure that leaves code in a better state.
- Putting tests above code means energy flows toward the test code and away from the production code.

chunks.heading: Red-green-refactor and where attention goes
chunks.text:
- DHH's observation: the dopamine of the loop comes from flipping red to green, not from the refactor step. It ends up red, green, (parentheses, refactor), which he compares to play video games, then eat your vegetables.
- The result is under-refactoring and too little focus on code clarity and cleanest-possible code.
- This is part of the same dynamic as test-induced damage: a pressure on attention rather than a mandate.

chunks.heading: Quantifiable metrics as a honey trap
chunks.text:
- DHH notes that test speed, coverage and ratio are easy to measure, while design quality is hard to quantify and subjective, so it is tempting to chase what can be counted.
- He says these are not even secondary for him when developing a system. Near the top he puts the design and clarity of the system, and above that building something valuable to a user.
- He calls it a "honey trap" and a "siren call," and says the point of naming it is to be aware when a team is chasing the wrong things.

chunks.heading: Tooling infrastructure and Cucumber
chunks.text:
- He objects to an over-focus on the testing infrastructure, which he says glorifies the test environment to the detriment of the code itself.
- Cucumber is his main example, with RSpec to a lesser extent. He says: "I really have a reserved a special place in hell for anybody who forces other people to use cucumber."
- The one exception is a narrow, "largely imaginary" sweet spot where tests are written together with non-technical stakeholders. He thinks seeing that in the wild is rarer than catching unicorns.
- He sees all of this as symptoms of TDD being a very addictive practice that can pull people into these traps.

chunks.heading: Why the dark side of TDD gets discussed now
chunks.text:
- DHH argues the upside of TDD has been explored in immense detail over the past decade, while the downsides have barely been discussed.
- He compares it to selling Rails: when you sell something that breaks existing paradigms, you present it in the best light. Once the sale is made, you should be willing to reveal the darker side.
- He says TDD has largely won as an accepted principle in his Rails circle, so it is no longer the same battle as a decade ago, and it is hard to shift the conversation because it has brought so much good. He acknowledges that many places still fight the initial battles.
- He says Rails was designed with testing in mind, as a framework built to be testable.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In the third Is TDD Dead hangout with Kent Beck and Martin Fowler, DHH argues that TDD's success bred overconfidence and led shops to drop QA. He says the costs of testing are rarely discussed, and that real-world feedback such as on-call and customer complaints catches what green tests miss.

chunks.heading: Programmers who test their own code become overconfident and drop QA
chunks.text:
- DHH says TDD was so successful at giving programmers confidence that many shops cut their QA people. Basecamp was one: it only added someone in QA about two years before this 2014 discussion.
- He thinks this gave programmers overconfidence in the quality they can reach through testing. Some then shipped software of lower quality.
- He grants the old model was broken: throwing code over the wall to a QA department you don't care about leaves someone else cleaning up after you. He thinks the pendulum has now swung too far the other way.
- His claim: "I don't think you can work on anything of material quality and produce great software without having somebody who's not you test it."
- A non-programmer tester is valuable because they don't know how you implemented it and aren't thinking about the happy path. They are just trying to break it before users do.
- He is disappointed that exploratory testing and non-programmer testing have drifted out of the conversation.

chunks.heading: A generation that equates quality with green automated tests
chunks.text:
- DHH sees a generation of programmers who never knew the 1990s battles. They have only known programmers being responsible for quality, and they read quality as automated tests. He calls that better than what came before, but a shallow understanding of quality.
- Green tests do not show you the real problems. Users upload things you never accounted for.
- His example: nobody reasonable would upload a 2 GB file into a field, but someone will. He had only tested with 5 MB files and never accounted for the back-end processing taking 50 seconds.
- 100% coverage with bugs still shipping produces cognitive dissonance in programmers, because "this is not supposed to be possible."
- Passing your own tests can feel good and become a plateau, so programmers don't see how many levels of quality remain above it.

chunks.heading: Production feedback: customer service and being on call
chunks.text:
- DHH treats real-world feedback as part of the feedback loop, beyond the tests you write yourself. It is often ugly, and people don't want to see it.
- A worse failure is when that feedback never reaches the programmers. This happens when customer service doesn't relay "the atrocities that you've pushed out into the world."
- For about 10 years at Basecamp there was an inherent conflict. Programmers didn't want to be on call or deal with customer complaints because it dragged on their work.
- He says that is exactly the feedback loop they need, in the same way TDD once showed programmers how poor their code was.

chunks.heading: Trade-offs: testing has costs, and nobody talks about them
chunks.text:
- DHH says the TDD conversation has shown only a positive bar: faster tests, more tests, better tests. Minutes beat hours, seconds beat minutes, milliseconds beat seconds.
- He argues that chasing improvement this way blinds people to the fact that a trade-off means giving up something valuable. The cost can be time, complexity or overhead.
- When he says "testing does damage," some programmers look at him as if the idea were inconceivable. They only see more tests, better tests, faster tests.
- He says you have to understand the drawbacks and what you give up, and decide whether those things are worth giving up.

chunks.heading: Diminishing returns and criticality
chunks.text:
- DHH compares test coverage to operations uptime. At Basecamp, reaching 98.5% uptime felt impressive and reaching 99% felt like a milestone. Each step further cost exponentially more.
- Likewise, going from 80% coverage to 99% is far more expensive, and each further nine costs exponentially more again.
- He uses criticality to decide how far to go. NASA launch software or pacemaker software should chase 99.999%. Glue code between services for an exploratory web app should not chase five nines of reliability or coverage.
- He sees a contradiction in holding both positions. You cannot say "we need 100% coverage because that's our design methodology" and also say the trade-off depends on the criticality of the domain.
- He also cannot reconcile the stance that you should never write a line of production code before a failing test with a real cost/benefit trade-off. To him those two don't go together.

chunks.heading: Accepting a quality trade-off deliberately
chunks.text:
- Responding to the point that startups can now run without QA, DHH agrees that is fine "as long as" you hold the mindset that you are willfully trading some quality for speed. His version is "run fast, break things, maybe we're not going to be around tomorrow."
- The problem he sees is not the trade-off itself. It is programmers who have internalized programmer testing so completely that they don't recognise the value of anything else.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues most information-system work is closer to writing than to hard science. He says TDD optimizes for ease of testing and metrics (coverage, ratio, speed) at the cost of architecture and comprehension. He favors coarser system-level tests and aiming for clarity by reading, writing and rewriting lots of code.

chunks.heading: Why DHH rejects the "computer scientist" self-image
chunks.text:
- DHH learned to program around age 20, about 3 years before he released Rails. He argues the you must have programmed for 10 years idea is a myth: "Turned out fine."
- He tried to learn programming three or four times (typing in magazine programs at 6, AMOS and Easy AMOS, assembler after the 1993 demo party at The Gathering) and failed each time because it was framed as computer science and hard science.
- He got an F on his high school math final and says math and physics never appealed to him. He credits this with "inoculating" him against believing he would discover algorithms or make low-level breakthroughs.
- What he wanted to build was information systems: tools, to-do lists, social networks. He says most programmers do the same and are nothing like Linus working on the kernel.
- He calls the computer science prism harmful for information-system work. A Steinway maker is not a great pianist, and a great computer scientist is not automatically a great writer of information systems.
- Picking heroes who are nothing like you "sets yourself up for a bad time for the whole ride."

chunks.heading: Software development is closer to French poetry than physics
chunks.text:
- DHH says most programs read like 17th century French poetry or forensics: subjective interpretation of what someone meant, not empirical truth.
- He calls "laws" such as the Law of Demeter pseudoscience when presented as universal truths about good programs, with the only debate being professional versus amateur.
- Believing you can discover laws of programming lulls you into treating certain practices as beyond debate.
- He rejects the claim that programmers working on subjective material can sneer at other subjective fields.

chunks.heading: Software methodologies are like diets
chunks.text:
- Diet books are among the most popular books on Amazon because people want to be told how to cheat the basics. DHH says software developers behave the same way.
- Diets rest on anecdotes, tiny sample sizes and uncontrolled variables, yet each announces an absolute truth (the 10-day green smoothie cleanse, the super shred diet).
- Most people feel a bit insecure about their body at some point, and most developers feel insecure about their code. That makes them ripe for someone to say "your code is dirty, you are an amateur, I have the path to clean code."
- This "hits a lot of people right in the imposter plexus."
- The real answer is boring and hard, like diet and exercise: read a lot of code, write a lot of code, aim for clarity.

chunks.heading: Why DHH rejects test-first design (TDD)
chunks.text:
- He calls TDD "the most successful software diet of all times." He tried it multiple times, felt guilty about it for a long time, and never saw better code come out when tests drove his design.
- For years he assumed he was doing it wrong. His point: "Just because everybody's doing TDD wrong doesn't mean that there's not anything wrong with TDD."
- TDD's principles are about test-first design, not about having tests. Having tests is just a side benefit.
- The measure of quality in TDD, he says, is whether code is easier to test. He calls that a poor measure with much higher ideals available.
- Kent Beck is quoted approvingly: "I get paid for code that works, not for tests. So, my philosophy is to test as little as possible to reach a given level of confidence." DHH thinks Kent's current view is more sensible than what most TDD advocates run with.

chunks.heading: Code examples where testability makes design worse
chunks.text:
- **Person#age**: the original uses `Date.today` directly and the test uses `travel_to` to stub the date, which is easy in Ruby. The "shaped up" version injects the date as a parameter with a default of today. DHH says it is easier to test but not simpler or clearer.
- Injecting the dependency down through several methods muddies the code further. He says arguing it's only one dependency is exactly the thinking that leads down a nasty path.
- **Rails controller**: a standard controller depends on a before action for permissions, builds an object, sends an email and responds. It directs the world, so it is hard to unit test in isolation. Extracting a `PersonCreationCommand` and injecting everything makes it testable, but he asks whether it is clearer for understanding what the system does.
- He compares this to Struts 1.2, where each action was its own object. They were easy to test and produced a million objects, so the system was harder to reason about. He calls the results zombie astronaut architectures.
- Same pattern with Active Record: pushing logic out so models are just data access objects, so tests are simple and fast, puts "test, test fast, oh, your architecture" in the wrong order.

chunks.heading: Test at a coarser level: models, controllers, and especially systems
chunks.text:
- DHH quotes James Coplien's white paper "Why Most Unit Testing Is Waste": "Splitting up functions to support the testing process destroys your system architecture and code comprehension along with it. Test at a coarser level of granularity."
- He is not against tests. He is against deriving design from unit tests. Regression tests after the fact are valuable.
- Rails already moved up a level: the directory is `test/models`, not `test/unit`, so model tests touching the database are not a problem. "You can make anything fast if it doesn't have to work."
- Basecamp lost real customer data (attachments lost when editing an object and its attachments) while being heavily unit tested at the unit level. All tests passed because there was no system test for that flow.
- Most TDD proponents focus on units where they drive design and little on the system level, which is what people care about: "Does the whole thing work?"
- Fixtures: people hate them when they want to isolate one unit, but fixtures spin up a small world and work well when you test at the level of models, controllers and systems.
- He still writes test-first occasionally, for example for a translator where input and desired output are clear. Most information-system design is not like that, because he is still working out what the system should do.

chunks.heading: Coverage, test ratio and speed are the wrong scoreboard
chunks.text:
- In arguments on Hacker News and elsewhere, he finds people judge design almost only by test coverage, test ratio and test speed.
- A 1:4 ratio (four lines of test per line of production code) makes the system five times as large and five times as complex to reason about. He asks why that is a point of pride.
- Fast suites with 100% coverage often test little of the system. Decoupling to isolate tests from HTML and the database adds indirection, and "this decoupling is not free" because of conceptual overhead.
- Why people cling to these metrics: they come from the engineering and hard-science prism, and they are easy to measure to six decimals. He cites the quote that something being easy to measure does not make it important.
- Cost is not value: people who invested heavily in testing defend it, but expensive and time-consuming does not mean valuable.
- Aaron Patterson trolled him at dinner with "TLDR, just don't test." DHH's reply: regression testing has value, test-first design rarely does.

chunks.heading: Write software like a writer: clarity above all
chunks.text:
- DHH says "software writer" is a more apt identity than "software engineer" for most of the work: adding features to Basecamp, doing forensics on bugs, reading a plug-in. He wears the engineering hard hat only for performance work (change, measure, keep or revert).
- Clarity means being succinct without being terse, using the smallest words and least conceptual overhead that get the job done. Convolution gives no bonus points in writing and should not in code.
- Putting clarity above testability settles many arguments. It is liberating: complaints that Active Record is too big or has too many methods stop mattering. "Is it more readable? Is it more clear? That's the only thing that matters."
- Ruby's `unless` was his lightbulb moment: it duplicates `if not` purely for readability.
- Clarity has no metric. "I know it when I see it." You develop an eye the way he did in photography after thousands of photos, by doing it a lot, not by memorizing patterns.
- To develop it: decide clarity matters first, then read a lot of code and write a lot of code.

chunks.heading: How DHH builds the eye: read code, rewrite code, delete
chunks.text:
- When starting Rails he read the entire Ruby standard library, partly because documentation was poor. Today `bundle open <gem>` opens any gem in the editor, and he encourages reading complete gems you did not write.
- By Sturgeon's Revelation, 90% of code is crap, and reading poor code teaches him the most about what clarity is. He rewrites bad classes and methods to find out what he cares about.
- In the code-submission arguments he has had online, applying three patterns to a poor piece of code usually just moved the same code into different boxes. The code was missing a rewrite, not patterns.
- "I didn't have time to write a short letter, so I wrote a long one instead" describes much bad code. Any first version is a draft.
- A high school teacher told him that if you wrote it down, you should rewrite it. He says most people skip that step with code.
- Rewriting means omitting needless concepts, patterns, practices and classes. The delete key is his "number one tool for improving code."
- His closing advice: forget about patterns and TDD for a while, focus on the code in front of you, and ask how to write it simpler.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH walks through a Basecamp 3 refactoring session, treating code comments as a smell and replacing them with clearer code (an extracted private constant). He also weighs conflicting aesthetic conventions and shows pushing a recurring pattern, create_or_find_by backed by a unique index, upstream into Rails.

chunks.heading: Code comments as a smell, and how to remove one properly
chunks.text:
- DHH treats code comments as "a bit of a smell". If you need prose to explain something, it usually isn't apparent from the code itself. In Ruby you should be able to encapsulate the explanation in the code.
- He admits a "mixed relationship": a comment is sometimes great for explaining something non-obvious, but more often it signals unclear code.
- Context: he was reading through the whole Basecamp 3 codebase on a branch called "thh refactoring 2018", revisiting earlier decisions he now thinks he can make better.
- The first model he opened was `Access`, the join between a person and a "bucket" (Basecamp's abstraction covering teams, projects and circles). It is the object checked to decide whether someone can view content.
- The only method in that class with comments was the one that removes inaccessible records. The comment explained a 30 second grace period before the irreversible, slow cleanup job runs, giving an accidental removal a chance to be undone.
- His diagnosis: the comment wasn't explaining the conditional, it was explaining a "somewhat magical integer", the `30.seconds`.

chunks.heading: Replacing the comment: explaining variable, then constant, then placement
chunks.text:
DHH walks through a sequence of small steps, each an improvement:

1. **Explaining variable.** Extract the number into a named local, e.g. a grace period for removing inaccessible records, and use it where the literal was. The comment can then be deleted.
2. **Constant.** He sees inline variable declarations as "another sort of smell" when the value never changes. A value that is constant on every run should be a constant.
3. **Visibility.** He asks whether the constant is general (public) or a private detail. Here it was private, so it moved under the `private` section.
4. **Proximity.** A constant should sit as close as possible to the method that uses it. He swapped the order of the two methods so the constant sits right beside the one that references it.

chunks.heading: Conflicting aesthetic rules, and why style checkers can't decide
chunks.text:
- His normal habit: order private methods like a "table of contents", in the order they are called. Here the callbacks were `after_destroy` (reconnect the user) and `after_destroy_commit` (remove the records).
- Moving the method next to its constant broke that ordering, and a constant floating "in midair" mid-class looked worse to him than a broken ordering.
- His point: two good principles conflicted (methods in call order vs. constants declared first and close to their usage). You have to pick which matters more in this case.
- Here he chose proximity of constant and usage over the table-of-contents ordering, since there were only two methods.
- He says an automatic style checker cannot encapsulate this kind of judgment. The goal is simply to make the code easier and more pleasing to read and to come back to.

chunks.heading: Reading the codebase to find things worth extracting into Rails
chunks.text:
- His stated mission at that time: read the entire Basecamp 3 codebase looking for pieces that suit extraction into Ruby and Rails.
- He treats Basecamp as the source of framework features, in line with extracting rather than designing frameworks up front.
- The example was `grant` on `administratorships`, the join model between an account and a person that records who may administer the account (grant access, add or remove people, and so on).
- He prefers modeling this as a domain object rather than an admin boolean: "I really like encapsulating these domain objects and being able to reason about them and giving them a place to live and giving them a whole concept rather than just giving them boolean."
- It is exposed through a small DSL via methods added to the association, e.g. `account.administratorships.grant(person)` and a matching revoke.

chunks.heading: Using exceptions for control flow vs. a better Rails primitive
chunks.text:
- A person only needs one administratorship. There is a unique index on the account/person pair in the migration, and the code also has to handle the case where someone tries to grant one that already exists.
- The existing `grant` rescued the uniqueness exception and returned the existing record. It was long and needed a code comment, which he flags as the same smell as before: "the fact that we need to explain what's going on means that it's not quite obvious what's going on."
- Rails' built-in `find_or_create_by` is the usual approach, but he argues it invites stale reads on a busy app. It starts a transaction, does a `where` lookup, then creates, and these are separate steps.
- On an app with Basecamp's usage, a stale read "certainly can happen".
- The better approach: try the insert first and rely on the database's unique index to raise if the row exists, then return the existing record.
- Rails lacked this, so he wants `create_or_find_by(person: person)`: the same idea as `find_or_create_by`, flipped, with the insert-and-rescue pattern encapsulated.
- With it, `grant` shrinks to an alias of `create_or_find_by`, which also makes the DSL nicer.

chunks.heading: Pushing the pattern upstream into Rails
chunks.text:
- He frames this as a small extension to put into Rails so the pattern is available to everyone going forward.
- He floats a bigger idea: perhaps this pattern "should be the default", and Rails should consider deprecating the `find_or_create_by` signature in favor of it.
- A small extra cleanup he made at the same time: the method should accept records directly rather than IDs, since it didn't need to deal with just IDs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH walks through the Basecamp 3 mentions feature, tracing it from controller through concern, callbacks, background job and eavesdropper class. He argues callbacks push auxiliary complexity off to the side so the main flow stays simple, and that opt-out via suppression is the key to using them safely.

chunks.heading: Callbacks keep auxiliary complexity off the main path
chunks.text:
- DHH loves callbacks because they move incidental complexity "off to the side". Most code can pretend it lives on a simple default path, and you dig into the specifics only when you want to.
- He defends side effects against the functional-programming bad rep: "I think side-effects are wonderful for a whole host of uses." They adorn or progressively enhance a main flow that stays free of that complexity.
- Example: Basecamp 3 mentions. The messages controller `create` action records a new message (subject and content) and says nothing about mentions or eavesdropping. That keeps the controller readable.
- He calls mentions an auxiliary concern. It "does not deserve center stage" but must be there and be easy to dig into.
- He invents domain words freely (mention, mentioner, mentionee, eavesdropper). He says inventing concepts is a joy of programming, as long as they are packaged up consistently and coherently.

chunks.heading: Tracing one feature through the callback chain
chunks.text:
- The flow for a mention in Basecamp 3:
  1. The messages controller records a new message through the recording bucket setup.
  2. A `Mentions` concern mixed into `Recording` runs after save and decides whether to eavesdrop.
  3. If so, it enqueues an `EavesdroppingJob`.
  4. The job is a thin shell around an `Eavesdropper` class, which scans content and creates `Mention` records.
  5. `Mention` has a callback that delivers after commit.
  6. Delivery is a notification (browser or native push via an ActionNotifier framework he plans to extract) plus a mailer email.
- Recording is the broad abstraction over all content types: messages, chat lines, to-do items. A concern on it applies mentions to all of them.
- He admits there is "a fair amount of indirection". But reading the controller stays clear, because you are mostly not concerned with the auxiliary mentions work.
- The `Mention` model skips delivery when the mentioner and the mentionee are the same person.
- Eavesdropper splits the work into small methods: create mentions, find the mentionees, extract mentionees from a recording. Plain text is scanned with a regex. Rich text has the mention already encapsulated as HTML produced by JavaScript.
- He finds the eavesdropping metaphor "perfectly delicious": a system sitting on the side, listening for new recordings and acting on mentions in them.

chunks.heading: Capturing dirty-state before the transaction closes
chunks.text:
- Dirty-tracking methods such as `changed_from_drafted?` (generated from the status enum) only work inside the original transaction. Once it closes, the change set is cleared.
- Eavesdropping must act on a saved object, so it runs in `after_commit`, when the change set is gone.
- His trick: an `after_save` callback checks the change set and stores the result in an instance variable (`@eavesdropping`, set via a method like `remember_to_eavesdrop`). The after-commit hook then reads that variable.
- He says he has tried several times to extract this into Rails without finding a good way.
- The conditions for eavesdropping: the recordable changed and is active or archived, or a draft became active.
- Drafts stay secret, so mentions in a draft must not notify anyone until it is published.
- Scanning only when content changed was an optimization found after launch. The launch version scanned every time. A comment touching the parent message recording triggers a save, and re-scanning then is wasted work done "all the time".

chunks.heading: Move non-blocking work into jobs
chunks.text:
- Scanning content and creating mentions does not need to happen in the request that saves the message. He pushes it onto a queue in a job, so the user is not held up.
- Recording the message is only a few database writes. Scanning every time would block the response.
- Mentions suits this well: a notification delivered a second and a half later makes no difference to the user.
- The concern itself does little. It checks whether to do the work, sets up the `mentions` association, and enqueues the job. The job delegates to the dedicated `Eavesdropper` class.
- Because the job runs outside the original request, the current person has to be passed along explicitly.

chunks.heading: Always give callbacks an opt-out: suppression
chunks.text:
- Callbacks belong on the default path, the thing that should happen most of the time. But there are cases where they must not run.
- He suspects people got bitten by callbacks in the past because they never considered how to opt out.
- Basecamp's concept is `suppressible`: a mixin that holds a flag for whether something is suppressed. Code can wrap a block in a suppression, and anything inside it that would trigger the callback is skipped.
- Example: `ProjectCopier` copies content from an earlier version of Basecamp into the current one, creating many recordings that may contain mentions. Copying should not notify anyone or create mentions, so the copier wraps its work in a block that suppresses the eavesdropper.

chunks.heading: Why not a service object or transaction script
chunks.text:
- He considers putting the scanning, eavesdropping and delivery logic in the controller, a service object or a transaction script. He does not think any of those makes it clearer.
- Because mentions is auxiliary, it belongs on the side, and a concern lets you treat it as one cohesive unit.
- Recording gets some new private methods, but that does not matter when reading the flow. He says this is a much easier way to read through things, and that the recording class is not burdened with the logic and setup.

chunks.heading: Globals and current, flagged for a later episode
chunks.text:
- A current person or current account is something you need over and over. Passing it all over the place "isn't actually that helpful".
- Globals "should not just litter all over your application", but he thinks they are misunderstood and overly feared in web programming, like callbacks.
- He plans separate episodes on `Current` and on the recording bucket pattern, which he calls the predominant and most powerful pattern in Basecamp 3.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH defends globals as a "sharp knife" for request-scoped context, showing how Basecamp's Current class (extracted into Rails 5.1) carries the current person, account and request details into event tracking without threading them through every call. He warns to keep Current small so it doesn't become a crutch.

chunks.heading: Globals are a sharp knife worth using in the right place
chunks.text:
- DHH argues that globals are considered harmful is overstated, and that they have a great place in many applications, especially web apps.
- Web apps operate inside a request cycle. Certain things are set up at the start of the request, and the code wants easy access to them throughout that request. Globals are "a wonderfully good fit" for this.
- He accepts that globals can be overused and turn into a mess. A thing that can turn into a mess is still worth using when it is the right fit.
- This ties to a Rails philosophy of providing "sharp knives". A framework or language is not sinning by giving you tools that could cut your hand off if misused, because they also give the precision to make something happen in an easy, readable way.
- He tells developers to use globals "with pride" for precision incisions, and not to be ashamed of them, while staying mindful of the drawbacks.

chunks.heading: Current: the Rails 5.1 feature that extracts Basecamp's request globals
chunks.text:
- `Current` (`ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes`) was extracted into Rails 5.1 after being used in Basecamp 3 since its inception.
- It is a very short class. It does two things: declares a handful of attributes available globally, and provides delegation plus a hook for resetting them when the request ends.
- Basecamp's `Current` holds two kinds of things:
  - `current account`: derived from the URL, since Basecamp 3 puts the account ID in the path. A piece of middleware does the lookup and sets it.
  - `current person`: set at login, whether through a form, OAuth, a cookie or other authentication methods. Plus the request details (request ID, user agent, IP address), set in a callback.
- Setting the person can also set other things. If the account has not been set (e.g. in jobs that are simply passed a person), setting the person sets the account through it. The same applies to the time zone, which is recorded on the person.

chunks.heading: How Basecamp populates Current through concerns
chunks.text:
- Basecamp's `ApplicationController` has many concerns mixed in and almost no code of its own. Each cross-cutting consideration of the base controller is encapsulated in a concern.
- `SetCurrentRequestDetails` is a simple concern that adds a `before_action`. It sets request ID, user agent and IP address from the request into `Current`. Every controller inheriting from `ApplicationController` gets this.
- The request ID is used to tie things together through logging. User agent and IP address are used for various forms of tracking.
- The `Authentication` concern follows the same pattern. Its main path is cookie authentication, for a logged-in person returning with cookies intact. Other paths are OAuth and API authentication.
- The cookie flow: a signed identity cookie holds an identity ID that cannot be tampered with on the user side. The code uses it to look up the verified user, records how the person authenticated (cookie, OAuth, etc., used for logging), then sets `Current.person`.
- Basecamp has a shared identity system across its products. DHH names Basecamp, Backpack and HEY-era siblings in his list: Basecamp, Backpack and Highrise.
- The payoff is that once `Current.person` is set, it is accessible anywhere in the application, to any class, at any time within the request.

chunks.heading: Example: event tracking as a side effect that needs the current person
chunks.text:
- Basecamp tracks events: changes in the system are recorded in a separate tracking class instead of being deduced from the objects themselves. He defers the full explanation to a later episode.
- Event tracking is a side effect and auxiliary complexity, something not to focus on all the time. It is implemented like the mentions feature from episode two: a concern, using callbacks, declaring an association.
- That concern is mixed into `Recording`, Basecamp's master metadata class over concrete types such as messages, to-dos and documents. He calls the idea of a concrete metadata class encapsulating shared behavior probably the most powerful pattern in Basecamp, deserving its own episode.
- Every time a recording is created, an `after_create` callback calls `track_event` with a `created` status. The creator of the event is taken straight from `Current.person`.
- The callback takes no arguments. Nothing about the creator has to be passed in, which is "incredibly convenient". Having to pass the creator in whenever a recording is created would be "a real annoyance".
