chunks.heading: Example: tying request details to every event for support investigations
chunks.text:
- Each event also records its request details: request ID, user agent and IP address, pulled from `Current` when the event is built or saved.
- This gives Basecamp a way to investigate after the fact: who changed something, under what circumstances, from what IP.
- An admin interface lets support look up who created something from an IP address, which helps work out what went wrong when a customer writes in for help.
- DHH stresses how deep in the call chain this sits. Passing request ID, user agent and IP from the controller action through recording creation down to event creation would be a hassle.
- His argument is that explicit passing would not make the code clearer, just more convoluted. It would put an auxiliary concern, being able to look up an event by request ID, centre stage in code like creating a message, where readers do not want to be bothered by it.

chunks.heading: When globals become a smell, and how to judge it
chunks.text:
- DHH acknowledges the temptation to stuff things into a global because it is easier, and says that can be a code smell: a sign the code is not factored correctly and globals are used as a crutch.
- In Basecamp's case, he says the team examined the alternatives and deliberately chose globals, concluding that passing the data around is not an advantage.
- Guideline: the `Current` class should stay small. If it ends up with "10, 15, 20 different things", he suggests you may be "off into the weeds" and should step back and see whether the code can be factored to rely on globals less.
- Good candidates are request-scoped, auxiliary details (current user, account, request metadata, time zone) that many layers need but that are not the point of the code reading them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH walks through how Basecamp tests a lockable Document feature. He defends tests that hit the real database and render real views over isolated unit tests with mocks, uses fixtures instead of factories, and keeps assertions minimal. Fast-enough tests that give confidence beat the fastest possible tests.

chunks.heading: Philosophy: testing is for confidence, not fast tests
chunks.text:
- DHH says he is not anti-testing: Basecamp has "tens of thousands of written lines of test code" and he is not comfortable shipping new features without a suitable amount of automated testing.
- His past "TDD is dead" criticism (the RailsConf keynote and the conversation with Kent Beck and Martin Fowler) was about what TDD and unit-testing dogma do to the code itself, not about testing.
- He rejects the classic unit-test ideal of testing one thing in total isolation with everything else stubbed out "in the name of speedy tests". He says it is not a good trade against the cadre of mocks, stubs and dummy objects it requires.
- "The purpose of developing software is not to have fast tests." The purpose of tests is high confidence that shipped features are of high quality and that the common paths don't break.
- He prefers testing the real things (real database, real HTML generation in controllers). Those are slower, but the cost can be mitigated and tests made "fast enough".
- He also values exploratory QA by humans who were not part of development, as a separate practice.

chunks.heading: Model tests: real objects, fixtures, minimal stubbing
chunks.text:
- The example is the Basecamp documents feature plus the lockable concern, which lets only one user edit a document at a time. The behavior lives in the shared `Recording` class, which many content types (documents, to-do lists, uploads) can use.
- Tests are not pure unit tests. Recording a document hits the database and fires callbacks from other concerns, and DHH says that doesn't matter because it is "fast enough".
- Principle: test the real thing and "mock and stub as little as you can get away with", so tests stay close to the metal and readable, without accidental setup complexity.
- Setup is minimal: a `setup` method sets the current person (via the Current globals pattern) so actions are attributed to someone.
- No factories. Basecamp uses stock Rails fixtures: a base world of ready-made records (for example a bucket, a project, a recording) to pluck from. Tests don't first set up what they don't care about.
- Only things specific to the test are created inline. In the versions test, the new documents are created in the test because they are particular to the feature, not fixtures.
- Lock tests live in `test/models/recording/lock_test.rb`. They ignore the many other concerns on `Recording`, which are allowed to run with their callbacks. The test focuses only on the one aspect, the lock association and its DSL.
- Versions example: documents are immutable and recordings are mutable. The test updates a recording, asserts the latest recordable is the new one, and asserts the previous version is still reachable. It uses `travel 5.seconds` between writes because versions are ordered by `created_at`, and real edits are always at least a second apart.

chunks.heading: Speed: fast enough, and why he accepts the cost
chunks.text:
- The document model tests (4 tests) ran in about 2 seconds, roughly half a second per test, and the lock tests (4 tests) in about a second. He acknowledges you could get to around 100 ms per test, but says "for me that's not worth the trade-off".
- Spring, the preloader, keeps a persistent Rails process so the app isn't booted on every run.
- Tests are single-core for now. He announces that Rails 6 will add parallelized test execution, which matters more for larger suites.

chunks.heading: Assertions: only assert and assert_equal
chunks.text:
- For model tests he sticks to two stock assertions: `assert` and `assert_equal`. He extracts domain-specific assertions only when they need a lot of setup or are complicated.
- He rejects the "one assertion per test" rule: "I don't ascribe to that idea at all." You should have all the assertions you need to feel comfortable about one aspect, and "there's no upper ceiling".
- The smallest thing to test in a controller is a whole action, so the whole action gets tested. His `create` test ends up with three assertions.

chunks.heading: Controller tests: integration tests, not isolated
chunks.text:
- He deliberately does not test a controller action in isolation with everything stubbed. That would run fast but "wouldn't test a whole lot and wouldn't test whether the pieces actually work together".
- Controller tests inherit from Rails integration tests, so they are effectively integration tests, and he prefers them comprehensive even though they are slower.
- Documents controller flow: the test first requests the `new` action and asserts a 200. The controller does almost nothing there, but the view renders the application layout, the show template, and compiles assets (JavaScript, CSS). That confirms the form works. A custom assertion checks the breadcrumbs.
- It then posts to `create` with the full parameters, follows the redirect, and asserts it lands on the new document page with an `h1` of "hello world".
- Speed: the 10 documents controller tests ran in about 7 seconds. He calls that "a very worthy trade-off" for testing the whole stack from HTTP request to database write.
- He stops short of driving a real browser, which adds "an order of magnitude of delay". Browser-driven tests are worth it only when you need to test JavaScript behavior; for plain HTTP requests and responses, checking the HTML programmatically is a fair trade-off.

chunks.heading: Generic controllers and fixtures through the recordings pattern
chunks.text:
- The locks controller is generic and acts on any recordable (documents, to-do lists, other content). He cites it as the payoff of applying concerns through generic objects to concrete ones.
- Its tests cover the scenarios: the page shows locked when another user (Jason) holds the lock, shows "already locking" when you hold it, and the unlock and force-unlock paths. The tests do not care which fixture recording they use, only that it is lockable.
- Integration tests use a `sign_in_as` style setup that sets up the current user. Each test has about two assertions on average, and several is normal.
- Fixtures keep this readable: there are only 4 document fixtures, and since every piece of content has a corresponding recording there are more recording fixtures (for example the introduction document). All the busywork is done up front, so a reader of the test doesn't have to wade through setup.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues programmers owe users real deletion, not a hidden flag, and walks through Basecamp's "incineration" code. Command objects traverse the account, buckets and recordings tree, scheduled 30 days out, with a trash stage, a short grace period and backup wipes.

chunks.heading: Why deletion needs its own domain concept ("incineration")
chunks.text:
- DHH points to a Patrick McKenzie tweet: at most companies, deleting your data just sets a flag. The data stays in the database and in backups, and can be accessed by employees years later or subpoenaed.
- He argues programmers have an obligation to retire that pattern: "make it disappear", scrubbed from databases and backups in a timely, reasonable way.
- Basecamp's privacy policy says that when you cancel an account, nothing remains on its servers after 30 days.
- This doesn't happen automatically. In a multi-tenant database all data is intertwined, so it's not drop database customers. You must walk the whole web of connections and cherry-pick what to remove without deleting the wrong things.
- Basecamp reserves the word "incinerate" for this specific, meticulous, tracked process, instead of overloading generic terms like delete or destroy (which already have specific meanings in Ruby, Rails and computer science). He also "just think[s] it's a cool word".

chunks.heading: Structure: an Incinerable concern plus command objects
chunks.text:
- The account is the root of the data tree. An `Incinerable` concern on Account separates this aspect of the account, a recurring theme in the series.
- The concern is a thin access layer: it sets a callback so that after the account is canceled (a method from another concern that handles the account lifecycle), the incineration is triggered.
- The incineration itself is a standard command pattern: pass in the account, then either run it or check whether running is possible.
- Domain-language sugar: the job exposes a `schedule` method, so callers write `IncinerationJob.schedule(account)` and the job knows its own delay.
- The delay constant (30 days) is used in several places, so it was pulled up into the Incinerable concern. DHH says normally it would live with the job, which owns the scheduling.
- Accidental complexity: Basecamp runs the incineration against the master database (the shared "Signal ID" account database) and lets it replicate from there.

chunks.heading: Scheduling 30 days out and the "possible?" guard
chunks.text:
- Policy: an account is incinerated 30 days after cancellation. That gives 30 days to regret the decision, during which support can still recover a file.
- If a customer demands immediate deletion, secondary support can run incinerate directly from the command line.
- Jobs are scheduled 30 days into the future, so Basecamp keeps a deep, long-running queue of far-future jobs. DHH calls this a little unusual. They could rebuild it by querying for overdue canceled accounts if jobs were lost.
- Because the job waits 30 days, things can change in the meantime (for example, the customer un-cancels). So the command has a second layer of defense, a `possible?` predicate, that checks:
  - the account is actually canceled and inactive
  - the incineration window (30 days) has elapsed
- Incineration never runs just because a job was scheduled; it runs only if it's still legitimately possible.

chunks.heading: Walking the tree: account, buckets, recordings, recordables
chunks.text:
- Deletion proceeds top-down through the tree, and the account itself is deleted last, after everything depending on it.
- Level 1, buckets: projects, teams, and "pings" (direct conversations). Each bucket has its own incineration command. At the end, the account and the shared account record are deleted.
- Level 2, the bucket is mostly metadata (name, etc.), so the real data starts at the recordings it contains.
- Level 3, recordings: this is where content lives (messages, to-dos, uploaded files). Each recording incinerates its dependents (children), then itself. The recordable holds the actual content, such as a message body or to-do description. It's the last stop in the tree.
- Each level follows the same pattern: a `run` method plus a `possible?` check.
- DHH notes a style nit in the code: the private methods should follow the "table of contents" order of how they're invoked, and he likes inserting an extra blank line to separate groups of related methods (predicates vs. carrying out the command). He says this is controversial even in Rails core and Robocop complains, so you'd have to turn that cop off.

chunks.heading: Reusing incineration for single deletes, and avoiding wasted queries
chunks.text:
- The same framework handles deleting one project, team, or message, not just account cancellation. Deleting part of the tree is a subset of deleting the whole tree, which gives reuse.
- Each node therefore has two valid paths: it can be incinerated by itself (it was trashed and is due) or as part of an ancestor's incineration. A node must not be deleted out of sequence while an ancestor is being traversed, so the check also looks at whether an ancestor is being incinerated.
- Performance detail: Active Record's `belongs_to ... touch` normally touches the parent on each child delete, which is an UPDATE per row. During incineration that is wasteful, since an account can have thousands, tens of thousands, or in rare cases hundreds of thousands of recordings. Incineration skips the touching.

chunks.heading: Multi-stage grace periods and backup expiry
chunks.text:
- For a single bucket, deletion has stages:
  - Trashed: visible in a trash can that account users can see and restore from.
  - Imminent: no longer visible to users, with a final 5-day grace period. A user who finds the data gone can write to support to pull it back out of the deletion queue.
  - Incinerated: gone from the active database for good.
- Support can't restore a single customer from a database backup in a multi-tenant system, because restoring to production would roll back every other customer to that point.
- Database backups are wiped after 30 days too, so the data can't be recovered, subpoenaed, or involved in any retrieval process.
- DHH's principle: give as many reasonable safety steps as possible while still honoring that data should actually disappear. Basecamp chose 30 days as the point at which it fully does.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH walks through a real Basecamp pull request (skipping reminders for already-answered questions) to show how to evolve code without degrading it. Keep generic classes stable by pushing type-specific logic down to the concrete classes via message passing, and choose names from everyday domain vocabulary.

chunks.heading: Replace type checks in generic classes with message passing
chunks.text:
- DHH frames a hard part of writing software well as keeping a design clean and intact as it changes. Little software stays as written. It is changed a lot, over a long time, by people who may not have seen the original implementation or have forgotten how it was done.
- His goal: learn to extend and rewrite code, "make things a little better along the way and at the very least not make them worse," without ripping up the whole codebase each time.
- His worked example is a Basecamp pull request. Recurring questions ("what did you work on today?") sent a reminder even if the person had already answered, which made the system look dumb. The fix was to skip the reminder when the question was already answered.
- The first version added a check to the generic `ReminderDelivery` class. It overrode the superclass's should we deliver predicate and added a type check: is the recording a question, and if so, has it been answered? It also added a lookup method on the entry.
- DHH flagged the tension: `ReminderDelivery` is a generic concept, used for questions and also for approvals, and it now knew about one specific data type.
- He says a type check like this is a smell and can be replaced with message passing and polymorphism, "one of those standard refactorings in object-oriented systems that you see over and over again."

chunks.heading: Move the specifics down as far as they will go
chunks.text:
- DHH's rule for the refactor: take the generic notion ("is this reminder still pertinent?") and push it down the hierarchy "as far down as we can get to the most concrete level possible."
- In the pull request, the deliverability checks stay on the reminder: is the schedule eligible, is the recording trashed, has the recipient been deleted from the system (no emails or notifications to deleted people).
- The new "is this reminder pertinent" question is not answered by the reminder. The reminder passes itself to the recordable (here the question), and the question decides whether an answer already exists.
- The delivery class's type check becomes plain indirection. The specific lookup now lives in the question and its answer/entry classes, not in the generic delivery code.
- The same pattern covers future cases. If another data type needs reminders and needs to say a reminder is no longer pertinent, that logic lives in that class.

chunks.heading: Why a generic class should stay on its own change schedule
chunks.text:
- DHH admits the original version is arguably clearer when you read the diff: everything is in one place at the point of delivery, while the refactor spreads the responsibility across several objects.
- He still prefers the refactor because `ReminderDelivery` should be on its own change schedule. It should not change whenever the strategy for deciding "has this question been answered?" changes.
- His examples of how that strategy might change: answered today, answered yesterday, or some other scope for the lookup. "Why should [the generic class] be changing on that schedule?"
- The aim is to keep generic parts of the system stable as it evolves.
- Long-term payoff: avoid mega classes that are large not because they do a lot, but because they accumulate type tags and special cases for different objects. "Push all the stuff down to the objects and let it live there and you'll have a cleaner system."

chunks.heading: Name methods in domain vocabulary
chunks.text:
- DHH first named the predicate `pertinent?`. His colleague Tom proposed `needed?`, which DHH took as simpler and closer to casual speech.
- "Does this thing need a reminder" is something people would say in conversation, so the method name should be as close as possible to the domain vocabulary, not just an adequate word.
- This is one of the benefits he describes of reviewing someone else's code. An editor or reviewer sees things from a little distance, and some things look obvious from there. He worked on the pull request with Tom, and says he could just as well have written the original himself.

chunks.heading: Prefer `blank?` over a leading `!` when the negation gets far from the condition
chunks.text:
- DHH's last review note was about the `needed?` implementation. A reminder is needed if there is not already an answer, written as a `!` negation in front of a long expression.
- The line is mostly a chain through the module hierarchy (question to answer to entry), then the lookup method, then the answer recording. The actual subject is far from the `!` at the start, so the reader has to remember we're negating this whole thing.
- His suggestion: use Ruby's `blank?` instead. It is longer and for sure slower but reads in natural order.
- This is a small example of the care he wants when changing a system: think about the impact left behind, and about what is generic versus what is specific.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why the Turbo team removed TypeScript: the people building it weren't enjoying the work, so they pulled it out in about 40 minutes. He frames static versus dynamic typing as a tribal, identity-driven fight, defends open source as a gift made for himself, and explains why internet backlash doesn't faze him.

chunks.heading: Dynamic vs. static typing as a matter of programmer happiness
chunks.text:
- DHH has preferred dynamically typed languages for his whole career. Ruby (used for about 20 years at 37signals) and JavaScript both fall in the camp he likes: loose, permissive, "freedom loving".
- He says TypeScript sits on top of JavaScript and gives it a typed experience, with benefits in IDEs and autocomplete. It also forces you to write code in a certain way, and he never liked that way of writing.
- His core test is enjoyment. He wrestled with the TypeScript type system on a new Turbo feature and asked the team whether anyone still liked working that way. The answer was "not me, not me, not me".
- He treats the dynamic vs. static split as a real schism in programming, one that has run for his 20-plus years in software and for at least 20 years before that.
- He still appreciates the statically typed side. He spent a couple of weeks in Swift, read the language manuals, and could see the benefits (IDE support and so on). He took some ideas away, then went back to Ruby with a sense of relief: "this is what me likes".
- He compares it to a vacation in Japan. A statically typed language is like a trip to a different, quirky, interesting country. You enjoy it because it is different, then you come home. A good trip doesn't mean you move.
- He doesn't want everyone to program the same way: "life would be so boring" if every chef used the same technique and the food all came off an assembly line.

chunks.heading: Why Turbo 8 dropped TypeScript
chunks.text:
- Turbo is the framework 37signals uses to build its applications. It exists to minimize the amount of JavaScript you write while still building highly interactive apps.
- The decision came from the team itself. A new group was working on Turbo for a major new release. The new feature, plus the question "does anyone like this way of working anymore?", showed that nobody did.
- The discussion had started several months earlier. The new feature brought it back.
- His reasoning: Turbo is mainly a tool 37signals uses internally. It has some external effects, but "if we're not enjoying ourselves why don't we just yank it".
- It was cheap to test. Alberto, one of the programmers, removed TypeScript from the codebase in roughly 40 minutes, and the result was a pull request (a diff).
- Seeing the diff settled it. DHH says it looked "so much nicer" and reminded him why he is "such a big fan of JavaScript". His response was "let's just ship it".
- His message to users was short: some people like the statically typed experience and that's fine, but the people working on Turbo don't, so they are taking it out. He is glad JavaScript exists in the form he likes.
- Internally there was no fallout. His line: "we had the knife we didn't like cutting with so much so we put it at the side and used another knife."

chunks.heading: Why the typing debate can't be argued to a conclusion
chunks.text:
- DHH loves technical debates and going into the weeds. He says this one is different because it carries "identity politics" stickiness.
- He says he has never seen a conversation between two programmers where one said "excellent point, I will now switch from statically typed to dynamically typed". People change their minds on this occasionally, but not from a single interaction.
- All the arguments have already been made over the decades, so he chose not to re-argue them. His position was "we're not going to change anyone's mind", so the team did what suited them.
- He thinks engaging with ideas is still worthwhile, because the debate sometimes produces breakthroughs. It breaks down when the discussion turns into tribal dynamics, where people say "you're an idiot because you like this knife" or "because you like statically typed".
- Jason Fried's observation (not DHH's): binary issues like air-cooled vs. water-cooled Porsches, or original paint vs. respray, give no gray space and so produce flame wars.
- DHH's view is that once the thread becomes personal, minds close and ideas stop moving: "it's actually the place where the discussion about ideas go to die".

chunks.heading: Handling internet backlash and social media dynamics
chunks.text:
- DHH says he has built up immunity to this level of vitriol. He has been in flame wars since the mailing-list days, and the intensity has ratcheted up slowly over 20 years.
- He compares it to bigger fights. 37signals spent two weeks battling Apple for hey.com's right to exist. Next to that, this was a small thing.
- He says the pile-on was partly about his reputation: people had already formed opinions about him. It also echoed the cloud exit, where he did the opposite of what "everyone" seemed to be doing, which confuses people's sense of the narrative.
- He sees the pattern on social media as a spectator sport. Outrage that targets people (one person calling another an idiot) spreads fastest, and people show up "with the popcorn" for what looks like a fight.
- He expects a news cycle of about 24 hours, plus maybe 36 more to crest, then a small ember. People cannot remember last week's controversy. Most of the "tourists" never knew what Turbo was.
- He suggests sports as a healthy outlet for the human urge to belong to a tribe, and says nerds who don't follow sports have nowhere else to put that energy. He now thinks he should get more into sports for the same reason.
- His practical advice: "you can also close Twitter" and most of the noise goes away, apart from some leakage into GitHub, such as frivolous pull requests meant to obstruct.

chunks.heading: Open source as a gift, not an obligation
chunks.text:
- Turbo is released under the MIT license ("do whatever the hell you want, but don't hold me responsible"). 37signals paid for Hotwire's development on company time, and he says they have spent "literally millions" on it. They give it away with no licensing deals and no revenue share.
- He describes the common backlash as people receiving a free gift and demanding a refund or a different gift. He has seen many open source maintainers quit over this.
- He is open about why he does it: "I'm predominantly doing open source for me". He enjoys sharing, but he is not a volunteer labor force building whatever others want. 37signals builds these tools because they need and enjoy them. Take them or don't, he says, "but could you not spit in the soup for everyone else".
- He recalls an early Rails slide that said "[expletive] you": if you don't like the gift, he'll keep making it for himself anyway.
- This episode did not change his view on open source. The loud voices on X are a small group, even if it is thousands of people. When he meets people directly or by email, they are appreciative and discussions are good.
- He reports many emails from people saying they also disliked TypeScript but were afraid to say so because opponents are so loud. He calls this preference falsification, and says being affirmed in a view that runs against the dominant narrative is valuable.
- He sees this as a recurring theme in 37signals' writing: Rework readers write in to say they also believed meetings are toxic or that inspiration is perishable but didn't think they could say it out loud. He says he likes saying aloud what others are hesitant to.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why AI finally clicked for him in late 2025: agent mode in the terminal, not autocomplete, produced work he kept about 80% of. He covers toil-reduction uses at 37signals, shipping AI features only when clearly useful, and staying optimistic without hype or doom.

chunks.heading: DHH on why AI agents changed his mind in late 2025
chunks.text:
- DHH says AI "really changed in the later half of 2025". Models kept improving, but the key shift was giving them more power in development.
- He moved from autocomplete-in-the-editor AI to terminal agents. In agent mode they run on their own from a plan, use the terminal, run bash commands, run code, and look things up on the web.
- He disliked the autocomplete mode: "Can you shut up for a second and just let me type the damn thought out of my head?" It interfered with how he works. He prefers a text editor to a heavy IDE and likes typing code by hand.
- He re-tested AI every month or at each model drop through early 2025. He saw promise but found it "not actually helping me", and he did not want to keep the work it produced.
- By the second half of 2025, agents were helpful enough that he wanted to keep the majority of what they produced.
- He writes that agents work "alongside you, not sort of on top of you". That change in feel mattered as much as the capability jump.

chunks.heading: How much of an agent's output he keeps
chunks.text:
- He often gets agent output that is "like 80% there".
- Sometimes he gets the last 20% by iterating with the agent. More often he jumps in and does it himself.
- His view is that if an agent does 80% of a problem, that is amazing. Even 20% is still amazing, as long as it isn't padded with junk that takes longer to pull out.
- He sometimes throws out the agent's solution and rewrites it from scratch, but the draft still gives him the blueprint of where to go.
- The ratio of makes a mess to solves it or gives a useful draft is shifting fast. Not every run is good: after a great result he has asked for something simple and gotten a mess.
- He wrote a post about "promoting" AI agents, with a double meaning. He recommends developers and designers working in code try agents, and he personally "promoted" the AI he uses from a text box he asked questions to into a worker whose output he can keep.

chunks.heading: Using agents on toil at 37signals
chunks.text:
Jeremy pioneered putting agents on programmer toil that is important but not exciting.

- **HackerOne security reports:** External researchers submit findings for bounties, which DHH says go up to $5,000 or possibly more for catastrophic finds. About 90% of reports are low quality ("sludge"), from humans or weak AI.
  - The agent gets the history of past reports and a score of the submitter, such as whether they have submitted nonsense before.
  - It pre-reviews each report so the team spends time on high-value ones. He compares it to spam detection applied to low signal rather than spam.
  - He says AI is "really good at filtering noise from signal".
- **Console access reviews:** Every two weeks they review the logs of programmers' access to production systems and data during customer investigations. The goal is to make sure no one accesses data beyond what customers have permitted.
  - Early reviews found sloppy habits, such as accessing too much data at once, which were fixed.
  - Recent reports typically find that all accesses, such as "42 accesses to personal information", were vetted and within jurisdiction.
  - He notes AI is "perfectly patient" doing the same check repeatedly and can be trained to spot the aberration.
- **On-call and performance investigations:** The agent is given access to logs, the exception system, and performance monitoring and asked what is going on. He says it pulls data and runs queries and sometimes comes up with the answer in a way that is "damn impressive".

chunks.heading: Why 37signals held off on shipping AI in its products
chunks.text:
- Early experiments to put AI into the product, around search, commands, and autocompletion, never felt like a slam dunk.
- DHH says launching them would risk being called AI slop: a sticker on the product that isn't uniformly better.
- He doesn't mind being late, because when 37signals ships it wants the result to be useful.
- Experience with agents over the last three or four months of 2025 gave the team renewed zeal to find places where AI delivers an unequivocally positive impact in the product.
- He is excited about one idea around Basecamp but won't give details, since "we may not launch it either".

chunks.heading: Peak experiences: debugging and multi-model drafts
chunks.text:
- **Debugging a Rails bug:** A bug in the latest Rails produced a weird artifact when opening a Rails console. He didn't want to dive in, so he handed it to Claude's Opus 4.5.
  - The agent pulled out a C debugger and attached it to the process, which he didn't expect.
  - Its first couple of hypotheses didn't pan out, but it kept going and pinpointed the problem and the commit where things went wrong.
  - It produced a patch he could drop into the Basecamp codebase as a workaround until Rails core is fixed.
  - He says he wouldn't have invested that time right then and would have worked around the bug.
  - He enjoys seeing the visible reasoning of the thinking models, whether or not it reflects what's happening underneath: "The show is spectacular."
- **Five drafts of an MCP connector:** He wanted to look at the MCP standard (which he says now "seems like maybe it's kind of fading") and see how to build it the Rails way.
  - He used OpenCode, a terminal UI that lets him use models from all providers at once, including Claude, Gemini, OpenAI's Codex, and open-weight models. It was just added to the default setup (Omarchy context implied, not stated).
  - He got five drafts from five different models with a loosely specified task: a connector with three tools, authenticated with a bearer token. Each ran about 2.5 to 6 minutes.
  - All five produced working solutions using the existing tests, which shocked him. He kept none, because he wanted to focus on the fluidity of the interface, but several had good ideas he hadn't thought of.
  - Combining them with his own work was much faster. He got to running software and hooked it to his MCP debugger to see hello world come back.
- He ranks this up there with his top computer experiences, comparable to playing Yie Ar Kung-Fu on a Commodore 64 at age five and publishing his first web page in ninth grade.

chunks.heading: Experts versus non-programmers, and the innovator's dilemma
chunks.text:
- DHH says non-programmers can get more out of AI than he can. Everything he asks AI to do is something he could do himself given enough time, whereas non-programmers get something they truly couldn't have built.
- He compares this to Excel and FileMaker Pro, which let non-programmers build programs for business tasks they couldn't afford or had no access to professional programmers to do. He notes Jason started in software with FileMaker Pro.
- He grants that AI-built software can be insecure or leaky, and says he'd hesitate to put his personal data into some of it. But he argues not everything is as critical as "a pacemaker or a bank".
  - Many programs sit at the low end of the "criticality ladder", where even catastrophic failure costs little and the upside of the program existing is worth it.
- He invokes the innovator's dilemma. Every disruptive technology starts out feeble, a toy that can't do top-end work, and then grows into it. Today's AI output needs supervision, but so what.

chunks.heading: His stance on AI hype and doom
chunks.text:
- He refuses to extrapolate. "Nobody knows where this is going", including whether LLMs are near the top of the curve, or whether AGI is five minutes or ten years away.
- He asks people to focus on how good AI is right now and what an achievement of mankind it is.
- He notes how fast image generation went from Midjourney v1 with seven fingers and mutant faces to hyperrealistic images in about two and a half to three years.
- He chooses optimism, hoping the new capabilities do more good than harm. He says it is easy to imagine the worst, since sci-fi has depicted it for 50 years, and he cites HAL 9000 in 2001: A Space Odyssey.
- His advice: unless you work at DARPA, the Pentagon, or a research lab, don't spend your time worrying about the end of the world. People worried about nuclear war in 1964 and it didn't happen. Be optimistic and enjoy the time you have.
- He says he goes to bed thinking "holy [expletive] this is amazing" and wakes up genuinely curious where it goes.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why 37signals is leaving AWS: the promises of smaller teams, lower cost and less complexity never materialized, and a $3.2M annual cloud bill could shrink dramatically on owned hardware. He argues for "sovereign clouds" in colocated data centers.

chunks.heading: Why DHH left the rental cloud: the promises did not hold
chunks.text:
- DHH says 37signals had been on the cloud for over a decade (S3 early, then compute clouds). Its fundamental promises never materialized: more with less complexity, lower cost, faster execution, smaller teams.
- He says they could not run with a smaller team or at lower cost. The one real advantage was spinning up "a hundred beefy machines" with a snap of the fingers, which he calls unique but very expensive, and not worth the premium for a stable, profitable company with predictable demand.
- hey.com (the email service launched a couple of years earlier) was running entirely in the cloud and performed fine. The disappointment was economics and the broken promises, not availability.
- He was once a "cheerleader" for the cloud inside the company. He bought the pitch that running your own hardware is like running a generator in your backyard instead of buying from the grid, and calls it a trillion-dollar argument. It took years to deprogram.
- He compares the situation to the emperor's new clothes: many people can't see the magic of the cloud but stay quiet because they assume everyone else does. He says 37signals is playing the little boy who says "he's naked."

chunks.heading: The cost trigger: 2022 numbers and the savings math
chunks.text:
- Philosophy came first; cost was the tipping point. When he ran the numbers, he says, "this is absurd."
- 37signals spent $3,201,564 on cloud in 2022, more than a quarter of a million dollars per month.
- About $2.4M of that was managed services (EKS, RDS, OpenSearch, ElastiCache). Half a million dollars went to RDS (managed database) and just over half a million to OpenSearch (managed logging and search).
- About $900K went to S3. He calls S3 the best-priced service and the most cumbersome to replace, partly because egress costs to get data out are "so astronomical."
- Their napkin calculation: the $2.4M could be cut to under $900K, including buying replacement gear, amortizing it over five years, and paying for hosting. He calls that "almost misdirectingly conservative."
- He thinks the real figure is closer to $2M a year saved, taking a $2.4M budget to roughly $400K. The stated target was at least $1.5M a year saved, possibly more.
- He calls $1.5M a year of extra bottom line "very material" for a medium-sized SaaS company.
- His advice is not to take his word: run your own numbers. 37signals published a full accounting of its cloud spend per application and per service.

chunks.heading: Why hardware economics shifted
chunks.text:
- Hyperscalers were supposed to buy hardware far cheaper and pass the savings on through lower prices. He says the opposite happened: services got more expensive, especially cloud-native managed services (managed databases, managed search).
- The cloud peaked while Intel stumbled, with roughly five years of CPUs that barely improved in performance per dollar.
- In the last three to five years ARM (Apple in particular) and TSMC advances have made computers much faster. Comparing cores and speed from a vendor like Dell against cloud pricing gave a "staggering" gap.
- He regrets not running that comparison two and a half to three years earlier. Faith in the cloud being the future made the spell hard to break.
- He says AWS is the most profitable part of Amazon, generating about $40 billion a year in profit, and "those profits don't come from nothing."

chunks.heading: Centralization and the philosophical objection
chunks.text:
- DHH says he was already down on big tech owning everything, starting with the app store duopoly (Apple and Google) and what it did to innovation. The web is a permissionless platform; mobile stores require begging a corporation for permission.
- Cloud consolidation undermines the internet's decentralized design. When AWS US-East-1 goes down, a large part of the internet goes offline. He says DARPA designed a system meant to survive nuclear attack.
- Handing all computing to three companies destroys that design, which he calls "utterly tragic."

chunks.heading: What a cloud exit actually involves
chunks.text:
- 37signals ran its own hardware in colocation alongside the cloud, so it knew how to buy and operate hardware. He says the industry has a "general amnesia" about this and has been scared into thinking you aren't smart enough to run your own servers.
- Cloud exit does not mean building your own data center. Below the scale of Meta, Apple and Google, nobody does. You rent space in a colocation facility and own the hardware inside it.
- Colocation is similar to the rental cloud experience, but lead time is a few weeks to receive and rack machines instead of minutes.
- Network and power are shared infrastructure either way. No one owns their own transatlantic cables. His line: own the core competencies and core infrastructure, not homestead with no connection to society.
- Two data centers were enough for 37signals. Adding a third would not be materially more complicated, and backup and coordination between sites works the same in a rental cloud or a sovereign one.

chunks.heading: Sovereign cloud and the migration
chunks.text:
- He prefers the term "sovereign cloud" to "private cloud" (which he associates with CIO white papers): you still use containers, VMs and the same stack, but you own the footprint.
- The cloud runs the same software everyone else does (Postgres, MySQL, Redis, containers). It has no special magic, only marginal extras such as automated backups.
- Work done to make apps cloud-ready carries over. Stateless app servers, shared state kept elsewhere, and containerized apps move to owned hardware just as well. Getting into the cloud took years; getting out was very fast.
- 37signals had seven cloud applications at the start of 2023. The move started in earnest in January and was due to finish around the end of May. The original Basecamp had been pulled out the previous week, and performance was better after leaving.
- The one new tool they built is MRSK (mrsk.dev), a deployment wrapper around Docker. He says Kubernetes suits running a large rental cloud but is horrendously complicated for a medium-sized company running a sovereign cloud.
- The plan was to leave S3 as the only lingering cloud footprint by the end of summer, and eventually reach zero spend on the rental cloud.

chunks.heading: Who should do the math, and banks as the example
chunks.text:
- DHH says "software is eating the world": a bank today is a software company, since its value is in operating software, not branches. Operating software is a core competency to keep in-house.
- His advice targets companies buying hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars of compute directly from rental clouds. Mere users of a SaaS product like Basecamp are not the audience.
- He says a bank that can't do a financial rent-versus-buy analysis, or can't amortize hardware over five years, is one he would not trust with his money.
- Banks have boring, predictable demand with no sudden spikes of millions of customers (KYC throttles growth), so they fit owned hardware well.
- He argues the rent-versus-buy break-even clicks in around five years of amortization for stable businesses.
- He calls hybrid setups "soft pedaling." He says run the math yourself, and expects most stable businesses to find zero rental cloud dollars is the answer. File storage like S3 is the likeliest exception for those without philosophical objections.
- Bank technologists are herd animals: many probably knew the math didn't add up but followed consultant hype. He expects the pendulum to swing back and conservative businesses to revisit cloud decisions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH's founding essay lays out nine pillars behind Rails: programmer happiness, convention over configuration, omakase, no single paradigm, beautiful code, sharp knives, integrated systems (the majestic monolith), progress over stability, and a big tent. It explains why Rails trusts programmers, favors shared defaults, and resists premature distribution.

chunks.heading: Optimize for programmer happiness as the first design principle
chunks.text:
- DHH says the first pillar of the Rails Doctrine comes straight from Ruby's core motivation: Matz's "original heresy" was to put the programmer's happiness above competing concerns like safety, uniformity, or purity.
- He contrasts Python ("one and preferably only one way to do something"), Java (protecting programmers from themselves) and Smalltalk (purity of message passing) with Ruby's expressiveness, sharp knives and keyword accumulation.
- Ruby makes the machine "appear to smile at and flatter its human co-conspirator", often via complex implementation hidden behind simple-looking code. He says these choices "were not free", which is why they are commendable.
- He describes discovering Ruby as finding "a magical glove that just fit my brain perfectly" and a "fountain of flow" (Csikszentmihalyi), which moved him from programming because he needed programs to programming for love of it. He says it set the course of his life's work.
- Optimizing for happiness is hard to measure at the micro level but clear at the macro level: the Rails community is full of people who report "better, more fulfilled working lives".
- He concludes it is "perhaps the most formative key to Ruby on Rails".

chunks.heading: The Principle of The Bigger Smile (Rails' version of Least Surprise)
chunks.text:
- Ruby's early Principle of Least Surprise (PoLS) meant behaving as expected. Example: Ruby's `irb` accepts both `exit` and `quit`, while Python's console says "Use exit() or Ctrl-D" even though it clearly knows what was meant.
- PoLS faded because it is subjective ("least surprising to whom?" Matz), and it fed fruitless bike-shedding on the mailing lists as the community grew.
- Rails follows an equivalent: the Principle of The Bigger Smile (of DHH). APIs are designed around whatever makes him smile more and broader.
- He admits this sounds "comically narcissistic" and says creating something like Ruby or Rails is at the outset "a deeply narcissistic endeavor": "I created Rails for me. To make me smile, first and foremost."
- Examples of silly lengths taken for the principle:
  - The Inflector, which maps Person to people, Analysis to Analyses, Comment to Comments. It was fiercely controversial early on and is now unquestioned.
  - `Array#second` through `#fifth` (and `#forty_two`), which critics decried as bloat versus `Array#[1]`.
- He still relishes writing `people.third` in a test or the console. It is "not logical", "not efficient", maybe "pathological", but it makes him smile and helps justify 12 years of involvement with Rails.

chunks.heading: Convention over Configuration
chunks.text:
- An early Rails productivity motto: "You're not a beautiful and unique snowflake." Giving up vain individuality lets you skip mundane decisions and move faster on what matters.
- Example: whether primary keys are "id", "postId", "posts_id" or "pid" is not worth recurrent deliberation. Thousands of such decisions only need to be made once, and Rails swings its machete at that jungle.
- Conventions also give a field for deeper abstractions. If `Person` reliably maps to a `people` table, the same inflection lets `has_many :people` find the `Person` class. Good conventions "pay dividends across a wide spectrum of use".
- They lower the barrier for beginners: much of Rails can be benefited from in ignorance, so great applications can be built "without knowing why everything is the way it is". A blank page and a thick textbook make it hard even to know where to start ("finding a thread to pull").
- For experts, an obvious next step for every change lets you move through the parts of an app that resemble every other app. "A place for everything and everything in its place. Constraints liberate even the most able minds."
- The peril: most worthwhile apps have some unique part, maybe 5% or 1%. He contends most impulses to be a unique snowflake are ill-considered and the cost of "going off the Rails" is under-appreciated, but enough of them are justified that each must be examined carefully.

chunks.heading: The menu is omakase
chunks.text:
- Omakase: letting the chef choose gives a good meal even before you know what "good" is. For programming, it means letting others assemble your stack.
- Convention over Configuration concerns how to use individual frameworks. Omakase concerns which frameworks, and how they fit together.
- He challenges "use the best tool for the job": picking the best tool requires a foundation for judging "best" with confidence, which is hard. Choosing each library in isolation is like picking each course of an eight-course meal; the objective is the whole system.
- Rails trades each programmer's individual privilege to choose every tool for "a better tool box for all". Three dividends:
  1. Safety in numbers: shared default setups make it easier to teach, help and debate ("We all watched the same show last night at 7"), and strengthen community.
  2. Everyone perfects the same basic toolbox: much software pain comes from component interaction, so shared configurations that fail the same way get fixed for everyone.
  3. Substitutions are possible but not required: you can delay swaps until you have developed a personal palate, then swap diligently and enjoy the rest of the shared stack.

chunks.heading: No one paradigm: Rails is a quilt
chunks.text:
- DHH says there is a strong emotional pull toward picking one central idea and following it to its logical conclusion. Rails is instead "a quilt", a composite of paradigms that would conflict if contrasted one by one. There is no championship with a sole winner.
- View helpers are by default one big pot of functions in a single namespace ("PHP soup"). He argues PHP had it right for rarely interacting functions. Presenter objects can fit when methods depend on each other, but that is the rare fit.
- Models are the "prime bastion of object-oriented goodness": finding the right names, increasing coherence and lowering coupling is the fun of domain modeling. Even there, Rails concerns (a specialization of Ruby mixins) give models a wide surface area with direct access to their data.
- Active Record mixes database interfacing with domain logic, which offends purists, but he says it is the practical way to build a web app that almost always talks to a database.
- Ideological flexibility lets Rails tackle a wide array of problems; overlapping paradigms "cover the flanks and guard the rear".
- The cost is conceptual overhead: you benefit from procedural and functional experience as well as OO, and from knowing JavaScript and SQL for the peaks. The mitigation is a "rush to Hello World", delivering real value early so people level up and treat learning as a joy.

chunks.heading: Exalt beautiful code
chunks.text:
- DHH says aesthetically pleasing code is a value unto itself and deserves a "full seat at the table of priorities", though it does not always trump other concerns.
- In Ruby, beauty is often at the intersection of native idioms and a custom DSL. His Active Record example: `belongs_to :account`, `has_many :participants, class_name: 'Person'`, `validates_presence_of :name`. It looks like a DSL but is just three class-method calls taking symbols and options, yet gives immense power. It also honors Convention over Configuration: `belongs_to :account` assumes an `account_id` column in the `projects` table.
- Migrations are the "essence of framework power": declare an `ActiveRecord::Migration` subclass with `#change` and the framework handles the plumbing, including running it forward with `rails db:migrate` and reversing it to drop the table. The programmer does not stitch the workflow together from libraries.
- Beauty can be subtle and about rhythm. `if people.include? person` focuses on the collection, while `if person.in? people` makes the person the subject. He finds the second more beautiful when the condition is about the person.

chunks.heading: Provide sharp knives
chunks.text:
- Ruby deliberately includes sharp knives, the best known being monkey patching. Critics predicted calamity from trusting programmers with it, for example overwriting `String#capitalize`.
- Nothing in Ruby stops that. Good sense is enforced "by convention, by nudges, and through education. Not by banning sharp knives from the kitchen and insisting everyone use spoons to slice tomatoes."
- The flip side is wonders like `2.days.ago`. If you would trade that for safety, he says, "Ruby is probably not for you." The language flourished because it trusted programmers and taught them to use capable tools, assuming most want to become better.
- He notes it is always about other programmers: "I've yet to hear a single programmer put up their hand and say 'I can't trust myself with this power, please take it away from me!'" He rejects that paternalism.
- Rails concerns are his current example. A thin layer of sugar over Ruby modules, they let one class encapsulate multiple related concerns. Critics say they give bloat-prone programmers new drawers for clutter, which is true, but he calls it a fallacy that withholding the feature leads to architectural bliss: "If you can't be trusted to keep the kitchen sink out of your overstuffed concerns, you're probably not going to end up with a shining beacon of elegance otherwise."
- The framework should be a patient tutor, and the only route to expertise goes through mistakes ("a bit of blood, sweat, and perhaps even some tears"). Rails is "an environment for chefs and those who wish to become chefs".

chunks.heading: Value integrated systems: the majestic monolith
chunks.text:
- Rails' first love is integrated systems, "majestic monoliths": a whole system that addresses an entire problem, from front-end JavaScript for live updates to production database migrations.
- The scope is broad but still understandable by one person. Rails aims to equip generalist individuals rather than segregate specialists into niches needing whole teams.
- The integrated system cuts needless abstractions, reduces duplication between layers (such as templates on both server and client), and avoids distributing the system "before we absolutely, positively have to".
- Complexity comes from new boundaries: method calls between objects are far simpler than remote procedure calls between microservices, which bring failure states, latency issues and dependency update schedules.
- Some distribution is necessary, for example an HTTP API for others. Handling inbound requests is easier than sending outbound ones ("your downtime is someone else's failure state").
- Worse is premature disintegration into services or microservices, driven by the misconception that a Modern Internet Application must be built many times over: server, JavaScript MVC client, each native mobile app. He says this is not a law of nature.
- Large chunks can be shared across apps, such as the same controllers and views for desktop web and embedded in native mobile apps, without giving up speed or user experience. The goal: "All the power of individually tuned and distributed applications with the ease-of-use and understanding of a single, integrated system."

chunks.heading: Progress over stability, and a big tent
chunks.text:
- Mature systems ossify because every change hurts someone who depended on past behavior. DHH says listening too closely to conservatism means never seeing the other side, so Rails must dare to break things occasionally. This is not a license for "needless or excessive hurt"; the 2.x to 3 migration left scars and left many behind, but "in the grand scheme of things, it was still worth it".
- The test: will Rails be better off in five years for today's changes, or for adopting another problem domain such as job queuing or WebSockets? If yes, "suck it up and do the work."
- Rails should push Ruby's progress too. It has moved through Ruby 1.6, 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 to 2.6 and helped everyone upgrade faster. Bundler, the asset pipeline and Spring were controversial but are now taken for granted because of Rails' insistence.
- Progress is about people: there are no lifetime seats in Rails Core or Rails Committers, which are for those actively making progress. New blood and fresh ideas are needed.
- Big tent: Rails would become insular if everyone had to defer to every tenet, so it has "so few if any litmus tests". Proof: RSpec thrives despite his "grave discontent" with it. Rails as an API for people who want separate clients and servers is welcome as a secondary mission, even though his personal focus is the integrated system including the view.
- A big tent does not mean being all things to all people: "welcome all people to your party, and allow them to bring their own drinks." It takes real work to be welcoming and to lower barriers to entry, and a thank-you for even a small contribution (a documentation typo fix) may start the next great feature contributor.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why he abandoned test-first TDD as a design practice while keeping automated regression testing. He argues that driving design from isolated unit tests produces over-engineered architecture, and that the testing mix should shift from unit tests toward slower, higher-level system tests. He also warns against replacing one testing dogma with another.

chunks.heading: Why DHH stopped writing software test-first
chunks.text:
- DHH credits TDD for opening his eyes to automated regression testing and the "tranquility of a well-tested code base" and the confidence it gives people changing software.
- He treats test-first as "training wheels" that taught him to think about testing at a deeper level, which he quickly left behind.
- Over the years he watched the test-first rhetoric get "louder and angrier" and more mean-spirited. He compares test-first fundamentalism to abstinence-only sex ed: "An unrealistic, ineffective morality campaign for self-loathing and shaming."
- He describes a yoyo cycle: he would try test-first for a few weeks, feel pride when he followed it, then drop it when it started hurting his designs, and feel despair, like "falling off the wagon."
- He regrets that in public he only alluded to not doing test-first, or even kept supporting it as "the right way."
- His declaration: "My name is David, and I do not write software test-first." He refuses to apologize for it or hide it.

chunks.heading: TDD as a litmus test and identity
chunks.text:
- DHH suggests test-first may have been a counterintuitive ram to break down the industry's "sorry lack of automated, regression testing," or a parable never meant as a literal description of day-to-day software writing.
- He argues it was soon corrupted into a hammer to beat down nonbelievers, declare them unprofessional and unfit to write software, and used as a litmus test.
- TDD was so successful that it is woven into programmer identities: "TDD is not just what they do, it's who they are."
- He expects "serious deprogramming" ahead for the community, and says it will take time.
- Rather than dance on its grave, he prefers to honor test-first's contributions as an important phase in history, then move on.

chunks.heading: What test-first does to system design
chunks.text:
- DHH says to take a hard look at what test-first does to the integrity of your system design, and that honestly considering it is "not an unqualified good" is like taking the red pill.
- The design justification for test-first is that unit tests drive code design. That pushes a primary focus on unit tests.
- To keep unit tests fast, people avoid anything "slow": the database, file IO, or going through the browser to test the whole system.
- The result is an overly complex web of intermediary objects and indirection. He calls some of the architecture "truly horrendous monstrosities": a "dense jungle of service objects, command patterns, and worse."

chunks.heading: How DHH tests Rails applications
chunks.text:
- He rarely unit tests in the traditional sense, where all dependencies are mocked out and thousands of tests can finish in seconds. He says it has not been a useful way to test Rails applications.
- He tests Active Record models directly, letting them hit the database, using fixtures.
- On top of that he has a layer of controller tests, but he would rather replace those with higher-level system tests through Capybara or similar.

chunks.heading: Rebalancing the testing spectrum toward system tests
chunks.text:
- Step one is admitting there is a problem; step two is rebalancing the testing spectrum from unit to system tests.
- The direction he sees: less emphasis on unit tests, since test-first is no longer a design practice, and more emphasis on slower system tests.
- He notes system tests no longer need to be so slow, thanks to advances in parallelization and cloud runner infrastructure.
- At the time of writing, Rails had no default answer in the stack for full system tests. He called that "a mistake we're going to fix," and suggested trying Capybara in the meantime to see where Rails was heading.

chunks.heading: Avoid replacing one testing religion with another
chunks.text:
- DHH warns against rushing into another testing religion and imagines the golden calf of 'system tests only!'. He says: "Please don't go there."
- His closing line: "Long live testing." The point is to keep testing and drop the dogma that test-first is the one true design method.
- He points readers to James Coplien's "Why Most Unit Testing is Waste" and to his own RailsConf keynote on Writing Software (Parts 1 and 2) for more.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues that the maxim "code hard to unit test is poorly designed" causes test-induced design damage: needless indirection added only for fast, isolated, test-first tests. Using Jim Weirich's hexagonal Rails demo as the example, he prescribes model tests with the database, integration-tested controllers, system-tested views, and design driving tests.

chunks.heading: Core claim: "hard to unit test" does not mean "poorly designed"
chunks.text:
- DHH rejects the TDD maxim that "Code that's hard to test in isolation is poorly designed." He grants it is sometimes true, since difficulty testing can point to tangled responsibilities.
- He denies it is always true. In his view you can have well-designed code that is hard to unit test.
- He treats the maxim as the source of "test-induced design damage": changes made to facilitate (a) easier test-first, (b) speedy tests, or (c) unit tests, which harm the clarity of the code.
- The harm is usually "needless indirection and conceptual overhead", code "warped out of shape solely to accomodate testing objectives."
- Faithful TDD'ers reject that this is possible. He says a true believer sees only good from these concessions, so TDD has been "rammed down people's throats as the savior of professional programming."
- He suggests the long absence of debate came from post hoc rationalization: if red-green-refactor is the guiding light for all design, any sacrifice seems trivial ("Who cares if you need two or three extra layers of indirection to unit test a controller?"). The "TDD is dead" uprising grew under that regime.

chunks.heading: Hexagonal architecture in Rails as a case of test-driven pattern application
chunks.text:
- His example is the late Jim Weirich's demonstration of hexagonal architecture in Rails. He notes Jim was a pragmatic programmer, did not necessarily buy into it as a general approach, and that he misses him dearly.
- The justifications in that talk are all about testing: faster tests without touching the database, and testing controller logic without dependent context.
- To get there, the simple controller is forbidden from talking directly to Active Record and must go through a Repository. The action is hollowed out into a Command object, which calls back into the controller through the Listener pattern.
- His verdict: "This is not better." The code suffered "tremendous design damage" for two goals, faster tests and easy-to-mock unit-tested controllers.
- He says the same rationalization runs through other attempts to draw boundaries between "your application" and Rails.
- The hexagonal pattern itself is not to blame. It may fit systems where the web is one adapter among many on equal terms (regular GUIs, voice control) that cannot just go through a web API.
- What he objects to is applying hexagonal, boundaries and ports-and-adapters to Rails apps for the purpose of testing: "test-driven pattern application."
- A Repository over Active Record only disconnects the app from the database for "fast test" purposes. If you ignored the tests, you would not look at the after code and say "BETTER!"

chunks.heading: Controllers and views: integration and system tests, not unit tests
chunks.text:
- Unit testing Rails controllers (or similar MVC) is a mistake in his view. A controller's job is to integrate the user's request with the model's response within the context of a session.
- Mocking all of that away just to check whether it sends this redirect or that notice "doesn't make the least bit of sense." Controllers are meant to be integration tested.
- People get pulled into unit testing by default because the testing pyramid prescribes the unit level as the focus.
- Unit testing views is "equally folly." That motivation drives interest in Presenters, which he says have occasional legitimate uses.
- The view is the top layer of the MVC cake, so the right testing metaphor for most of it is end-to-end system testing.
- Resist extracting session logic (such as permission checks) or auxiliary views (like emails) into a command object just to mock boundaries and get "fast tests."
- "It's skinny controllers, not anemic controllers, we're looking for. And private methods on controllers are not evil."

chunks.heading: Model tests should hit the database
chunks.text:
- The fear of letting model tests talk to the database is outdated. Decoupling is "simply not worth it any more, even if it may once have been."
- Rails now runs a persistent console process, so the 1.2s framework boot overhead from Jim's example is gone.
- Test fixtures combined with transaction-wrapped test cases make database-backed tests very fast. He promised a separate post on "Effective test fixtures".
- Technique: avoid expensive setup per case by tailoring prototypical fixtures to each case, changing the single piece of state needed.
- If model tests are still slow, he asks whether you are "testing like the TSA." Delete redundant or anemic tests, since a test base needs regular pruning like the rest of the code.

chunks.heading: Outside-in BDD does not fix it
chunks.text:
- BDD proponents may say the goal is outside-in rather than testing units. He is "in general far more sympathetic to the goals of BDD."
- But as long as it is done under the test-first regime, it still tends to lead to excessive mocking and artificial boundaries, at least in the usage he has seen in the wild.

chunks.heading: Where to put testing emphasis, and letting design drive tests
chunks.text:
- His three-part summary for Rails/MVC:
  1. Test models with intricate logic through model tests, not separated from the database.
  2. Test controllers with integration tests.
  3. Test views through system/browser tests, especially when JavaScript powers the view.
- The emphasis depends on the app. A simple model layer with a complex UI should be system-test heavy and model-test light: "This is not a sin."
- If controllers do little interesting work, they may not need test-driving at all when system tests cover them. With little notable JavaScript, integration tests may be the right place.
- Principle: "you do not let your tests drive your design, you let your design drive your tests." The design points to which MVC layer deserves the most tests.
- Once design is no longer driven primarily by tests, the question changes: "how can I make it better" means "how can I make it clearer, not how can I test it faster or more isolated."
- Closing advice: "The design integrity of your system is far more important than being able to test it any particular layer. Stop obsessing about unit tests, embrace backfilling of tests when you're happy with the design, and strive for overall system clarity as your principle pursuit."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues the TDD rule that unit tests must not touch the database is a relic of 1990s hardware. With SSDs, local databases, Spring preloading and transactional fixtures, Basecamp's model tests run in seconds, so abstracting away the database only causes test-induced design damage.

chunks.heading: Slow database tests are a 1990s heuristic
chunks.text:
- DHH rejects the TDD rule that a "unit test" must not touch the database or other external interfaces like the file system. The rule was justified by speed, and that justification no longer holds.
- It was probably true "in 1997" when tests connected to a mainframe database or "some Oracle abomination". In 2014 you can run MySQL or PostgreSQL locally off a fast SSD, and nearly every development machine has lots of RAM, an SSD and a fast CPU.
- General principle: heuristics adopted in one era of computing do not necessarily apply in the next. Anything based on a definition of "slow" should be revisited frequently, because "sound lessons can turn unsound very quickly".
- Avoiding the database in tests is far from free in most MVC systems. It needs extra indirection and layers that scar the code base and hurt clarity (see his "test-induced design damage" essay).
- That damage may have been worth it when a full database-hitting suite took hours. It is not worth it when the suite takes a few minutes.
- His advice: "Don't pervert your architecture in order to prematurely optimize for the performance characteristics of the mid-nineties." Embrace modern hardware and keep a code base "unharmed by test-induced design damage".

chunks.heading: Basecamp test suite numbers
chunks.text:
- All Basecamp model tests run in 80 seconds: 3333 assertions, all hitting the database, all going through Active Record, all using Rails test fixtures.
- The entire suite runs in 4 minutes 30 seconds. It includes controller and integration tests that also go through the database and fixtures.
- That suite has a 1:1 test:code ratio.
- These figures are the evidence that a database-backed suite is fast enough for a good feedback cycle.

chunks.heading: Run only the tests for the code you changed
chunks.text:
- Anticipated objection: 80 seconds is too long to wait after every model change. DHH's answer: nobody should run the whole harness for every line change in a model.
- He runs just the suite for the model in question.
- If you have so little confidence in the locality of your changes that you must run everything each time, "the tests are indeed telling you that the system has overly high coupling".
- Run the full 80-second suite when the feature is ready to check in, or when taking a break, to make sure nothing broke in a far-away model.
- Combined, the two modes (targeted while working, full suite before check-in) give confidence to change things "without the anxiety of breaking stuff left and right". He says that is "the true power of testing".

chunks.heading: Spring and persistent test processes
chunks.text:
- For large Rails apps, running a single model's tests used to be painful because Rails booted the whole application each time. Basecamp took about 5 seconds to boot, which was enough to be annoying.
- Rails adopted a persistent test process through the Spring preloader.
- He compares reloading the whole application and framework on every test run to CGI: it was a bad model for any complicated web application, and it is a bad model for running tests.
- With Spring, the entire test suite for the Basecamp Person model (52 cases, 111 assertions) runs in just under 4 seconds from start to finish. He calls that plenty fast for a great feedback cycle.

chunks.heading: Why fixtures are fast: transaction rollback
chunks.text:
- Part of the speed comes from Rails test fixtures. Default Rails fixtures are reset per test case so each case runs in isolation, but this is done with a transaction wrapper.
- Before each test case: BEGIN TRANSACTION. At the end of the case: ROLLBACK TRANSACTION.
- DHH calls this "crazy fast", with no setup penalty per test.
- He lists fixtures as a "killer Rails feature" and one reason hitting the database in every test stays cheap.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues tests have real costs, so developers must learn what not to test. He gives seven blunt rules for a typical Rails app (no 100% coverage, watch test ratios and time spent, skip testing framework basics, mostly test-after) and calls blanket coverage "TSA-style testing". He backs it with Kent Beck's "test as little as possible to reach a given level of confidence".

chunks.heading: Tests have a cost, so the benefit must exceed it
chunks.text:
- DHH argues that testing has a price, the way every line of code does: "it takes time to write it, it takes time to update it, and it takes time to read and understand it."
- The benefit derived must be greater than the cost to make it. In the case of over-testing, he says that is by definition not the case.
- He frames the question as: "What's the cost to prevent a bug?" If it takes 1,000 lines of validation testing to catch the one time someone removed `validates_presence_of :name`, it was not worth it.
- The exception is critical systems (his joke example is an airport control system launching rockets to Mars). Most applications are not that.
- He rejects the "if we catch just one bug, isn't it worth it?" argument. In his words: "This line of argument is how we got the TSA", which squandered billions "fondling balls and confiscating nail clippers."
- He calls the result "coverage theater of quality" and says very few applications run at a level of criticality that warrants testing everything.

chunks.heading: Learn what not to test early, before bad habits set in
chunks.text:
- Discovering test-driven development feels like entering a better world with less stress and insecurity, and DHH says that is worth celebrating.
- The harder lesson is knowing what not to test. A beginner need not worry on day one, but should start picking it up by day two.
- Humans are creatures of habit. Forming over-testing habits early makes them hard to shake later, and "shake them you must."
- Over-testing is hard to call out because it does not boil down to a catchy phrase. Test-first and red-green are succinct and sexy, which helped TDD reach center stage.
- Testing only what is useful "takes nuance, experience, and dozens of fine-grained heuristics."
- He wishes one or two of the hundreds of TDD getting-started books focused on taming the beast rather than repeating the same bowling and bacon examples.

chunks.heading: Seven rules of thumb for testing a typical Rails app
chunks.text:
DHH presents these as deliberately nuance-free opinions for a typical Rails application:

1. Don't aim for 100% coverage.
2. Code-to-test ratios above 1:2 are a smell, above 1:3 a stink.
3. You're probably doing it wrong if testing takes more than 1/3 of your time, and definitely wrong if it takes more than half.
4. Don't test standard Active Record associations, validations, or scopes.
5. Reserve integration testing for problems that come from integrating separate elements. Don't integration test what a unit test can cover.
6. Don't use Cucumber unless you live in the "magic kingdom of non-programmers-writing-tests."
7. Don't force test-first on every controller, model, and view. His own ratio is typically 20% test-first and 80% test-after.

chunks.heading: Test as little as needed for a given level of confidence
chunks.text:
- DHH endorses Kent Beck, "the man who deserves the most credit for popularizing test-driven development."
- The quote he leans on: "I get paid for code that works, not for tests, so my philosophy is to test as little as possible to reach a given level of confidence."
- Beck's corollary, which DHH endorses: "If I don't typically make a kind of mistake (like setting the wrong variables in a constructor), I don't test for it."
- The goal is working software, and tests are a means to that end.

chunks.heading: Weigh both criticality and likelihood of a mistake
chunks.text:
- In reply to a commenter arguing for testing anything that would cost money if it failed, DHH agrees criticality matters but says it is not the only factor.
- "If you don't also consider the likelihood of a mistake, you're definitely TSA testing."
- A trivial declaration that you are unlikely to get wrong is not worth a test, even when the nominal consequence of failure sounds serious.
- He applies the same heuristics to everything he writes, whether a framework used by thousands (Rails) or an app used by millions (Basecamp).

chunks.heading: Client-side testing costs more, so test less there
chunks.text:
- DHH agrees the burden of automated testing on the client side is much higher, and says "much TOO high."
- Applying the cost/criticality logic ("much greater cost, much lower criticality = much less testing"), 37signals does not test nearly as much on the client side as on the server side.

chunks.heading: Integration tests and Cucumber don't replace design
chunks.text:
- Integration tests are for problems arising from integrating separate elements, not for re-covering what unit tests already cover. Cucumber is not required to write integration tests.
- Pushing back on claims that Cucumber or integration tests help "design" the app, DHH says figuring out what the app should do is what designers are for. If you haven't worked that out before writing tests, "it's too late."
- He sees little value in pinning down a feature with an a priori integration test: a feature can be implemented in many ways depending on how the design is constructed.
- He says that argument mainly helps teams without designers, and dislikes the idea that designers just produce the CSS.
- He asks how integration testing helps design a system's internals, given that its whole point is to treat the system as a black box.
- For unit tests, the way tests help him is by ensuring he doesn't regress while refactoring. He considers that the key attribute of testing and files it under "don't create bugs", not "helped me design."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH frames Rails as an omakase meal: a small team of chefs picks the ingredients and APIs into one opinionated, personal full-stack framework.
