Substitutions are allowed within reason, but loud demands from people who haven't contributed carry little weight; influence is earned by showing up with code.

chunks.heading: Omakase: a framework as a curated menu, not à la carte
chunks.text:
- DHH contrasts à la carte environments (pick your own ORM, template language, routing library) with Rails, which is "omakase".
- In Rails, "a team of chefs picked out the ingredients, designed the APIs, and arranged the order of consumption" for a full-stack framework.
- The menu is "personal and quirky". It "isn't designed to appeal to the taste of everyone, everywhere."
- He admits à la carte is a popular way to consume software. It also demands that you already know what you want, and he notes you rarely get your horizons expanded by always ordering the same thing.

chunks.heading: Substitutions are allowed, within reason
chunks.text:
- Omakase does not mean no exceptions. Patrons can swap parts out.
- Examples he gives: don't like test/unit, bring your own rspec. Don't like CoffeeScript, delete a single line from your Gemfile.
- Defaults are a starting point. Opting out of a default should be cheap, so disagreeing costs little.
- The menu is also open to suggestions: "Good ideas are good ideas regardless of where they come from."

chunks.heading: Friendly suggestion versus belligerent diner
chunks.text:
- The line between the two shows up when a suggestion is declined. The right reply is "I'm sorry, but hotdogs don't really fit our sushi menu... But thanks for the suggestions!"
- Many arguments carry on after that point. He mocks the shouting version: "BUT I REALLY DON'T LIKE UNAGI!!! ... TAKE IT OOOOOOFFFFF!!"
- His answer to that is to sit down and "have a sake". The default course does not get changed to appease it.
- If you disagree about a feature, the conclusion is likely to be 'then don't eat that'.

chunks.heading: Why the head chef's taste decides the menu
chunks.text:
- When a dish is included, "it's usually based on our distilled tastes and preferences."
- He cites his own experience: a decade working on Rails and "well in the excess of ten thousand hours" poured into it.
- He claims this doesn't make his tastes right for you, but "it certainly means that they're well formed."
- He rejects "my opinion is as valid as yours" as applied to the menu: "Your opinion is valid _for you_, but most certainly not for the menu I've designed in this restaurant."
- The weight of an opinion scales with time spent in the establishment. First-time patrons, and people far from the kitchen, carry less, especially when the opinion is loud and obnoxious.

chunks.heading: Vote with your feet
chunks.text:
- Your standing power is to leave. "If most things on the menu disgust you, what on earth are you still doing at the table? The door is right over there."
- To shape the menu over the long term, you have to work your way up to it.
- He gives a concrete example: three more people were added to the Rails core group "this week" who did exactly that.
- They arrived in one of two ways: with a "what can I do to help?" directive, or with "here's a dish I've designed, have a taste and see if you like it."
- His claim: "Nobody ever got to have a meaningful impact on the direction of Rails by contributing no code and just showing up in a Github comment thread and yelling about the evils of CoffeeScript."

chunks.heading: Why people argue about defaults anyway
chunks.text:
- His "pet theory" is that yelling feels like meaningful activism in the moment. People haven't followed day-to-day project work, but it's a chance to "paint some signs and get on the barricades."
- He mocks the shifting target: "Turbolinks? Or was it CoffeeScript we're protesting this week? Or Bundler?"
- He treats this as futile behavior.

chunks.heading: Evaluating a framework by the bigger picture
chunks.text:
- His test for a prospective user is two questions: "Do I generally like what's being served in this establishment?" and "Can I express my differences as exceptions or substitutions to the few things I don't care for?"
- If both answers are yes, give the maintainers "the benefit of assuming that they are working on what they truly think is the best way to go."
- You don't have to like everything. You can still drop the idea that a disliked default is "a conspiracy to make the world love unagi as a sick joke."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues microservices/SOA suit organizations with thousands of developers, and copying them is cargo culting. Small teams should build an integrated "majestic monolith" that removes needless abstraction and stays understandable by individuals, as Basecamp does with about 12 programmers across six platforms.

chunks.heading: Why the monolith fits small teams and not behemoths
chunks.text:
- DHH separates patterns about code from patterns about "how the code is being written, by whom, and within which organization." The Majestic Monolith is the second kind.
- Micro/services oriented architecture (M/SOA) breaks an application into many smaller parts, each run as its own application, with the constellation solving the larger problem.
- He calls M/SOA "a great pattern" for Amazon, Google or any organization with thousands of developers. Each service can be its own team with its own timeline, staff and objectives, evolving somewhat independently. At that scale there is "simply no other reasonable way" to coordinate effort, or everyone steps on each other and endless merge conflicts follow.
- M/SOA fits the organizational shape of very large corporations. The mistake is copying them: "hey it works for The Most Successful, I'm sure it'll work for me too."
- He calls this cargo culting. Patterns that suit organizations orders of magnitude larger are often the exact opposite of what suits you. The same goes for non-technical patterns: you shouldn't run HR like a 50,000-person company when you have 50.

chunks.heading: Why premature services are a bad trade
chunks.text:
- Prematurely turning an application into services violates "the #1 rule of distributed computing: Don't distribute your computing!" if you can avoid it.
- Every time you extract a collaboration between objects into a collaboration between systems, you accept "a world of hurt with a myriad of liabilities and failure states."
- Examples of that pain:
  - what to do when services are down
  - how to migrate in concert
  - the cost of running many services in the first place
- He says the pain is worth it when you have no choice, but most people do have a choice.

chunks.heading: What a majestic monolith is
chunks.text:
- It is "an integrated system that collapses as many unnecessary conceptual models as possible." It eliminates as much needless abstraction as you can swing a hammer at.
- It is a big no to distributing your system unless that truly prevents you from doing what needs to be done.
- "Monolithic" is usually said in derision. DHH says to embrace it with pride.
- The point is to choose a monolithic design with intent, not drift into one: "Any monolith worth erecting is worth making majestic!"
- An accidental monolith cannot meet the goal of beautiful, understandable, succinct code. It "just gotta be majestic."

chunks.heading: Basecamp as the case study
chunks.text:
- DHH has written Basecamp as a majestic monolith since 2003. Basecamp 3 extends the pattern to the web and all native platforms.
- Platforms: web, iOS, Android, Mac, Windows and email (6 in total).
- Team: about 12 programmers (many busy keeping decade-old systems running) and 7 designers, counting Jason, his partner and CEO.
- Size of the app:
  - hundreds of screens
  - 200 controllers with 900 methods
  - 190 model classes with 1,473 methods
  - this counts only what is inside `app/*`, not the front end such as the Trix text editor
- Scale and commitments: millions of users, plus a back catalogue of apps committed to being maintained "until The End of the Internet."
- His summary: "a very broad scope, deep commitments, and a very small budget."
- That situation is incompatible with a labour-intensive pattern like M/SOA. It is also incompatible with writing 100% native apps, but it fits the hybrid application model "like a glove."
- He believes the only way a team of about 12 programmers can cover six platforms concurrently is to choose and commit to the Majestic Monolith.

chunks.heading: Understanding, ownership and code quality
chunks.text:
- A majestic monolith presumes that the people who work on it also understand it. Knowledge and responsibility are easier to silo with a proliferation of smaller systems.
- He saw this with the few external shared services Basecamp has, such as Basecamp ID (shared authentication for all generations of the app): "Oh, you gotta talk to Jeff about that."
- This puts "immense pressure on making the application understandable and changeable by individuals, not teams." That forces you to take the time to turn a long letter into a short one.
- Slipping standards matter more in a shared monolith: "you're not just pissing in your own corner, you're pissing all over that majestic monolith we all have to polish every day."
- The mission is code that makes you smile when you write it and when you later extend or patch it.

chunks.heading: Rails philosophy and the limits of architecture
chunks.text:
- The pattern reflects Ruby and Rails' view of programmers: given the right incentives and nudges, most will rise to the occasion and write beautiful code.
- Systems should be "a red carpet invitation to become a better, more productive programmer."
- He doesn't worry about people who use the tools and patterns to hurt themselves. Maybe everyone needs to do that once or twice before appreciating the ropes that guide them.
- The Majestic Monolith "doesn't pretend to provide a failsafe architectural road to glory." Programmers under oppressive influences can turn any architecture, in any tool, into a big pile of mud.
- Worrying too much about saving people who are likely out of reach is unproductive and pulls the ones who do care down the wrong path.
- His summary: if you run a small team, not a tech behemoth, embrace the monolith and make it majestic.

chunks.heading: Does it still hold? DHH's 2019 answer
chunks.text:
- In a comment, a reader asked in 2019 whether the view still stood, given a very small team (about 5) considering M/SOA and whether tooling had improved enough to make it manageable.
- DHH replied that he saw no fundamental improvement that alters the equation.
- His rule of thumb: "Integrate your systems until it's impossible for one person to hold it all in their head."
- He said Basecamp and their other apps had still not reached that point.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues most web apps should start and stay as a Majestic Monolith, whose limits are far higher than architects imagine. If scale or team size ever demands it, extend into a Citadel: the monolith stays at the center, supported by a few small Outposts for divergent slices. Basecamp's Campfire poller is the example.

chunks.heading: The Majestic Monolith as the default architecture
chunks.text:
- DHH argues the vast majority of web applications should start life as a Majestic Monolith: "A single codebase that does everything the application needs to do."
- This contrasts with a constellation of services, whether micro or macro, that carves the application into little islands each doing a piece of the work.
- He says the vast majority of applications will be served well by the monolith for their entire lifespan.
- The limits of the pattern are "much higher than most people like to imagine when they fantasize about being capital-a Architects."
- He expects the pendulum to swing back as more people realize the chase for microservices "ended in a blind alley". The monolith is waiting for "microservice refugees".

chunks.heading: When a monolith may need help, and what to try first
chunks.text:
- Two situations he names where a monolith might need support:
  - Very large teams that constantly trip over each other. He adds that many very large organizations use the monorepo pattern, so size alone is not proof.
  - Performance or availability problems under extreme load that cannot be fixed within the monolith's technology choices.
- His rule: the first instinct should be to improve the Majestic Monolith until it can cope.
- Only after having tried that and failed should you look to the next step.
- The next step is the Citadel, not a wholesale carve-up into services.

chunks.heading: The Citadel pattern: a monolith at the center with Outposts
chunks.text:
- The Citadel keeps the Majestic Monolith at the center, supported by a set of Outposts.
- Each Outpost extracts a small subset of application responsibilities.
- Outposts let the monolith offload a slice of divergent behavior for organizational, performance, or implementation reasons.
- The key contrast with microservices: you extract a single Outpost, not the whole app. "We didn't try to carve the entire app up into little services, each written in a different language."
- The Citadel is there to give peace of mind that the pattern will stretch if an app ever hits "that jackpot of becoming a mega-scale app".

chunks.heading: Case study: Campfire's polling Outpost at Basecamp
chunks.text:
- Campfire, Basecamp's old chat app, was built in 2005 when Ajax was still novel, so it used polling rather than persistent connections.
- Every connected client fired a request every three seconds asking "are there any new messages for me?".
- Most replies were "no", but each still required authenticating the request and querying the database.
- That service had very different performance characteristics from the rest of the app: roughly 99% of all requests at any given time.
- It was also a very simple system. In Ruby it was, by his recollection, about 20 lines. That made it a perfect Outpost candidate.
- Because it could usually be written in a few hundred lines in any language, rewriting this Outpost in high-performance languages became a hobby. It was written in C, C++, Go, Erlang, and a few others he may be forgetting.
- The rest of the application stayed a Majestic Monolith in Ruby on Rails.
- Later, Campfire was retired. Basecamp 3 has chat built in using Action Cable inside the monolith, and it needs no Outposts to scale.

chunks.heading: How Outposts talk to the monolith
chunks.text:
- Campfire's poller integrated through the database. It fetched directly from the monolith's database, so no additional chatting between services was needed.
- HEY's inbound email intake is another Outpost-style setup:
  - Postfix receives the inbound email and can buffer it on disk if the app is down.
  - It then POSTs the raw email to a monolith controller, via a dead-simple HTTP request in a shell script called by postfix.
  - The raw email goes onto Action Mailbox, which decides whether to record or reject it. All of that logic lives within the monolith.
  - The emails themselves are stored in encrypted cloud storage.
- He says both integration styles (shared database, or HTTP POST to a monolith controller) work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues programmers should trade brevity for clarity in variable and method names, citing long Basecamp method names as examples. Names should express intention rather than implementation, which removes most need for comments. In replies he credits Kent Beck's Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns as the bible on this.

chunks.heading: DHH names for intention, not implementation
chunks.text:
- DHH argues that many programmers prefer short variable and method names, and rarely recognize it as trading clarity for brevity.
- He says writing terse code can still be a joy while spelling things out in abundant detail. Modern languages are expressive enough that what you save in boilerplate can be spent on clarity.
- He cringes at abbreviations like `ext` for extension and `cp` for copy. Worse are application-specific abbreviations "sure to be forgotten two months after you left the project".
- On very long names: being exceedingly clear can seem silly at first, even when the name is longer than the operation it labels. The silliness fades the first time you return to the code and know exactly what it does.
- In the comments, he answers a worry that a name is almost as long as its code: "The method name explains the intention, the code the implementation." He says he has often had names longer than the implementation, especially when explaining variables.
- His example: `someone_else_just_finished_writing?` is "completely divorced from whether we implement this using events and how long 'just' is." The name states the domain intent, so the implementation can change without renaming.

chunks.heading: Examples from the new Basecamp codebase
chunks.text:
DHH offers three long method names from the new Basecamp code as models:

- `make_person_an_outside_subscriber_if_all_accesses_revoked`: a one-line body, `person.update_attribute(:outside_subscriber, true) if person.reload.accesses.blank?`.
- `shift_records_upward_starting_at(position)`: runs `positioned_records.update_all "position = position - 1", ["position >= ?", position]`.
- `someone_else_just_finished_writing?(document)`: checks the document's current version event, returning true when it was not by the current creator and `event.updated_at > 1.minute.ago`.

Each name tells the reader what the code is for, and the body tells how it is done.

chunks.heading: Comments as a code smell
chunks.text:
- DHH says that if you work hard at being clear in naming, you will rarely need comments.
- His rule: "Comments are generally only needed when you failed to be clear enough in naming. Treat them as a code smell."
- The practical effect is to move explanation into names instead of prose that sits beside the code.

chunks.heading: Line length and the 80-character convention
chunks.text:
- He calls the "Church of 80-character Lines" ridiculous and says it pushes programmers toward terse names.
- His point is that line-length limits cause the brevity-for-clarity trade, so he would drop the limit before shortening a name.
- Laborious boilerplate is what a good language removes; the lines it frees are meant to buy clarity.

chunks.heading: Books and prior art he endorses
chunks.text: - He calls Kent Beck's *Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns* "the bible on this", and says he has never read a book with so much good advice about programming in such a small volume. It is "golden".

chunks.heading: Tooling: no heavy autocomplete needed
chunks.text:
- Asked whether long names depend on IDE autocompletion, DHH says most methods are not called often enough to warrant automation.
- He uses plain escape-key completion in TextMate and says that has been fine.
- Long names are not a typing burden in his workflow, so the clarity gain costs almost nothing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues that abstractions like Active Record have compressed the database into an appliance, so beginners can build database-backed apps without learning SQL. Progress means making yesterday's fundamentals optional, unpackable on demand, and lowering barriers to entry. Experienced programmers shouldn't cling to hardships the next generation doesn't have to endure.

chunks.heading: Conceptual compression: abstractions that hide fundamentals
chunks.text:
- DHH calls this "conceptual compression": advances in (leaky) abstractions have compressed the conceptual overhead of the database so far that beginners no longer need to learn SQL before building database-backed applications.
- It used to be taken as self-evident that you had to speak the database's native language, and care about your particular database engine, before you were qualified to use it. He says that is no longer so, and he calls that "amazing".
- In Rails the abstraction is Active Record, an object-relational mapper (ORM).
- ORMs were long derided as an unreliable, even harmful, aid of "the lazy or the weak", something "Real Programmers" shouldn't lean on because it would break down soon and you'd better know all your relational theory. He says that is "the past".
- The same compression already happened with memory management and garbage collection: pointers, destructors and mallocs were once foundational, and now application programmers rarely think about them.
- He concedes SQL abstraction isn't yet at the level of memory management, and some frameworks and environments are further along than others, but it's getting closer.

chunks.heading: Evidence from Basecamp: no SQL in the application logic
chunks.text:
- Basecamp 3 has about 42,000 lines of code and "not a single fully formed SQL statement as part of application logic". It serves millions of people.
- It leans on the ORM abstraction and "hardly even thinks about it the vast majority of the time".
- The first version of Basecamp had a bunch of `find_by_sql` calls; the latest versions have none. He calls that progress.
- DHH used to write SQL statements every day. Now he writes them maybe once a month, or less, against a major application at a scale most beginner apps never reach.

chunks.heading: Unpack concepts when you need them, then compress again
chunks.text:
- Knowing SQL is still nice to have, just as a strong mental model of memory management is helpful. The point is that you no longer need it to start making applications.
- SQL is a concept you can "unpack when you need to", further down your career. Once learned, you can compress it back down and spend most of your mental capacity on other things.
- You can't learn everything or hold every concept fully expanded in your head, "and moreover, you shouldn't".
- Compressing formerly fundamental concepts makes room for new, grander abstractions. He describes those as the leaps of progress that make programmers more efficient and effective.

chunks.heading: The database as an appliance and a commodity
chunks.text:
- His analogy: the relational database is "a glorious invention", but for most programmers it doesn't need to be more than an appliance. Take the time to learn how a drying tumbler works because it may save a service call one day, but it's not a requirement for getting your clothes dry.
- Appliance status is "not a dig, but an honor": the technology and abstraction are so good that most programmers don't think about it daily.
- It also makes the database a commodity. Basecamp uses MySQL "basically only for historical and operational reasons". He says they could switch to PostgreSQL tomorrow and he "wouldn't really give a damn", because nothing in the application relies on a particular database brand.
- Software is always built on layers of abstraction: CPUs, 1s and 0s, assembler, C compilers, database drivers, memory management and more. As the industry progresses, fewer people need to know all of them, and he says "thank heavens for that".

chunks.heading: Why low barriers and generalists matter
chunks.text:
- Improving conceptual compression is hard but "incredibly rewarding" work. The more effectively yesterday's concepts are compressed, the lower the barriers to entry, and "we need low barriers if we are to get more people started making applications."
- He names SQL as perhaps the brightest example of conceptual compression over the past decade or so, but says application work is full of others.
- Compression is needed more than ever "to starve off specialization, and to preserve the power of individual generalists to make complete applications."

chunks.heading: Next target: front-end build pipelines
chunks.text:
- He sees an explosion of conceptual expansion and experimentation on the client side of web applications in 2018. It is exciting, with many new ideas churning rapidly, but also "needlessly intimidating in many ways".
- Not everyone should have to spend hours or days learning to configure build pipelines. He expects leaky abstractions to get good enough that this tooling is relegated to appliance status too, and says "That will be a good day."

chunks.heading: Against the fogey instinct
chunks.text:
- Some programmers instinctively scoff, saying it's irresponsible to write code before knowing the historical fundamentals. DHH calls this a key pitfall of experience: falling in love with the trials you suffered, rather than rejoicing that the next generation doesn't have to endure them.
- He compares it to an old person complaining about the price of gas or milk because their frame of reference is anchored in the past. Broad-based progress sometimes needs generational churn, which he says is about years of experience rather than physical age.
- His closing instruction: "Don't be a fogey. Don't fight the conceptual compression. Help make it happen."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH announces Turbo 8 is dropping TypeScript. He explains he likes modern JavaScript, dislikes the compile step and type gymnastics, and argues programmers pick a typing camp early and rationalize it. He still respects TypeScript users and values compatibility.

chunks.heading: Dropping TypeScript from Turbo 8: the decision
chunks.text:
- DHH announced in September 2023 that Turbo 8 drops TypeScript, and says he is glad to do it.
- He has never been a fan of TypeScript, "not after giving it five minutes, not after giving it five years".
- Many people love adding explicit, compiler-checked types to JavaScript, and he acknowledges TypeScript has been a big success for Microsoft.
- He frames the move as a personal preference for his own code, not a call to convert anyone.

chunks.heading: Why he prefers plain modern JavaScript
chunks.text:
- He likes JavaScript, calling it his second favorite language after Ruby, though "a distant second".
- He did not always feel this way. Proper classes and the other improvements since ES6 made it "a real joy to write".
- He does not think JavaScript suits most server-side web app work, but respects people who feel differently.
- Browsers can interpret modern JavaScript with no compiler at all, which he sees as good fortune.

chunks.heading: What bothers him about TypeScript
chunks.text:
- It adds an explicit compile step, which gets in the way of running JavaScript directly in the browser.
- It "pollutes the code with type gymnastics" that add very little joy to his development experience and often considerable grief.
- His summary of the experience: "Things that should be easy become hard, and things that are hard become `any`."

chunks.heading: Why people rarely change their mind on typing
chunks.text:
- He points back to his essay "Programming types and mindsets".
- Few programmers want their opinion on typing changed.
- Most people are drawn strongly to typing or to dynamic languages early in their career, then spend the rest of it rationalizing "The Correct Choice" to themselves and others.
- He is not trying to persuade anyone, in line with that view.

chunks.heading: Compatibility: mix and match
chunks.text:
- He credits the TypeScript team for realizing a full take-over of JavaScript was never going to happen, so complete compatibility with JavaScript was built in from the start.
- Dropping TypeScript from Turbo does not stop anyone from writing client code in TypeScript or using libraries that employ it.
- He calls this ability to mix and match "wonderful".

chunks.heading: JavaScript as a language of necessity
chunks.text:
- He contrasts Ruby, a language of choice on the server, with JavaScript, a language of necessity on the client.
- Dialects can be compiled into JavaScript, but running code in the browser still means running JavaScript.
- Given that, he sees being able to write it "free of any tooling, and free of any strong typing" as a blessing.
- His sign-off: TypeScript can bring rigor and satisfaction to its tribe, while the rest of us enjoy JavaScript "free of strong typing", in the spirit it was originally designed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH responds to the backlash after Turbo 8 dropped TypeScript. He separates good-faith technical objections from pile-ons by outsiders, argues a project may choose its own tools without being attacked, and notes TypeScript is still JavaScript, a superset that adds an appearance of type safety to a weakly, dynamically typed language.

chunks.heading: DHH's reaction to the TypeScript backlash after Turbo 8 dropped it
chunks.text:
- DHH describes the response to 37signals dropping TypeScript from Turbo (Sept 2023) as a "full-on meltdown" and "open source hooliganism".
- He separates two groups: active contributors and users of Turbo who had legitimate technical objections, whom he is happy to debate in good faith, and people with no stake in Turbo who showed up "spoiling for a fight".
- The second group carried most of the debate. They framed anyone who dropped TypeScript as incompetent or malevolent, defending the "honor" of the language.
- Behavior he cites:
  - Pull requests to add TypeScript back
  - A pull request to delete the Turbo repository
  - An issue to remove him from the project
  - Pile-ons of emojis, rockets and "LGTM"s
- He points out that 37signals founded and funded Turbo and remains its primary maintainer.

chunks.heading: Why he saw the backlash as unjustified
chunks.text:
- The decision was one project, mostly overseen by one company, removing TypeScript from its own code and explaining why.
- It left ample room and spirit for others to reach different conclusions for their own work.
- He says a reaction like this might have had a sliver of justification only if the decision had been a tirade against TypeScript, a wholesale denigration of its users, or a petition for Microsoft to shut it down. It was none of those.

chunks.heading: Evangelist versus dogmatic crusader
chunks.text:
- DHH smiles at people with passionate preferences. He sees it as good that people care enough about their craft to extol their favorite tools.
- He draws a "fine line" between a passionate evangelist and a dogmatic crusader.
- Crusading for technology is old: he recalls Newsgroup flamewars over the Sony PlayStation versus the Sega Saturn, fought by overzealous nerds citing "The Facts".
- He admits he used to dance that line himself in the early days of Ruby on Rails.
- Even so, he says he would have found it "absolutely inconceivable" to show up in someone's open source repository to deface its "collaboration organs".
- He calls this a new variety of open source advocacy, closer to hooliganism than to 1990s console flamewars, and "entirely unbecoming for a profession like ours".
- He expects most people who genuinely care about TypeScript to look back on it with ambivalence or shame.

chunks.heading: TypeScript is JavaScript, and the bikeshed
chunks.text:
- DHH calls the animosity "a weird exhibition of self-loathing in the choice of technology".
- His description of TypeScript: "a superset that sprinkles an appearance of type safety on top of a weakly- and dynamically-typed language."
- He sees the rage toward people who use the plain JavaScript subset as an example of the ferocity and viciousness of minor differences.
- He invokes the bikeshed parable: when stakes are low, debate gets nastier.
- Whether to use compiler-based type checking is, in his words, "so ultimately unresolvable" that it invites hooliganism. It lets people drop inhibitions for a match, repeated season after season. He calls it "the exercise of the Id".

chunks.heading: His position on tool preference and open source culture
chunks.text:
- He is glad if people found their calling in TypeScript, and calls himself an "unapologetic superfan of Ruby".
- His ask: find another way to express enthusiasm than defacing collaboration spaces or slandering people who "JavaScript differently" with accusations of incompetence or malice.
- He frames this as a matter of open source culture and professional conduct, not a verdict on whether static typing is right for everyone.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH says he is a dynamic typing person who loves Ruby for its poetic syntax, and he dislikes static typing. He used to evangelize dynamic typing as a mark of better education or competence. He now sees typing preferences as matters of faith and personality, and values multiplicity in programming paradigms.

chunks.heading: Types are a matter of mindset, not correctness
chunks.text:
- DHH says the static vs dynamic typing schism has run for his whole career, and "very few" of the million arguments from either side ever convinced anyone.
- He calls these arguments "rationalizations masquerading as reason" in matters of faith: "The rider will always justify the way of the elephant."
- Converts tend to "shout the loudest rationalizations of all": "The shorter the faith, the brighter the flame."
- Functional vs object-oriented programming falls in the same category. Poles on both axes have delivered excellent software over the decades (and awful stuff too).

chunks.heading: DHH's own position: dynamic typing and Ruby
chunks.text:
- He is "unashamedly a dynamic typing kind of guy", and that is why he loves Ruby.
- Ruby takes full advantage of dynamic typing to allow the "poetic syntax that results in such beautiful code".
- Ruby with explicit, static typing would be "like a salad with a scoop of ice cream. They just don't go together."
- He does not enjoy static typing, and objects animate [his] mind's eye.
- His line in the sand: he never wants to "soil [his] Ruby with type hints" or write all front-end code in TypeScript.

chunks.heading: Why he stopped evangelizing
chunks.text:
- He admits he used to hold the evangelical position for dynamic typing, to the point of a "One True Proposition affliction".
- He read lack of enthusiasm for dynamic typing as a sign of missing education, experience, or competence. He calls that "folly".
- He compares it to convincing an introvert they would love parties if they loosened up, and that shouting in crowded rooms for hours is actually fun.
- He describes himself as a "recovering solutionist" who now smiles at people incredulous that anyone could prefer JavaScript over TypeScript, because he recognizes that zeal from his own past.

chunks.heading: The case for multiplicity in programming
chunks.text:
- He has come to appreciate "the magnificence of multiplicity". Programming would be an "awful endeavor" if everyone were confined to one paradigm.
- Human nature is too varied to accept such a constraint on creativity.
- His analogy: imagine all visual art in cubism or realism, or all novels in Hemingway's short, direct style. It would be a bore.
- Uniformity would "ruin the magic of programming", which he calls a unique fusion of art and engineering.

chunks.heading: Limits of the relativism and coexistence
chunks.text:
- Not every programming disagreement is equal-but-different mindsets. He says "there are limits to this relativism", but static vs dynamic typing and functional vs OO sit within them.
- People can express themselves equally well from either end, but being ambidextrous is rare. The evidence is the "utter disbelief" each side expresses that the other might hold a reasonable position.
- He accepts that others "illuminate their creativity with just as much intensity" using functional constraints and explicit types.
- His coexistence deal: as long as he never has to add type hints to Ruby or write all front-end code in TypeScript, he can happily coexist with people who adore Go or can't stand JavaScript. "Vive la différence!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues that Rails system tests, despite high hopes in 2016, remain slow, brittle and full of false negatives. He keeps a small top-level smoke test, relies on model and controller tests for business logic, and prefers human exploratory testing for UI logic and feel. HEY is cutting its roughly 300 system tests way down.

chunks.heading: Why DHH thinks system tests have failed
chunks.text:
- DHH introduced the default system test setup in Rails 5.1 in 2016 with "high hopes". The theory: tests that drive a headless browser through the real interface give more confidence that the whole machine works, and as black-box tests they should survive implementation changes.
- In practice he has found none of this true. System tests "remain as slow, brittle, and full of false negatives as they did a decade ago."
- His bottom line: "I've wasted far more time getting system tests to work reliably than I have seen dividends from bugs caught." Most of the time they are no longer worth the effort.
- He gives several reasons for the malaise:
  - Browsers are complicated.
  - UI driven by JavaScript is prone to timing issues.
  - Working out WHY a black-box test failed is often surprisingly difficult.

chunks.heading: What automated testing is for, and why system tests don't serve it
chunks.text:
- DHH says we automate testing for three reasons: a quick feedback loop on changes, catching regressions, and most of all, becoming confident that the system works.
- These goals are valid, but he argues system testing is not the best way to fulfill them.
- Business logic is better and more cheaply tested with model and controller tests, not system tests.
- The sticky problem is testing UI logic, which means testing JavaScript. He says he is "not sure we're there yet on the automated front."

chunks.heading: What to keep: a small top-level smoke test
chunks.text:
- DHH is not saying to throw out every system test. He says to cut "probably most of them."
- System tests work well as a top-level smoke test. Their end-to-end nature tends to catch not domain model or business logic problems, but a configuration or interaction problem that stops the system from loading at all.
- Catching that kind of failure early and cheaply is good.

chunks.heading: Human tests beat automation for UI logic
chunks.text:
- The method that gives DHH the most confidence that UI logic is good is not system tests but "human tests": literally clicking around in a real browser by hand.
- Half the time, UI testing is not only "does it work" but also "does it feel right". In his words, "No automation can tell you that."
- He recommends embracing the human element of system testing (linking 37signals' piece on the value of human exploratory testing).
- He leaves open that AI might take over this task one day, but says "as of today, I think we're better off dropping the automation."

chunks.heading: Applying it at HEY: cutting 300-odd system tests
chunks.text:
- HEY has some 300-odd system tests today. 37signals is doing a "grand review" to cut that number way down.
- DHH says the sunk cost fallacy kept the team running "this brittle, cumbersome suite for too long."
- The plan is to cut losses and reduce system tests to a much smaller part of the confidence equation, leaning on model and controller tests for logic and manual exploration for UI behavior.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues against chopping features into tiny, short-lived pull requests. Letting a PR run as long as a complete feature needs (weeks, up to six under Shape Up) lets reviewers see trade-offs and design decisions in context, protecting design standards and cohesive architecture. Merge-conflict costs are real but manageable for most teams.

chunks.heading: Why DHH prefers large, long-running pull requests
chunks.text:
- DHH's favorite part of code review is seeing "all the trade-offs, design decisions, and changes in context together."
- That is hard when a feature is chopped into "itty bitty pieces as independent pull requests under pressure never to let them run longer than a week."
- At Basecamp, pull requests run as long as they need to cover a complete feature or fix: from a few weeks up to six weeks, because the team follows Shape Up.
- He argues the PR-size debate "focuses mostly on the cost, not on the value." The value is "tremendous to any organization that seeks to keep high design standards and a cohesive architecture."

chunks.heading: The merge conflict trade-off and how to manage it
chunks.text:
- DHH admits the approach has a cost: the longer a PR runs off the main branch, the greater the chance of merge conflicts.
- His mitigation is to keep the pull request up to date by frequently merging main into it.
- He accepts that very large organizations with high traffic on the same bits of code might hit a point where this doesn't cut it, but asks "is that really you?"
- At Basecamp it has never been a serious problem. Several teams have often worked on the same product in close proximity. Conflicts occasionally happen, but he can't remember the last time they seriously impeded the work.
- He acknowledges the cost still exists and may grow with organization size.

chunks.heading: Externalities of piecemeal code review
chunks.text:
- DHH frames fragmented review as a source of negative externalities.
- His metaphor: high design standards and a cohesive architecture "bank the rivers of clear code." Pouring in partial, I-haven't-seen-the-end pull requests pollutes those pristine waters.
- Each one looks like a harmless drop in the river, but if you keep it up, "eventually the rivers no longer run clear."
- The damage isn't obvious right away, which is why it accumulates.

chunks.heading: What gets lost when you review pieces without the whole
chunks.text:
- Code that didn't embrace a key insight that would simplify everything when viewed from 30,000 feet.
- Code that doesn't leave the campsite in a better condition than it found it, because cleanup is deferred to "another pull request, on another day (by no one ever)."
- Code that has already shipped and now feels like too much of a hassle to change.

chunks.heading: Reviewing your own work against the full diff
chunks.text:
- DHH treats code review as something a programmer can do to themselves, not only something done by others.
- On substantial work, he hops back and forth between TextMate and the complete GitHub diff for all the commits.
- In that back-and-forth, "you see the shape of the code, pick up on bad smells, and ultimately decide whether you're happy with the whole."
- This self-review depends on having the whole feature in one pull request.

chunks.heading: Guidance: when to split pull requests
chunks.text:
- DHH's advice: "don't chop up your pull requests until the cost of doing so definitively outpaces the value."
- He says what works for "mega corps working on million-line code bases" probably isn't fit for smaller systems.
- Smaller systems "still have a fighting chance at keeping their structural integrity," and large PRs help protect it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH says the hardest part of working with juniors, and with AI, is the premise trap: flawed assumptions in a first draft go unquestioned until too much time is sunk into polishing. Current AI is a superb junior that writes overcomplicated, subtly defective code, so seniors shouldn't delegate whole systems to it.

chunks.heading: The premise trap in collaboration
chunks.text:
- The hardest part of working with junior programmers, in open source or at work, is avoiding the "premise trap".
- The trap is when the fundamental assumptions baked into the first draft of the code go unquestioned until far too much time has been spent improving the implementation.
- DHH sees the same dynamic with AI: it is "like a superb junior programmer", with encyclopedic knowledge of syntax and APIs but the same tendency toward overly-complicated, subtly-defective solutions.
- The fix is to question the premise of a draft early, before polishing the implementation.

chunks.heading: What AI-written code looks like today
chunks.text:
- DHH has yet to see any AI model he has used over the past year produce great code in domains he knows very well.
- There are occasional glimmers, as with promising juniors, but taken as a whole the solutions almost always need material rework, and that is when the premise trap "claps".
- The same problems show up in both Ruby and JavaScript output, so he doubts it is specific to one language.
- Recurring problems:
  - Pulling in needless dependencies.
  - Overly-verbose presentation.
  - Architectural dead ends.
- He hears the same from non-programmers using AI to build whole systems: a prototype appears in minutes, which is "an incredible rush", but getting it to something reliable becomes a one-step-forwards-two-steps-backwards dance. He compares it to getting catfished by a barely qualified junior on Upwork.

chunks.heading: Why the models write mediocre code
chunks.text:
- The training data is the cause: endless basic online tutorials, simplified Stack Overflow answers, and the fact that a fair chunk of internet programming content is made by "the blind leading the blind".
- Senior human programmers started on the same information diet.
- They moved up to mastery by working on proprietary code bases, where the trade-offs absent from tutorial-style code reveal themselves and demand to be weighed "with finesse".
- DHH thinks the next big leap under the current paradigm probably won't come until models are exposed to a vast corpus of proprietary, corporate code. How that would happen is not clear to him.

chunks.heading: How senior programmers should use AI
chunks.text:
- Treat AI as you would a junior programmer.
- It is rarely going to save time to ask it for an entire system, or even a subsystem, if you care about the final quality of the architecture or implementation.
- Verifying the assumptions baked into its approach takes as much time as understanding the choices would if you did the work yourself.
- This is the premise trap applied to AI: reviewing and reworking a flawed foundation costs as much as building it right.

chunks.heading: Staying bullish without lowering standards
chunks.text:
- He reads the junior-programmer parallel as potentially bullish: AI may follow the human progression tree and graduate to senior-level competence in code aesthetics, novel problem reasoning, and architectural coherence. He hopes so.
- He remains bullish on AI writing code for everyone, but realistic about its current abilities.
- Risk to watch for: senior programmers, himself included, being lured into signing off on slop.
- Leaning too much on AI writing code for you, rather than teaching it how, saps stamina for continued learning.
- He closes with: "May this piece age badly within a few short years!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues microservices-first is rarely justified and that most systems should start and stay as a majestic monolith. For teams already in the mess, he gives a five-step recovery plan: stop adding services, consolidate critical flows, keep true performance hotspots, prune esoteric languages, and partition with modules rather than networks.

chunks.heading: How DHH defines when microservices make sense
chunks.text:
- DHH admits there may be cases where a microservices-first architecture makes sense, but calls them "few and far in between".
- He says the vast majority of systems are better served by starting and staying with a majestic monolith.
- He cites the Prime Video case study, which "blew up the internet" the day before the essay, as the latest illustration.
- GitHub and Shopify run their main applications as monoliths with millions of lines of code and thousands of programmers collaborating on them.
- His test: if you don't have many more millions of lines of code or thousands of programmers on the same code bases, "exercise extreme caution before even thinking about microservices".
- Maybe at Netflix or Amazon scale some areas make sense.

chunks.heading: Why "it depends" is not enough, and what microservices actually depend on
chunks.text:
- DHH says microservices, like any programming pattern, are a tool. "It depends" is technically correct but helps nobody make better decisions, so guidance must say WHAT IT DEPENDS ON.
- Using microservices well usually depends on two things:
  - **a)** A large, complex system that has successfully evolved from a small, simple system.
  - **b)** The ability to identify a part of a clearly modularized design with strong boundaries and no critical-flow dependencies as an extraction candidate. Proceed only IF there are large performance gains from switching implementation approach, OR organizational benefits from placing the module with a whole team that can't easily collaborate with the rest of the system makers.
- Other justifications are possible, but they should be "clearly articulated, rigorously examined, and critically challenged" before embarking on microservices.
- Otherwise you can YOLO and splinter the design, and return to the majestic monolith "when the hangover hurts enough".

chunks.heading: Recovering from premature microservices: stop digging and consolidate critical paths
chunks.text:
- **Stop digging.** You can't clean up a mess while still making more of it.
  - Don't introduce new microservices.
  - Pick one existing microservice to be the epicenter that carries all new functionality.
  - Its gravitational pull should eventually swallow most of the other microservices. The key is not making matters worse.
- **Consolidate critical, dependent paths first.** The worst microservice madness is splintering a single, coherent flow (signup, checkout, visiting a single piece of content) across multiple systems.
  - Changes then require coordination across systems, synchronization issues, and more.
  - Start consolidating microservices into macroservices, on the way back to the monolith, here.

chunks.heading: Recovering from premature microservices: leave hotspots for last, prune languages
chunks.text:
- **Leave isolated performance hotspots for last.** Microservices done right target a narrow, isolated, performance-critical segment that benefits from a rewrite in a clunkier but faster language.
  - Example: a Rails app with one screen that sees wild load spikes and can't be cached, so you use Rust or Go there. "Well done, you've microserviced with honors!"
  - Caveat: make sure you actually benchmarked to prove the productivity regression was worth it.
- **Prioritize dropping the most esoteric implementations.** Microservices' promise of isolation feeds CIO dreams of "best-in-breed" and the programmer urge to experiment.
  - The result can be 3-5-7 programming languages, even more frameworks, and parallel dependency tracks. This is "murder for conceptual comprehension" and produces the symptom of "nobody understands or can work on the whole system".
  - Rule: most systems should have no more than two backend languages at once. One general-purpose language tuned for programmer productivity, used 99% of the time, and one high-performance language for the last 1% of hotspots, should they ever appear.

chunks.heading: Partition with modules, not networks, and start simple
chunks.text:
- DHH calls it a fallacy that if you can't architect a large system with modules and namespaces, you can solve it by partitioning with network boundaries. "No, no, no."
- Building a large, resilient, performant system is hard. Designing one for a novel problem space on day one is impossible.
- He quotes John Gall: "A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that works. The inverse proposition also appears to be true: A complex system designed from scratch never works and cannot be made to work."
- Simplicity means not inviting distributed systems, "the beast of complexity", to the first dance. A justified distributed system is only possible in good conscience if you started with a simple, monolithic design.

chunks.heading: Reading list and learning order for architecture
chunks.text:
- For breaking large problem spaces into domain models, the key tome is Eric Evans' *Domain-Driven Design*.
- Graduate to that strategic level only after mastering tactical programming:
  - Kent Beck's *Smalltalk Best Practices* (for object-oriented languages).
  - Martin Fowler's *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture*.
- His analogy: many eager programmers start an Iron Man before they've done a 5K run. He admires the gumption, but says the industry has done them a disservice by not being clearer about the dangers of microservices earlier.
- He doesn't believe, as a general rule, in "learning speed limits". You can always start learning, and if it changes how you view earlier choices, you can change your approach from that day forth.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH traces a recurring pattern: vendors profit from complexity, so each time a wave (J2EE, WS-*) is flattened by simpler tools like Rails and JSON over HTTPS, the merchants of complexity regroup around the next frontier. He argues Kubernetes and its ecosystem are the current iteration, with the ratio of good ideas to bullshit out of whack.

chunks.heading: Why J2EE, WS-\*, and now Kubernetes keep happening
chunks.text:
- DHH started programming during the J2EE heyday (late 90s/early 00s): expensive, hard-to-learn application servers, monitoring tools and "boxes upon boxes of other fancy solutions" that needed "an army of contractors, consultants, and sales people" to buy, configure and run.
- All of it did what a Perl CGI script or PHP page could do: pull data from a database and render it as HTML.
- His diagnosis: there were good ideas underneath, but "the ratio between Good Idea and Bullshit was completely out of whack."
- He treats this as a recurring cycle. Merchants of complexity "migrate to the next" market whenever one dries up, and "the struggle between profitless simplicity and profitable complexity is eternal in the world of software."
- When things become too easy and approachable, there is no room for the enterprisey services, sales and solutions to prosper, so the incentive is to rebuild the complexity elsewhere.

chunks.heading: Rails as the original answer to J2EE
chunks.text:
- The original mission of Rails: "to liberate the good ideas from the bullshit," flush out the nonsense, and compress the remaining intrinsic complexity.
- The goal was that "mere mortals without an advanced degree in enterprisey gibberish" could use the real ingenuity that was present.
- It worked. Rails brought a deep catalogue of solid patterns from J2EE and elsewhere (he links Fowler's Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture) to programmers who would never have had the patience for the original wrapping, and gave those already versed in the patterns a simpler environment.
- It also drained much of the enterprisey swamp. There was no room for commercial vendors selling convoluted wares to an ecosystem running commodity hardware, commodity databases, web servers and simple open-source frameworks.

chunks.heading: WS-\* ("WS-DeathStar") and how JSON over HTTPS beat it
chunks.text:
- After Rails arrived, the next complexity gold rush was Web Services, WS-\*, which he called "WS-DeathStar" at the time.
- It sought to complicate the basic mechanics of making applications talk to each other over the internet. Examples he names: WS-SecurityPolicy, WS-Trust, WS-Federation, WS-SecureConversation.
- It mushroomed into "a cloud of impenetrable specifications," seemingly written by and for holders of the same advanced degrees in enterprisey gibberish.
- It imploded, like J2EE, "under the pressure of the plain alternative: Just sending JSON over standard HTTPS to servers running whatever on the backend."
- Practitioners argued for years over how pure something had to be to be called RESTful, but "it didn't really matter. The internet voted with its web requests."
- Fragments of the old world remain (SOAP references, some bank on an original J2EE stack). The wide internet belongs to Rails, JSON, REST, and commodity databases and web servers.
- He sets JavaScript aside as "an interesting hybrid case" that needs its own exploration, but aligns it more with the rebels than the empire.

chunks.heading: Kubernetes as the latest Death Star
chunks.text:
- The latest frontier is containerized running of software in the cloud. He ranks the initial advancement and popularization of containers as "one of my favorite milestones of progress in our industry."
- The merchants of complexity saw that simplicity "as a bug to quickly correct" and used "their impressive tractor beam of bullshit to pull us back towards the ever-reconstructing Death Star."
- He grants that there are good ideas inside Kubernetes and the tools, services and standards following in its wake, but says the bullshit ratio is "already completely out of whack."
- The actual goal is modest: run an application on some hardware in a reasonably efficient manner, and be able to easily redeploy it when it changes.
- Contrasting what Kubernetes requires, both within your application and to operate control planes, with "the breakthrough simplicity of the original Docker advancement" is, in his words, "damn depressing."
- It is also predictable: the complexity is immensely profitable, and renewed demand for "advanced degrees in enterprisey gibberish" drives the same expansion of jargon, specifications and techniques seen with J2EE and WS-\*.

chunks.heading: Why complexity looks reasonable while you are inside it
chunks.text:
- In hindsight it looks silly. He points to early-2000s WebSphere manuals and the incantations once required just to reach Hello World, and challenges readers to digest WS-\* specifications: "It's technical masochism."
- In the thick of it, the complexity seems "if not reasonable, then at least excusable": "Yes, this is all horrendously complicated, _but_ look at what we can do!"
- The pattern is to offer reasons (he jokes "17 reasons") why the simple approach is "just naive or unsophisticated."
- He frames this with the Emperor's New Clothes: if you can't see the splendor of the king's fine threads, "surely it is you, little boy, who is mistaken."

chunks.heading: Practical stance
chunks.text:
- His advice: "Beware carnies dressed as storm troopers. The circus empire is always coming to town."
- Keep "a safe distance, a skeptical mind, and one hand on your wallet."
- The test he applies each cycle: does the tool still deliver the simple core job (data to HTML, apps talking over HTTP, running and redeploying an app) at a sane cost in complexity, or has the Good Idea to Bullshit ratio gone out of whack?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH credits Kent Beck's XP mottos, "the simplest thing that could possibly work" and "you aren't gonna need it", as the drivers of all his programming work. He pairs them with a cultivated outsider's ignorance to break paradigms (Rails, Hotwire, Kamal) and get from nothing to working software in days.

chunks.heading: Origin: Extreme Programming and the agile movement
chunks.text:
- DHH calls himself "a programming child of the agile software movement." Kent Beck published *Extreme Programming Explained* in 2000, just as DHH was starting out.
- Having had just enough exposure to Big Upfront Design and waterfall to appreciate the shift, he saw XP as a monumental break from the traditional approach. Beck's methodology "x-rayed the ills of the traditional approach."
- What attracted him most was Beck's "irreverent insistence on practicality": plenty of vision and principles, but all of them lead to running code.
- He sees XP as one expression of a larger paradigm shift. In 2001 several of his programming heroes published the Agile Manifesto: Ward Cunningham, Martin Fowler and Dave Thomas among them.
- The manifesto points that still excite him: "individuals over processes" and "working software over comprehensive documentation."

chunks.heading: The two mottos that drive all his programming work
chunks.text:
- Beck made the lofty agile ideals more practical still, with two mottos:
  - "the simplest thing that could possibly work"
  - "you aren't gonna need it" (YAGNI)
- DHH says that to this day these are "the mottos that move all my programming work forward."
- Their job is to be pithy mental antidotes. It is easy to get lost in sentiments like "but wouldn't it be nice if..." and "we'll probably also need...", and you need a counter ready.
- He admits sticking with this intent is always a struggle. Human nature seems primed to dwell on all potentialities rather than activate the instinct for action, so the mottos help.

chunks.heading: Pairing the mottos with cultivated ignorance
chunks.text:
- DHH argues the mottos pair well with a "cultivated strain of ignorance" when you want to tackle existing problems from first principles.
- His examples of being an outsider to the incumbent paradigm:
  - An outsider to J2EE, which let him pursue Ruby on Rails.
  - An outsider to JavaScript, which let him chase Hotwire.
  - An outsider to Kubernetes, which let him sail with Kamal.
- His conclusion: "It's easier to break the paradigms if you're not enmeshed in them on the daily."

chunks.heading: Going from nothing to working software in days
chunks.text:
- Even when you're not busting paradigms, he calls the mottos paramount.
- They are how you go from nothing to working software "in days, not weeks or months."
- The tactic is cutting straight to the chase for the epicenter of the solution (he links Basecamp's *Getting Real* chapter on epicenter design).
- He reports seeing this in action on a new product at 37signals (March 2023), marveling at how quickly the team went from concept to code.

chunks.heading: Why he recommends reading Beck, and the payoff
chunks.text:
- DHH strongly encourages reading Beck's *Extreme Programming Explained* if you haven't.
- Whether XP as a complete methodology is right for you is irrelevant. "The mere audacity of the prescriptions will expand your horizon."
- The benefit is trained eyes: you learn to look for the simplest thing that could possibly work.
- His claim: "Few changes in perspective will unlock that hallowed 10x potential like this."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues most hard problems in business, design, or programming can be restated as easy ones by questioning assumptions, reweighing trade-offs, and abandoning sunk costs. He names this as 37signals' key principle for making big things with tiny teams, taught through constraints like 6-week cycles and two-person teams.

chunks.heading: Core principle: restate hard problems as easy ones
chunks.text:
- DHH argues that most hard problems in business, design, or programming don't have to be solved. Almost all can be restated as easy problems if you "dare question the assumptions, reweigh the trade-offs, and stop diving after sunk cost."
- He ranks this above every other principle at 37signals: it is the key to keeping pace, making big things happen with tiny teams, and avoiding "motivation-killing slogs."
- The rule is a stubborn refusal to solve hard problems of any kind unless there truly is no other choice. He says there almost always is another choice.

chunks.heading: Cultivate an allergy to hard problems
chunks.text:
- He says to build a higher sensitivity to the cumbersome and to park the part of the ego that treats doing hard things as a point of pride.
- He notes this is deeply unnatural to ambitious, creative, diligent people, which makes it a rare trait.
- It usually appears natively only in people whose constraints forced it on them, such as bootstrapped founders.
- Practical reframing moves he names:
  - Question the assumptions behind the problem.
  - Reweigh the trade-offs.
  - Stop diving after sunk cost.

chunks.heading: Teach the habit through artificial constraints
chunks.text:
- DHH says the aversion can be taught by adopting constraints tight enough to require it.
- Example 1: the 6-week cycles in Shape Up, the project-shaping method used at 37signals (Basecamp and HEY).
- Example 2: deliberately small teams, smaller than you might think is needed. Virtually everything at 37signals is built by two people: one designer and one programmer.
- Constraints only work if backed by a mandate from the top: when push comes to shove, the right answer is not to throw more people or effort at the problem, but to do the opposite.

chunks.heading: Less is the answer
chunks.text:
- His stance on scope pressure is "Less is the answer, less is the way."
- Instead of adding resources to a struggling problem, cut the problem down.
- He frames this as the way a tiny team makes big things happen.

chunks.heading: Where to find purpose
chunks.text:
- DHH advises finding purpose "in pace and progress," not in "heroic tales of climbing impossible mountains."
- This is aimed at the ego trap of equating hard-won effort with value, which he says drives teams into slogs that kill motivation.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues that style is an integral part of code as expression, and that Ruby's many ways to do things make it a language for writers. Linters are good when authors and teams enforce their own style, which is why Rails ships RuboCop with his omakase defaults as a starting point, not an edict.

chunks.heading: Linting as personal style, not mandate
chunks.text:
- DHH is skeptical of programmers' hostility to style. He rejects the idea that aesthetics conflicts with substance and says this shows up most in the debate over linting.
- Linting means applying a consistent style to source code, "like following Strunk & White's grammatical guidelines for prose, but automatically enforced by a linting program."
- Adoption has grown with cloud-based continuous integration, which runs tests, and now linting, on every pull request.
- He dislikes the Go approach, a built-in linter (gofmt) applying one universal style set by the language designers. He calls it "the most totalitarian approach," a decree "barely two feet removed from a compile error," and says he doesn't like it "one bit."
- His position: linters are excellent for authors and teams to enforce their own style on their own codebases, as long as nobody forces their stylistic preferences on him.

chunks.heading: Code as prose: the Newspeak and single-shade argument
chunks.text:
- He compares a minimalist, single-style language to Newspeak from Orwell's 1984, not for political reasons but because of its pursuit of no redundant terms, ambiguities or flair.
- Analogy: "Imagine every novel written in the same style, Hemingway indistinguishable from Dickens, Tolkien from Rowling." It would be "awfully gray" to enjoy English with only one shade of prose.
- He answers the objection "code isn't prose, its compile target is the computer" by disagreeing: "The best code to me is indeed its own form of poetry, and style is an integral part of such expression."
- He says this is truest in Ruby, and that he strives to write code "as an author" more often than as an engineer.

chunks.heading: Ruby vs Python: many ways to do it
chunks.text:
- Python's motto: "there should be one – and preferably only one – obvious way to do it." He says Ruby is "the exact opposite": there are many ways to do almost everything.
- He cites this as why reading and writing Ruby is a delight for people who write code as authors.
- Closing line: "Ruby is for writers." Ruby's rich, expressive syntax would be "a damn shame" if narrowed to "a single, pre-approved trail."

chunks.heading: Example: `unless` over "if not"
chunks.text:
- He finds the "if not" expression clumsy, though it is a mainstay of most programming languages. His example of the conventional form:

```ruby
def ensure_privileged_access
  if !person.admin?
    redirect_to root_url,
  end
end
```

- The Ruby alternative he prefers:

```ruby
def ensure_privileged_access
  redirect_to root_url unless person.admin?
end
```

- He doesn't claim it is poetry, but finds it "far more pleasant to read."
- Scaling metaphor: a single line is a sentence, several make a paragraph (method), then an essay (class), then a whole book (system). "It matters how that's written."
- People who prefer the literal style can encode that preference in a lint rule, and he would have no problem with it.

chunks.heading: RuboCop in Rails and the omakase defaults
chunks.text:
- The next version of Rails ships with a default linter, RuboCop (he jokes it is "cleverly called" that).
- The purpose is not to let him or anyone mandate a style, but so teams "can find and enforce your own."
- For those without a personal or team style yet, Rails includes the preferences he has developed over two decades, writing hundreds of thousands of lines of Ruby with the team at 37signals, published as rubocop-rails-omakase.
- He calls this the "omakase menu": a starting point for developing one's own sensibilities, "not a permanent edict on what those should be."

chunks.heading: Style is idiosyncratic
chunks.text:
- His core claim: "the essence of style, it's invariably idiosyncratic. We wouldn't even be talking about style if it was all the same for everyone all the time."
- Practical stance: tools should help authors and teams express and consistently enforce their own style, with sensible defaults offered but never imposed.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why 37signals is leaving AWS and Google Cloud after years of running Basecamp and HEY there. The cloud only pays off for tiny apps or wildly irregular load, the promised ops savings never materialized, and owning hardware is cheaper and better for a decentralized internet.

chunks.heading: Why DHH is leaving the cloud: the core conclusion
chunks.text:
- Basecamp has had one foot in the cloud for well over a decade. HEY has run there exclusively since launch two years earlier.
- 37signals has run extensively on Amazon's cloud and Google's cloud, on bare virtual machines, and on Kubernetes.
- His conclusion: "Renting computers is (mostly) a bad deal for medium-sized companies like ours with stable growth."
- The savings promised in reduced complexity never materialized, so 37signals is making plans to leave.
- He describes the cloud as mostly "renting computers", even though it is sold as futuristic "computing on demand".

chunks.heading: When the cloud actually makes sense (and why it doesn't for 37signals)
chunks.text:
The cloud excels at two ends of the spectrum. Only one end was ever relevant to 37signals.

- **Simple, low-traffic apps:** fully managed services save real complexity when you have no customers. This is the path Heroku forged, now paved by Render and others. It carries you far even with some customers. Bills that balloon with usage later are a "Good Problem" and a reasonable trade-off.
- **Highly irregular load:** wild swings, towering peaks, a baseline that is a sliver of peak needs, or no idea whether you need ten servers or a hundred. 
  - Example: HEY's launch. 300,000 users signed up in three weeks against a forecast of 30,000 in six months. The cloud was ideal for that.
- Neither condition applies to 37signals today, and neither ever did for Basecamp.
- By staying in the cloud, they pay "an at times almost absurd premium" for the possibility that these conditions might apply.
- His analogy: paying a quarter of your house's value for earthquake insurance when you don't live near a fault line.

chunks.heading: The cost argument: HEY's database and search bill
chunks.text:
- HEY pays over half a million dollars per year to Amazon for database (RDS) and search (ES) services.
- He grants that processing email for many tens of thousands of customers means a lot of data to analyze and store, but still finds the bill absurd.
- His framing question: how many "insanely beefy servers" could you buy on a budget of half a million dollars per year?

chunks.heading: Rebutting "but you have to manage the machines"
chunks.text:
- The standard argument: the cloud is simpler, and savings show up in labor costs.
- DHH's answer: "Anyone who thinks running a major service like HEY or Basecamp in the cloud is 'simple' has clearly never tried."
- Some things get simpler, others more complex. On the whole, he has yet to hear of organizations at their scale materially shrinking their operations team just because they moved to the cloud.
- He calls the "you don't run your own powerplant either" and "are infrastructure services really your core competency?" analogies a marketing coup, coated in "NEW-NEW-NEW paint" so that only luddites would consider running their own servers.

chunks.heading: Cloud provider margins
chunks.text:
- Amazon is "printing profits" renting servers at "obscene margins".
- AWS profit margin is almost 30%: $18.5B in profits on $62.2B in revenue, despite heavy investment in future capacity and new services.
- He expects the margin to rise further because Amazon said it plans to extend the useful life of its servers from four years to five, and networking equipment from five years to six.
- He is fine with renting being expensive. His objection is that it is never presented as renting.

chunks.heading: Decentralization and the duty to swim against the stream
chunks.text:
- Beyond cost, he calls it "downright tragic" that this "decentralized wonder of the world" now largely runs on computers owned by a handful of mega corporations.
- If a primary AWS region goes down, "seemingly half the internet is offline along with it. This is not what DARPA designed!"
- He considers it a duty for 37signals to "do our part to swim against the stream."

chunks.heading: Why owning hardware fits 37signals, and the call to others
chunks.text:
- 37signals has a business model "incredibly compatible with owning hardware and writing it off over many years".
- Its growth trajectories are mostly predictable.
- It has expert staff who might as well operate their own machines as Amazon's or Google's.
- He thinks plenty of other companies are in similar boats.
- Running your own servers is not too complicated: "Up until very recently, everyone ran their own servers, and much of the progress in tooling that enabled the cloud is available for your own machines as well."
- "Everyone and their dog did it to get the internet off the ground, and it's only gotten easier since."
- He urges people not to be dazzled by entrenched cloud interests into believing self-hosting is too complicated: "It's time to part the clouds and let the internet shine through."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH answers the recurring objections to 37signals' cloud exit: team size, security, reliability, scaling, and cost. His core claim is that the cloud's promised savings and ease of use never materialized, and that owning hardware is mostly the same operational work done cheaper, with the same team and open source tooling.

chunks.heading: Cost and scope: why DHH left the cloud
chunks.text:
- DHH's company 37signals announced a cloud exit in 2022 and finished in June 2023. The 2022 cloud budget was $3.2 million.
- He says the bill had already been "highly optimized, monthly scrutinized, heavily haggled." It used to be twice as large, and optimizing further was "a ton of recurring work."
- 37signals bought about $600,000 of Dell servers. It conservatively estimated $7 million in savings over five years.
- By September 2023 the exit had already secured $1 million per year in savings. The bill kept dropping as reserved instances (prepaid for a year) expired.
- The hardware in two data centers totals 4,000 vCPUs, 7,680GB of RAM and 384TB of NVMe storage.
- DHH says it is easy for a mid-sized or larger company to spend 2-3-4x what 37signals did for the same customer count, so most companies have even more to save.
- Customers "scarcely noticed anything" during the move.

chunks.heading: Why the savings are not eaten by payroll
chunks.text:
- 37signals did not change team composition after the exit. The same people who ran HEY and Basecamp in the cloud now run them on owned hardware.
- DHH calls the idea that the cloud means you hardly need operations staff "the central deceit of the cloud marketing." He has never seen reduced operations headcount at 37signals or at other large internet applications.
- About 90% of the expertise needed to run your own hardware is the same as in the cloud, at scale (millions of users, hundreds of thousands of dollars in monthly bills).
- The skills are not lost knowledge: the internet started in 1995 and the cloud only became the default around 2015, so companies ran their own hardware for twenty-plus years. He says it is not "some archaic knowledge that's been lost to the ages."
- A team does not need "a world-class team of super engineers." He says it would be hubris to claim 37signals has special insight.

chunks.heading: What owning hardware actually involves
chunks.text:
- Almost nobody builds their own data center. Outside hyperscalers and mega companies (Google, Microsoft, Meta), companies rent cabinets, a room or a floor from a provider like Equinix. Power, fire suppression and physical security are the provider's job.
- 37signals uses a white-glove service, Deft, for racking and stacking. Deft unpacks the boxes from Dell, installs the servers and the IP address comes online. It is "just like the cloud, even if it isn't instant."
- The operations team "basically never" sets foot in the data centers and works remotely from around the world.
- Procurement takes longer than the cloud. DHH grants that nothing beats the cloud for "10 servers online in Japan" in 30 seconds. His view is that for a business like 37signals, that premium is not worth it, and waiting a couple of weeks is tolerable.
- Planning a European HEY outpost with Deft, which would be an experiment.

chunks.heading: Reliability, performance and security are the same problems
chunks.text:
- **Reliability:** it is "largely a function of redundancy." In the cloud 37signals used two geographically dispersed regions with redundancy in each. It now has two dispersed data centers, each able to carry the full load, with replicas of every critical piece. His rule: you should be able to lose any computer or component at any time without a problem.
- **International performance:** the old setup was two US regions plus a CDN with edge nodes worldwide. The new one is two US data centers plus an international CDN. He says the hard part of a global footprint is application design (multiple write primaries, replication lag), not hardware.
- **Security:** most security problems come from the application and its direct dependencies, and the work is "not any materially different" whether you own or rent the computers. He says the cloud can give "a false sense of security."
- **Patching:** containerized delivery means little manual machine patching. Updates are packaged in Dockerfiles, and deploying a version on a newer Ubuntu is the same on rented or owned machines.
- **Kamal:** in February 2023 DHH bootstrapped Kamal in a few weeks to deploy without giving up cloud-era container innovation.

chunks.heading: Cloud-native, serverless and managed services
chunks.text:
- He rejects the Cloud Native, not lift'n'shift argument as "cloud marketing nonsense." It rests on the belief that serverless functions and on-demand tooling make things cheaper.
- His analogy: if you need a pound of sugar, you will not save money buying single-wrapped cubes.
- He points to two earlier posts: "Don't be fooled by serverless" and "Even Amazon can't make sense of serverless or microservices."
- 37signals replaced managed services with open source equivalents: RDS became MySQL 8 and OpenSearch became open source Elasticsearch.
- Service contracts and licensing fees: nothing. Everything needed to run internet applications is available as open source.
- Support is optional. 37signals has used Percona's MySQL specialists on and off, which does not change the equation.
