- His advice on vendors: avoid the most enterprisey outfits. If banks or governments are on their client list, look elsewhere, "unless you just like setting money on fire."

chunks.heading: Hardware lifespan, spikes and when the cloud still makes sense
chunks.text:
- **Replacement cost:** the math assumes servers last five years. That is conservative: 37signals has had servers run 7-8 years. The $600,000 purchase was already paid off by the savings, so a new round of hardware would still leave the company ahead.
- **Moore's Law:** hardware from Dell and others has become much cheaper and more powerful in the last 4-5 years, while managed-service prices barely move. This is why he says much of the cloud is a worse deal each year.
- **Spikes:** because owned hardware is cheap, you can "dramatically over provision" for headroom with little effect on the long-run budget.
- **When cloud fits:** if you regularly face 5-10x or higher spikes over baseline, you may be a good candidate for cloud. That was Amazon's original reason (Black Friday, Cyber Monday). The saying is "buy the baseline, rent the spike."
- **Capacity planning for most companies:** buy powerful machines a fair step ahead of your growth curve, watch usage, and an unplanned expansion can usually be online in about a week.

chunks.heading: GDPR, privacy and why 37signals went to the cloud
chunks.text:
- **Privacy:** the cloud gives no real regulatory advantage, and for European companies it is a negative. The big hyperscalers are American, so the US government can legally compel Amazon, Microsoft or Google to hand over data wherever the servers are. For strict GDPR compliance, DHH suggests owning hardware in a European data center provider.
- **Why they joined:** 37signals "bought the marketing pitch" of cheaper, easier and faster. Only faster came true, and provisioning a fleet quickly is something it rarely does.
- Economies of scale and ease of use never materialized: managed services still needed management, and Moore's Law gains were not passed on as savings.
- He is glad they gave the cloud "a proper go" because they learned and improved processes, but wishes they had done the math "a couple of years sooner."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why 37signals dropped its experiment with full-time managers and went back to none. Management is spread across senior individual contributors, which keeps it minimal, avoids Parkinson's Law, and depends on hiring "managers of one". He also names the limit: poor-performance cases must bubble up to the top.

chunks.heading: Why 37signals runs with no full-time managers
chunks.text:
DHH says 37signals is back to its original configuration: no full-time managers whose sole function is to organize or direct the work of others. After experimenting with several management roles over a few years, the company reverted. Everyone who manages does so on the side, next to their primary work as an individual contributor, including DHH and Jason Fried.

- Managerial work still exists: yearly performance reviews, onboarding new colleagues, scheduling on-call coverage, and supervising junior work.
- Instead of concentrating these duties in a few full-time managers, the load is distributed among senior staff.
- He says the arrangement works, and that "the result is astounding" when it does.
- After "twenty-plus years of running a company like this," he says he no longer has any interest in working any other way. The couple of years with a more traditional structure were "a wonderful experience because it cemented this fact."
- His stated resolve: "We're going to make this company work without full-time managers or die trying."

chunks.heading: How management is minimized: automation and one mentee each
chunks.text:
Distributing management duties incentivizes a minimalist approach to it.

- Instead of a recurring schedule of weekly one-on-ones, 37signals drives status updates and check-ins with automated questions (Basecamp's automatic check-ins feature).
- Instead of assigning five, six or seven reports to a single person, every lead and principal programmer is responsible for one mentee.
- Managers are primarily senior individual contributors, not a separate career track.

chunks.heading: Parkinson's Law and the zero-hour management week
chunks.text:
DHH argues a part-time, distributed model avoids Parkinson's Law (work expands to fill the time available).

- With no fixed forty hours for managerial duties to expand into, management stays small.
- Everyone doing a small share of the management "would usually rather get back to their own work as quickly as possible."
- Some weeks the managerial overhead is literally zero, because everyone is busy getting their work done and nobody needs anything.
- He says this is impossible in a traditional setup: a full-time manager can't scale their interventions down to zero hours a week and still feel like they're doing their job.

chunks.heading: Managers of one, and why the boss should also be the better doer
chunks.text:
The model depends on hiring, mentoring and promoting "managers of one": people with the competence and drive to set their own agenda and follow it autonomously.

- They don't need weekly one-on-ones with a manager to stay on track.
- They thrive on long stretches of uninterrupted time.
- This is the kind of person 37signals seeks to hire and develop.
- DHH finds it easier to steer that development when someone's primary manager is also their professional superior. You learn faster and "frankly respect that person more."
- He references Steve Jobs's quip about professional managers who "knew how to manage, but they didn't know how to do anything." He wouldn't go that far, and acknowledges many professional managers have solid experience doing things, but he thinks the principle holds when managers are not better at doing things than the people they manage.

chunks.heading: Where the model strains: conflict and poor performance
chunks.text:
DHH calls it a trade-off. The hardest managerial burden to distribute broadly is dealing with conflict and poor performance.

- Plenty of senior staff are willing and able to mentor and manage juniors and peers on a solid trajectory who act as managers of one.
- A much smaller group welcomes dealing with reports who can't keep up or repeatedly get lost.
- So the arrangement has to acknowledge its limits: someone else in the organization must be able to direct, or even take over, when an employee needs strong, repeated "redirecting feedback" (he calls it a euphemism).
- Those cases "will have to bubble up to the top."

chunks.heading: Poor performance as a root-cause signal
chunks.text:
DHH argues that cases bubbling up is not really a cost, because it exposes upstream problems.

- If poor performance keeps bubbling up, there is a fundamental problem somewhere in the process, which can usually only be addressed definitively by the top.
- Questions he asks: Are we not hiring the right people? Are we unclear in our expectations? Are we too diffident in our feedback?
- These are "root cause problems that require root cause reparations."

chunks.heading: Scale limits and the payoff
chunks.text:
DHH is explicit that this would be difficult to maintain at grand scale.

- With hundreds or thousands of employees, you naturally yearn for more structure and hierarchy.
- That isn't the case at around 60 people, which is where 37signals is.
- The payoff: small teams of highly competent managers of one "can progress at an unbelievable pace."
- Left to just do their job, they get it done and are rewarded with job satisfaction from making a direct, personal difference. In his words: "There's nothing better than shipping quickly alongside peers you respect highly."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues that well-meant efforts to fight imposter syndrome have drifted into celebrating incompetence and copy-paste programming. He says programmers should treat lookups as part of learning, accept that the craft has depth and uneven talent, and aim to become the wizard rather than the bedazzled audience.

chunks.heading: Core argument: stop celebrating incompetence
chunks.text:
- DHH argues the programming world has taken "a bad turn down a blind alley by celebrating incompetence" in its effort to fight imposter syndrome and gatekeeping.
- He says you don't have to reduce the profession to "a clueless gang of copy-pasta pirates" to make new recruits feel welcome.
- His objections: it undermines the aspiration to improve, and it reduces the work to magical thinking. "It is not good."
- He frames this as a critique of the prescription, not the diagnosis. Imposter syndrome and gatekeeping are real problems in programming.

chunks.heading: Why programming has imposter syndrome and gatekeeping
chunks.text:
- A high percentage of programmers are self-taught, unlike many other professional fields. DHH counts himself among them.
- Without a diploma from a prestigious institution saying "you know things, and you're good at things", occasional self-doubt is natural.
- That doubt is sharper when some people in the profession use their diplomas as a logical fallacy to prove they're right and others are wrong.
- Even so, he says you can't let the doubt win.

chunks.heading: Don't make "I have no idea what I'm doing" a professional identity
chunks.text:
- Don't adopt the "I HAVE NO IDEA WHAT I'M DOING" dog as a professional identity.
- Don't embrace being a copy-pasta programmer whose chief skill is looking things up on the internet.
- Treat looking things up as part of a learning process to understand what's going on, not merely a shortcut to solve today's problems.
- "If you never dig deeper, your competence will be stuck at the surface."

chunks.heading: Responsibility of experienced programmers
chunks.text:
- Influential programmers with hard-earned skills and accumulated knowledge, who repeatedly create good software, should resist posing as "a know-little, copy-pasta dummy, JUST LIKE YOU".
- Any gain from being relatable to a struggling newcomer must be weighed against infusing the industry with "a sense of futility of deep learning".

chunks.heading: Programming magic is just things you don't know yet
chunks.text:
- "The magic of programming is largely just things you don't know yet."
- Once learned, it stops being "I have no idea how it did that or why it works" and becomes "I can make the computer do exactly what I ask it to do!"
- The goal is to become the wizard, not the bedazzled member of the audience.
- Mastery doesn't happen overnight. The profession has real depth, and we should have the confidence to say so while still celebrating how easy it is to get started and welcoming people onto the path to becoming a wizard.

chunks.heading: Accepting limits and unequal outcomes
chunks.text:
- You can't become an expert at everything, and accepting your boundaries is fine.
- It is not fine to think you shouldn't be on some path toward mastery if you intend to make programming your career.
- Not all apprentices end up with equal talent or competence, as in every other human pursuit.
- His analogy is chess: the basic rules take minutes to learn, a lifetime to master, and not everyone becomes a grandmaster even when trying very hard.

chunks.heading: The need for competent programmers
chunks.text:
- "The world has never had a greater need for programmers than it does today. It's never had a greater need for competent programmers than it does today."
- He calls for dropping the "overly self-deprecating nonsense that nobody knows what they're doing, and trying to learn things in depth is not for us."
- His closing message: you're not a clueless dog banging at the keyboard with no prospects of improving; you're "a human of tremendous capacity to become good at what you do. Embrace that."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH argues "vibe coding" appeals mostly to programmers stuck in unpleasant languages, and that Ruby's programmer-happiness premise makes writing code itself the enjoyable part. He uses AI as a pair programmer for lookups and questions but refuses to permanently give it the keyboard.

chunks.heading: Programming should be enjoyable, and DHH wants to keep writing the code
chunks.text:
- DHH argues that part of the appeal of "vibe coding" (leaning back and prompting AI through a whole project) is that many development environments are deeply unpleasant to work with.
- Programmers stuck with cumbersome languages and frameworks naturally want to give up the coding part of software development. DHH says: "If I found writing code a chore, I'd be looking for retirement too." He doesn't find it a chore.
- He used to treat coding as a necessary but inconvenient step toward getting programs. That changed when he learned Ruby and built Rails.
- His view is that programming "should be a vibe", meaning fun, and should resemble English closely enough that line noise doesn't obscure the underlying ideas and decisions.
- Code should allow a richness of expression that serves the human reader instead of favoring the strictness the computer prefers. Ruby does this.

chunks.heading: Ruby's premise of programmer happiness, and why it matters more with AI
chunks.text:
- Ruby's entire premise is "programmer happiness": writing code should be a joy.
- Historically Ruby traded run-time performance, memory usage and other machine sympathies for that happiness.
- DHH says that trade-off has largely gone away: after thirty years of constant improvement, Ruby is "now incredibly fast and efficient, yet remains a delight to work with."
- He sees disgruntled programmers finally realizing that an escape is possible from "nasty syntax, boilerplate galore, and ecosystem hyper-churn". He says that ethos "couldn't shine brighter now."
- He holds that the instinct behind vibe coding is correct: "Programming _should_ be a vibe! It should be fun!"
- The wisdom Ruby was founded on, and a big part of AI's appeal to programmers, is that programming should "favor and flatter the human."

chunks.heading: Why AI hiding the unpleasant parts is not a fix
chunks.text:
- DHH says the appeal of AI is that it hides away the unpleasantness of bad languages: syntax, boilerplate and framework churn.
- He compares this to "cleaning your room by stuffing the mess under the bed". The mess doesn't go away.
- The better answer is to use an environment (Ruby and Rails, in his case) where the mess isn't there to begin with, rather than papering over a painful stack with AI.

chunks.heading: Why he won't hand AI the keyboard
chunks.text:
- DHH has no interest in giving up writing code. It isn't the unpleasant part he wants AI to take off his hands.
- He rejects the idea of becoming "a project manager for a murder of AI crows". He has had the option to move up the manager ladder for most of his career and has steadily refused, "because I really like writing Ruby! It's the most enjoyable part of the job!"
- He says he'd retire before permanently handing AI the keyboard to drive the code.

chunks.heading: How he does use AI: as a pair programmer
chunks.text:
- DHH converses and collaborates with LLMs all day long.
- His uses: looking up APIs, clarifying concepts, and asking stupid questions.
- He calls AI "a superb pair programmer", with him still driving.

chunks.heading: Where he thinks AI could go
chunks.text:
- DHH allows that wanting to write code might one day become a quaint concept, like tending to horses for transportation in the modern world: done as a hobby but devoid of economic value.
- He says he doesn't think anyone knows how far the intelligence and creativity of these "insatiable token munchers" can be pushed, and he wouldn't bet against their advance.
- Even so, his position for now is that programming should stay enjoyable for the human doing it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH reacts to Salesforce announcing it will train Slack AI models on customers' private messages and files by default, with opt-out only via a special email. He reads it as a symptom of companies so afraid of missing the AI wave that they will trample trust and privacy for any edge in the chatbot race.

chunks.heading: DHH on the AI gold rush: fear-driven desperation and privacy transgressions
chunks.text:
- In May 2024, DHH wrote that he had "never seen so much paranoia in technology about missing out on The Next Big Thing as with AI."
- He says companies seem "less excited about the prospects than they are petrified that its going to kill them."
- He leaves open whether that fear is justified ("maybe it's not"), but calls the desperation it produces "incontestable."
- His case in point is Slack, which Salesforce owns.

chunks.heading: Slack's default opt-in training on private messages
chunks.text:
- Salesforce announced it would train Slack AI models on customers' private messages, files and other content.
- Training is on by default. Opting out required sending a specially formatted email to feedback@slack.com.
- DHH mocks the "feedback" address as the kind of process that invites a quip about "knuckle-sandwich feedback to their face."
- His reading of the motive: executives in a brainstorm decided that the way to catch up to big players like OpenAI is to ignore privacy concerns altogether.
- The logic he lampoons: if you can't beat OpenAI at scanning the sum of public human knowledge, scan the confidential conversations instead (new product strategies, unannounced layoffs, private 2025 financial projections).

chunks.heading: The autocomplete-for-layoffs critique
chunks.text:
- DHH imagines a CEO typing an announcement of a 30% layoff and Slack autocompleting it with "the most anodyne distillation from five competitors doing the same."
- The CEO would only edit out a competitor's name (his example is Asana) and save "at least 8 minutes typing out the corporate slop yourself."
- He treats this as the product vision such training buys: bland, averaged corporate text built from other companies' confidential communications.
- Whether that vision looks bright or dystopian, he says, depends on how well one's "inner compass is tuned to the kind of AI KPIs pushing product managers in charge of acquired chat products at large tech companies."
- The point implied: AI metrics driving acquired-product PMs, not user trust, are what produce decisions like this.

chunks.heading: Prediction: more trust and privacy violations in the race
chunks.text:
- DHH's broader point is that this reflects "the broad paranoia and desperation in the AI gold rush."
- He expects "more such flagrant transgressions of trust and privacy" because things are moving fast.
- The trigger he describes is low: any "sliver of a chance" that a data grab gives an edge in building a better chatbot.
- He closes with "Buckle up!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH explains why terminal-based coding agents finally won him over after autocomplete left him cold. He treats agents as a team whose finished work he reviews, not a pair programmer, while staying skeptical of pure vibe coding and of claims that agents write 90% of code.

chunks.heading: DHH promotes AI coding agents from helpers to real contributors
chunks.text:
- At the end of 2025, AI agents "really came alive" for him.
- Part of the reason is better models. The bigger reason is that agents were given tools that go beyond pure reasoning.
- Coding agents now control the terminal, run tests to validate their own work, search the web for documentation, and use web services through skills taught to them in plain English.
- He argues the code from this generation is "leagues ahead" of what the predecessors produced at the start of 2025.
- He says he is ready to give the current agents "a promotion". They are no longer just there to help him learn, answer questions, or check his work. They can produce production-grade contributions to real-life code bases.

chunks.heading: Models and harness he uses: OpenCode with Opus 4.5, Codex 5, Gemini 3 and open-weight models
chunks.text:
- Models he names as new and strong: Claude Opus 4.5, Codex 5, Gemini 3, and the Chinese open-weight models MiniMax M2.1 and GLM-4.7.
- He says the gains show up when these models run in a modern terminal harness that gives them autonomous powers (terminal, tests, web search, skills).
- His harness of choice is OpenCode, a terminal interface for coding agents. He likes that it:
  - switches seamlessly between all of the models
  - captures sessions for sharing
  - looks "astounding" when theme-matched with the rest of Omarchy
- OpenCode becomes a default in the next version of Omarchy.
- His advice: download OpenCode, throw real work at Opus or the others, and see where things stand for yourself.

chunks.heading: Why agents work for him and autocomplete did not
chunks.text:
- He never cared for in-editor AI autocomplete, the format pioneered by GitHub Copilot and Cursor. It left him cold.
- His reason: "When I code, I want to finish my own thoughts and sentences." He compares autocomplete to an overly zealous pair programmer who keeps stealing the keyboard to finish the code he was in the middle of writing. He expressed this on the Lex Fridman podcast in summer 2025.
- Autonomous agents feel different. It is more like working on a team than pairing:
  - the agents do their work autonomously
  - he reviews the final outcome
  - he offers guidance when asked

chunks.heading: Supervised collaboration is real today; pure vibe coding is not
chunks.text:
- He says supervised collaboration is here now. He has worked alongside agents to:
  - fix small bugs
  - finish substantial features
  - produce several drafts of major new initiatives
- Pure vibe coding remains "an aspirational dream" for professional work, for now.
- The paradigm shift "finally feels real" to him, though results depend on what you work on and what you expect.

chunks.heading: Pushing back on the hype: 90%+ AI-written code and the end of programmers
chunks.text:
- He rejects the claim that agents will put professional programmers out of work in five minutes. If you bought that pitch, he says, you will be disappointed.
- He is "nowhere close" to the claims, made by some online, of agents writing 90%+ of the code.
- He does not know what code those people are producing to hit such numbers. It is far from what he can achieve if he "holds the line on quality and cohesion".
- He forgives the excitement anyway. The leaps agents made in 2025 are "simply incredible", and he calls this the most exciting thing computers have been made to do since they were connected to the internet in the '90s.
- He understands why people extrapolate to 2026 or 2027 and get dizzy.

chunks.heading: Why programmers should not tune it out
chunks.text:
- He acknowledges why some programmers want to ignore AI:
  - the hype drones on relentlessly
  - the most fantastical claims are still unsubstantiated
  - there is real uncertainty about where this leaves the profession
- He says none of that is reason enough to miss the moment.
- His message: "You gotta get in there." Try it yourself and relish "the privilege of being alive during the days we taught the machines how to think."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH follows up his Rails World keynote claim that programmers should stop writing most code by hand. He frames AI agents as fast, capable new coworkers rather than a threat, expects a boom in software as development costs fall, and says only those who refuse to collaborate with agents should worry.

chunks.heading: Rails World 2026 message: put down the pencils
chunks.text:
- At Rails World (two weeks before October 6, 2026), DHH told programmers it is "time to put down the pencils."
- His claim: the vast majority of code will no longer be written by hand. Coding agents are now good enough that having humans type out lines of Ruby, Rust, or C++ is "not an economically viable enterprise going forward."
- He polled the room on who still writes a material amount of code by hand on a weekly basis. Only a handful raised their hands.
- His read on the reaction: the room already knew this, but many were still shocked to hear it said out loud.

chunks.heading: AI agents as new coworkers, not just another tool
chunks.text:
- DHH argues AI "isn't just another tool." He compares it to "gaining some new coworkers" who are exceptionally good and fast at a wide range of tasks.
- These coworkers still need help with some things, and you may occasionally disagree with their choices.
- He calls them "clanker colleagues" and says it is fine to be skeptical about the areas where they still get things wrong.
- Treating agents as collaborators, not as an instrument, is the framing he recommends for working with them.

chunks.heading: Why programmers feel threatened
chunks.text:
- DHH acknowledges the shock: programming has barely been a professional career for a generation, and it is being completely transformed.
- He says that is unsettling even for people who have watched technologies come and go.
- The threat is partly about status. Programmers were treated as "precious priests" whose incantations were needed to get even the lowest-hanging fruit out of a computer, and that was barely "five minutes ago."
- The perceived risk of disintermediation, with agents appearing as competition, is hitting some programmers hard.

chunks.heading: The optimistic case: a bloom in software development
chunks.text:
- DHH does not think anyone willing to lean into the future needs to worry much. The condition is to make the most of the "intelligence explosion" and apply existing skills to what comes next.
- He predicts "an absolute bloom in software development" as the price of development plummets.
- His reasoning: everyone will realize how much automation is still left to do in the world, so demand for software grows as the cost falls.
- Closing line: "Don't go down with the pencils. There's so much to build. We need you."

chunks.heading: Who should actually worry
chunks.text:
- DHH says the only programmers who need to worry are those who refuse to embrace the progress of the age of agents, or who drag their feet on it.
- Skepticism about where agents still get things wrong is acceptable to him.
- Refusing collaboration with agents is, in his words, "not a viable career path for almost anyone."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: DHH presents Rails 7 as the closest realization of "The One Person Framework": a toolkit powerful enough for one individual to build a modern app and a competitive business. Conceptual compression and integrated defaults (Hotwire, import maps) let a single developer avoid the sprawling big-tech toolchain.

chunks.heading: Rails 7 as "The One Person Framework"
chunks.text:
- DHH calls Rails 7 "the version of Rails I've been longing for," the one where "all the cards are on the table" and there are "no more tricks up our sleeves." He frames it as the culmination of years of progress on five fronts at once.
- The ideal he is chasing is The One Person Framework: "a toolkit so powerful that it allows a single individual to create modern applications upon which they might build a competitive business. The way it used to be."
- He sees this release as the closest Rails has come to that ideal.
- He says it still makes him giddy: more than twenty years into web development, a big release "still makes me giddy like nothing else."

chunks.heading: Why the conventional path is too heavy for individuals
chunks.text:
- Becoming an expert in all the latest tools and techniques takes a huge amount of learning.
- He calls the conventional path, "as paved by solutions extracted from giant tech companies," a journey "akin to The Oregon Trail": "You might well die of dysentery before you ever get to your destination!"
- His framing of the fight: "You simply can't play by the same rules against an opponent exponentially stronger than you."
- Rails 7 is meant as "the wormhole that folds the time-learning-shipping-continuum," letting you travel grand distances without knowing "all the physics of interstellar travel." The goal is to give "the individual rebel a fighting chance against The Empire."

chunks.heading: Conceptual compression as the engine
chunks.text:
- The key mechanism behind the One Person Framework is conceptual compression.
- His analogy: a video codec that throws away irrelevant details so you can download the film in real time rather than buffer for an hour.
- He dedicated an entire RailsConf keynote to the idea.
- In practice, a developer gets powerful capabilities without having to master every underlying layer first.

chunks.heading: Hotwire and import maps as Rails 7 defaults
chunks.text:
- Stimulus and Turbo, together known as Hotwire, are integrated directly as the new defaults in Rails 7.
- Import maps arrive alongside them, which means "you no longer need to run the whole JavaScript ecosystem enchilada in your Ruby app."
- Turbo's roots go back to 2012 with the first release of its predecessor, Turbolinks.
- Stimulus originated in a Christmas spike he did almost exactly five years before this essay, out of frustration with the many different ways Basecamp was doing JavaScript sprinkles at the time.
- This long-running work is "now finally ready for the big stage of being Rails defaults."

chunks.heading: Backend upgrades: encryption
chunks.text:
- The backend gets "really nice upgrades," especially the encryption work done for HEY.
- This lets data be encrypted while it is live in the database. 37signals calls it "at-work encryption" on the HEY security page.

chunks.heading: Swimming against industry specialization
chunks.text:
- He acknowledges uncertainty: "Will it succeed? Who knows."
- The headwind is "so many vested interests in the subdivision of expertise." Specialisms are getting ever narrower, and the One Person Framework deliberately goes in the opposite direction.
- Still, he argues that if there was ever an opening to "at least tilt the direction of the industry, now is it."
- His mood: "What a glorious time to be working in web development."

Programmers are often skeptical of aesthetics because they frequently associate it with veneering. A thin sheen of flashy marketing design covering up for a rotten or deficient product. Something that looks good from afar, but reveals itself to be a disappointing imitation up close. They're right to be skeptical. Cheap veneers are the worst. But discarding the value of aesthetic on behalf of cheap imitations is a mistake.

Not just because truly beautiful objects and concepts inevitably reveal a deeper and designed experience. That's the whole "I'm writing you a long letter because I didn't have time to write you a short one". Making something beautiful takes extra steps. Steps that are commonly also associated with extra care the rest of the creation.

No, the primary reason I appreciate aesthetics so much is its power to motivate. And motivation is the rare fuel that powers all the big leaps I've ever taken in my career and with my projects and products. It's not time, it's even attention. It's motivation. And I've found that nothing quite motivates me like using and creating beautiful things.

I don't think that would come as any surprise to people of the past. The history of creation is in part a tale of pursuing beautiful outcomes and rewards. But in our age, we've managed to deconstruct and problematize so much of what is self-evidently beautiful that it's harder to take the chase for granted.

It's in the context of this age that I labor for programmers to rediscover beauty. Beautiful code, beautiful patterns, beautiful tools. Not to create a single, mono culture of aesthetics. That's never going to happen. But to elevate the work of making things look not just good, but sublime. To revel in it, to celebrate it.

And beauty isn't binary. It's the journey of a thousand little decisions and investments in making something marginally prettier than it was before. To resist the urge to just make it work, and not stop until you make it shine. Not for anyone else, even, although others will undoubtedly appreciate your care. But for yourself, your own motivation, and your own mission.

When Ruby on Rails was launched over twenty years ago, I was a twenty-some young programmer convinced that anyone who gave my stack a try would accept its universal superiority for solving The Web Problem. So I pursued the path of the crusade, attempting to convert the unenlightened masses by the edge of a pointed argument.

And for a long time, I thought that's what had worked. That this was why Ruby on Rails took off, became one of the most popular full-stack web frameworks of all time, inspired countless clones, and created hundreds of billions in enterprise value for companies built on it. But I was wrong. It wasn't the crusade that did it.

Since those early days, I've talked to thousands of programmers who adopted Ruby on Rails back then, and do you know what virtually every one of them cite? That original 15-minute blog video. Which didn't contain a single comparison to other named solutions or specifically pointed arguments against alternatives. It just showed what you could do with Ruby on Rails, and the A/B comparison automatically ran inside the mind of every programmer who was exposed to that.

That's what did it. Showing something great, and letting those who weren't happy with their current situation become inspired to check it out. Because those are the only people who is able to convert to your cause anyway. I've never seen someone who was head'over'heels in love with, say, functional programming be won over by arguments for objected-oriented programming.

You simply can't dunk someone into submission, and it's usually counterproductive if you try. But you can absolutely attract people who aren't happy with their current circumstances to give an alternative a chance, if you simply show them how it works, and allow them to conclude by themselves how it would make their programming life better.

What I've also come to realize is that programmers come in many different intellectual shapes and sizes. Some of those shapes will click with functional programming, and that'll be their path to passion. Others will click with vanilla JavaScript, and be relieved to give up the build pipelines. Others still will find their spirit in Go. This is great. Seriously. The fact that working for the web allows for such diverse ecosystem choices is an incredible feature, not a bug.

I found my life's work and passion in Ruby. I have friends who've found theirs in Python or Elixir or PHP or Go or even JavaScript. That's wonderful! And that's really all I want for you. I want you to be happy. I want you to find just that right language that opens your mind to the beautiful game of coding in your most compatible mode of conception, as Ruby did for me.

This is not the same as just saying "everything has trade-offs, use what works best". That to me is a bit of a cop out. There is no universal set of trade-offs that'll make something objectively "work best". Half the programming conundrum lies in connecting to an enduring source of motivation. I wouldn't be a happy camper if  I had to spend my days programming Rust (but I LOVE so many of the tools coming out of that community by people who DO enjoy just that).

It also doesn't mean we should give up on technical discussions of advantages or disadvantages, but I think those are generally more effective when performed in the style of "here's what I like, why I like it, so look at my code, my outcomes, and see if it tickles your fancy too".

Programming is a beautiful game. I would give up all the fancy cars I have in a heartbeat, if I was made to choose between them and programming. The intellectual stimulation, the occasional high from hitting The Zone, is such a concrete illustration of Coco Chanel's "the best things in life are free, the second best things are very expensive". Programming is one of those "best things" that is virtually free to everyone in the Western world (and increasingly so everywhere else too). 

So let's play that beautiful game to the best of our ability, in the position that flatters our conceptual capacities the most, and create some wonderful code.
